items.title: Vance says he will decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 US presidential run
paragraphs: US Vice-President JD Vance has said he will make a decision "sometime next year" about whether or not he will run for president in 2028.
In an interview with Fox News, Vance would not provide a timeline on making a determination, but signaled he is not in a hurry to make up his mind.
"I haven't made a decision. We'll figure it out sometime next year," Vance said. When pressed by host Laura Ingraham, he added: "When I make a decision, I'll be all in on whatever that decision is."
The comments came amid growing interest in Vance's next moves in the weeks since voters handed both President Donald Trump and Republicans a resounding defeat in the midterm elections.

People in Vance's orbit who have spoken to the BBC said the November elections did not change the timeline around his decision-making process for 2028. He is expected to run but allies believe he could wait several months to make a final decision.

Speculation about Vance's White House aspirations began the moment President Trump selected him as his 2024 running mate. The pick positioned Vance, who entered the White House as one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, as the most likely heir to Trump's Make America Great Again (Maga) movement.
But while serving in office, Vance has carefully avoided discussing his own political ambitions.

He kept that up during the midterms, when supporters frequently interrupted his campaign speeches to urge him to run in 2028. Vance's stock response was that Republicans needed to focus on the election at hand in November.
But with the midterms in the rearview mirror, and Republicans eager to move on from their 2026 drubbing, the next election at hand is now the 2028 presidential race.

Vance would likely jump to the top of the Republican primary field whenever he launches his bid, should he choose to run. But the contest is expected to be a competitive process with a large field of candidates.
Numerous other high-profile Republicans are rumoured to be interested in running or have said publicly that they are mulling a White House bid.
The list includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, outgoing Florida Governor and 2024 hopeful Ron DeSantis, and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, among others.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio on several occasions, while also insisting that he is not sure who he will endorse in 2028 - or if he will weigh in at all.

The president's endorsement would be influential with the Maga base. But the midterms revealed widespread frustration with many of his second-term policies, complicating the path forward for potential candidates like Vance who are tied to Trump's agenda.

Vance blamed the midterm results on the war with Iran in a post-election social media post. In it, he also mapped out a plan for winning back Republican voters, which included ending the war and focusing on the economy.
The message was widely seen as a first step by Vance to distance himself from Trump ahead of a 2028 run.
In the Fox News interview, Vance reiterated his view that the war came with a "political cost", but said it has not damaged his relationship with Trump.
"There's no daylight" on the Iran war between Trump and senior administration officials including himself, Vance said.

He added that Trump would not let the conflict become a "forever war" and said the administration would not let the war, which was launched by the US and Israel in February 2026, even become "a two-year commitment".

Vance also discussed the nationwide air traffic outrage last week, which brought air travel across the US to a standstill for several hours. The vice-president called on lawmakers to fix the issue in the final weeks of the current congressional session.

He also touched on the scandal engulfing Nvidia, its former CEO Jensen Huang and its implications for US-China relations. Vance said there was still no "clarity" about the accuracy of reports that a woman with whom Huang reportedly had an affair with was indeed a Chinese spy.
"There is a lack of clarity about it. I don't know and [Trump] doesn't know whether this woman was a spy or not," Vance said.

items.title: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?
paragraphs: Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.
This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".
US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.
But with 97% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.
BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.
The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.
This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.
Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest state
Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.

A New York Times story, external published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.
Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.
President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".
But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed.
"There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.
Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot
Senator Sullivan was joined by President Trump at a campaign rally ahead of the vote
Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference.

"There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.
On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:
- Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent
There was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.
A sample ballot for the US Senate election in Alaska
As of Monday, Peltola holds 49.94% of the vote.

In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.
Democrat Mary Peltola's said on Saturday she will "decisively be elected" as Alaska's next senator
Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".
Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.
We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.
A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second.

"The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."
Additional reporting by Wesley Stephenson and Daniel Wainwright

items.title: David Jones’ total debt is over $400m including millions owed to staff, administrators confirm
paragraphs: Upmarket retailer David Jones collapsed into administration earlier this month owing well over $400m, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas.

About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol broke down the 188-year-old chain’s massive debt pile, including an estimated $180m owed to suppliers and $11m to employees.

There is also about $33m in unredeemed gift cards held by shoppers, which the retailer is still accepting, and significant sums owed to secured creditors including the retailer’s main financier, Hilco.
David Jones collapsed into voluntary administration in early November after years of steep losses left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent and supplier payments.
The retailer is set to shutter half of its 38 department stores by the end of the year, triggering mass job losses under a sweeping restructure.
Under a dual appointment, FTI Consulting has day-to-day control of operations, while administrators McGrathNicol seek a buyer or fresh injection of capital.

David Jones recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year, according to updated figures disclosed to creditors. It lost a further $69m in the first four months of the new financial year leading up to the administration.
Creditors were told that the funding pressures it was facing, coupled with reputational damage, was affecting its ability to get stock for the Christmas trading period.
Guardian Australia has reported that some suppliers are owed money from stock sent as early as April.

items.title: Rio Tinto agrees to pay US$250m to begin repairing ‘devastation’ left by Panguna mine
paragraphs: Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago.

Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville.
But the sprawling mine pit, once a mountain, remains a scar in the middle of the island, with vast pillars of rubble at risk of collapse, and polluted rivers running bright blue with toxins.

Rio Tinto was forced from the island and has never returned, but in recent years has been part of a detailed consultation process with landowners and government. It has now agreed to voluntarily contribute US$250m (A$370m) towards the remediation of the mine site.

Theonila Roka Matbob, a former cabinet minister in Bougainville’s autonomous government and Panguna community leader, said the fund was a vital contribution towards repairing the “devastation left by the Panguna mine”.

“We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but the establishment of this fund gives us the chance to find solutions to the huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation.

“No amount of money will restore the damage caused to the environment in Panguna, but this sets a foundation for us to invest in addressing the environmental issues and invest in our children’s futures as well.”

Roka Matbob said the most fundamental remediation was to improve “accessibility” for the people living around Panguna – “accessibility to clean drinking water that is safe and secure … and infrastructure, in bridges that makes people’s access to trade, to school, to health[care], much easier. This is one critical area that immediately needs attention.”

The president of Bougainville, Ishmael Toroama, seeking to become the world’s newest head of state at the forefront of a long-running independence movement on the island, said the money would make a “meaningful difference” to villages and communities that had suffered from the impacts of the mine’s pollution.

“This work will deliver benefits not only for people today, but for future generations. Continued engagement with our communities will be essential to ensuring the work responds to local priorities and delivers lasting outcomes.”

The Rio commitment has emerged from the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment consultation process, which was initiated in response to a human rights complaint brought by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, with Roka Matbob as the lead complainant.
Keren Adams, the HRLC’s legal director, said establishing the fund had taken years of work.
“It is a testament to the courage and persistence of community leaders, and the willingness of all parties to engage in difficult but constructive dialogue,” she said.
“The significant funding contributed by Rio Tinto creates a real opportunity to now address an environmental disaster that has remained unresolved for decades.”

Mark Davies, Rio Tinto’s chief safety and technical officer, said the establishment of the fund was an “important milestone … intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation”.
“Community engagement is an important next step to identify priorities and we remain committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”
The quarter-of-a-billion dollars will not be sufficient to entirely remediate the mine site, but it is being seen as a major step towards rehabilitation.
The funding commitment for Panguna comes at an acutely sensitive time for the restive Bougainville island.

The mine has become inextricably linked with the Bougainville’s political future: restarting operations at Panguna – believed to still hold at least $60bn in unrealised reserves – is seen by many, including the president, as the fundamental financial basis for the island’s independent future. Indian miner Lloyds has been granted a 25-year large-scale mining lease, but any future mining is years from starting.
Bougainville, a group of islands off Papua New Guinea to the north of Australia, has been variously controlled by Britain, Germany, Japan, Australia and PNG.
It declared independence in 1975 as the Republic of North Solomons, but was absorbed into the newly independent PNG weeks later.
Its close ethnic ties and proximity to the Solomons archipelago means it has always sat uneasily with Port Moresby’s rule.
That discontent came to a violent head in 1988 after a long-running dispute over the lucrative Panguna copper and gold mine.
The mine, carved from a mountain in central Bougainville, was critically important to PNG, at one point generating more than 45% of the country's national export revenue.

Multinational Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly US$2bn from the mine over 17 years of operation. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands had been destroyed by it.
Under the leadership of a former mine worker, Francis Ona, disaffected Bougainvilleans ran a sabotage campaign which forced the mine’s closure in 1989.

The PNG Government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war that ran for a decade, and saw as many as 20,000 people die.
PNG later hired international mercenaries to end the conflict (the notorious Sandline affair), before a peace agreement was signed in 2001.
In a 2019 referendum, 97.7% of Bougainvilleans voted in favour of independence. Many argue that reopening Panguna mine will be key to the island’s economic future as an independent nation.

Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it.

Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as “the crisis” – that ran for a decade. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were killed, roughly 10% of the island’s population.

A recent environmental impact assessment found the abandoned mine remains an acute threat to people’s lives, including from landslides, levee collapses and floods. Untouched, the river delta will stay polluted for a century.

The future of Bougainville’s independence campaign is now before the PNG parliament, which will decide whether or not to recognise a UN-backed independence referendum held on the island in 2019, in which 97.7% of voters were in favour of Bougainville seceding and becoming an independent country.
The PNG parliament, which heard lengthy and impassioned debate over Bougainville last month, appears almost certain to vote against recognising the referendum result.

But Toroama, who has staked his presidency on achieving political independence, has said, regardless of the parliament’s decision, Bougainville will enter a period of “self-government” from September next year, before seceding, breaking away from PNG as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.

items.title: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
paragraphs: Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.
"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.
Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.

Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.
Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".
He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.
"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.

He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.
He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year.
"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote.
Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing".
"[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters.
Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.

His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.
At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence.
Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics.

Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march, demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, insisting that Khan be given proper medical care.

items.title: Truck driver fired for ‘unsafe’ use of smartglasses in first reported sacking over device in Australia
paragraphs: A Toll truck driver was fired from work in Victoria after using smartglasses to snap photos at an LPG terminal, in what was described as an “intrinsically unsafe” incident.
It is the first reported case in Australia of a worker dismissed for using smartglasses in a workplace.

The employee, Ricardo Martins Silva, was fired from Toll Transport in July 2025, after eight months with the company as an LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) tanker driver, the federal circuit court heard. His role was to drive a loaded LPG tanker for Origin Energy from the Long Island Point terminal in Hastings, Victoria, for onward delivery.

A federal circuit court judgment last week stated that on 17 June 2025, Martins Silva raised concerns about a truck allocated to him, telling superiors the truck had too much vibration and was jumping excessively.

The judgment stated he was advised to take a different truck, and when he went to the terminal, he took photographs using his smartglasses, and sent them to a superior with a message stating: “I’m going to take the truck back to Dandenong and I’m leaving! There’s no more time for deliveries today!”
The Esso worker at the terminal told Toll that any use of electrical equipment on-site is “intrinsically unsafe” due to the risk of an explosion caused by electrical spark.

Martins Silva was prevented from taking on additional work until an investigation into the incident had been completed, and Origin Energy later asked the employee be removed from work as soon as possible because “his attitude is poor” and “not doing planned deliveries because he is ‘tired and stressed’ is not acceptable”, the judgment read.

Martins Silva sent emails between 17 and 19 June raising concerns about his role, truck allocations and safety issues. The worker on 20 June submitted a complaint about his employment, including safety, and impact of working conditions on his health, among other things.
On 22 June, the employee was advised he was stood down, the judgment stated.

At a meeting on 24 June, what Toll termed as “the glasses incident” was raised with the employee. He was told it was regarded as a “critical safety breach” and that Toll had commenced an investigation process due to its seriousness.

By 30 June, the company decided Martins Silva should be suspended from employment citing, among other reasons, the seriousness of the glasses incident. On 9 July, the employee was informed that taking a photograph with the smartglasses was in breach of Toll’s code of practice, and his contract of employment. His employment was terminated on 18 July, the judgment stated.
Martins Silva claimed the action was in breach of the Fair Work Act, arguing Toll’s actions were as a result of complaints he had made.
The federal circuit court found in the ruling last week that the glasses incident was “on any objective view a serious incident”.

“On the day he wore the smart glasses, Mr Martins Silva was plainly aware of the risks of what he was doing – he went so far as to seek to mitigate the risk by covering his smartglasses with safety glasses,” the ruling from federal circuit justice Karl Blake stated.
“The glasses incident was not concocted or made to look more serious than what it was. It was objectively very serious.”

Martins Silva had conceded in cross examination that he knew at the time he had done the wrong thing, Blake’s judgment stated, but had written to his employer at the time that his judgment had been affected by the unresolved trauma of a truck fire in which he had been injured in March 2025.

Blake found Martins Silva was not dismissed because he made complaints but “because he wore smartglasses” at the terminal and his employer was of the view that it amounted to a serious safety incident. The application was dismissed.

While the case had focused on safety concerns, since the arrival of Meta’s Ray-Bans and cheaper alternatives such as the Kmart Anko brand glasses, governments have faced pressure to ban the devices over privacy concerns.
Councils across Australia have banned the glasses from some public spaces including gyms and pools, while the federal government is considering bans in government offices.

items.title: Failed asylum seekers face removal without five-day notice period
paragraphs: The government is to change the law so that it no longer has to give failed asylum seekers notice before they are removed from the country.
Currently, people are given five working days' notice but ministers believe this leads to last-minute appeals which delay the process.
Under the new rules, once an asylum claim fails, the Home Office would have six months in which to remove the applicant without telling them in advance.
The move was criticised by the Refugee Council which said: "Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety to people."
Imran Hussain, the director of the refugee charity, said: "The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns.
"If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer."
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood will make the change by amending the Immigration and Asylum Bill which is currently going through Parliament.
The amendment will scrap the notice requirement for those who have exhausted the asylum appeals process.
Instead, the Home Office will have the power to remove people immediately, a power that will remain in place for up to six months.

The Home Office has not said how many additional people it thinks it will be able to remove but has pointed to Denmark where the number of migrants awaiting removal more than halved over five years to under 1,000 after a similar policy was introduced.
The previous government, led by Sir Keir Starmer, had pledged to clear the asylum backlog.
In June 2026, there were 40,168 people waiting for an initial decision on asylum application claims and a further 90,341 waiting for the outcome of an appeal in the courts.
Between July 2025 and June 2026, 38% of asylum decisions led to the applicant being granted refugee status.
Forty percent of all asylum claims come from people who arrived in the UK by small boat.
The remaining 60% of claims are made by people who arrived in the country by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and subsequently applied for asylum.

Anna Turley, minister for border security and asylum, said: "We are ensuring those migrants who have exhausted their right to appeal can be removed promptly, rather than being given an opportunity to frustrate their legitimate removal from this country.
"This bill will restore order and control to the system, ensuring it is swift and fair."

items.title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
paragraphs: Gamers have long been known to book time off work for major releases.

When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding, external more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.
Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing , externaltaking several days off to play.
GTA 6 is no exception, but it appears to characteristically be taking things to a whole new level.
For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.
It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.

According to the HR firm, one person put "new GTA is coming out! I will be spending a week on the sofa in my pants!" as the reason for their leave request, while another said: "play the new GTA - I've waited a billion years".
A third said in their request: "GTA Release - I'll put my notice in if this is denied."
The company added it had no way of tracking if the requests had actually been approved by employers.
Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.

Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.
This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.
According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.
Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.
"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.
"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.
It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.

But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.
GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither has Sony nor Microsoft.

Louise Wooldridge from analyst firm Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".
Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.
Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.
"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.
A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.
Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.
Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game.
"So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video.
After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter what the cost or extra effort.

items.title: Iranian Kurdish opposition groups reject amnesty-for-surrender deal
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

Iranian Kurdish opposition leaders based in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region have ruled out turning themselves in to Tehran as part of potential amnesty deal, citing lack of trust in Iran to guarantee their safety.

Their comments come after Iraqi officials reported progress in negotiations involving Baghdad, the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and Iran over the future of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups that have a maintained presence in northern Iraq for decades.

Iraq's Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein confirmed last week that one of the options discussed during the trilateral talks included potential amnesty for the Iranian Kurdish armed group members who wished to return, if they felt safe.

Amanj Zibaee, a member of the central committee of the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran (KDPI), an armed opposition group seeking greater autonomy for Kurds in Iran, and the party’s representative in Erbil, told VOA that his group categorically rejects the prospect of surrendering to Iranian authorities.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran makes many promises but offers nothing in practice. Surrendering to it is something we completely reject, and it is not even an option we have discussed,” he said.
Zibaee said his party would wait for an official announcement over the proposal discussed between Baghdad, Tehran and Erbil before determining its response.
“Once the Iraqi government and the Kurdistan Regional Government officially announce their positions, the KDPI leader will make an appropriate decision,” he said.
He said his organization has acted responsibly and has not used Iraqi territory to attack Iran, a key demand by Baghdad.
“We have never used the Kurdistan Region of Iraq as a base to launch attacks against a neighboring country. We have acted responsibly, and we will continue to do so,” Zibaee said.
Khalil Nadri, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Freedom Party, also dismissed the possibility of accepting an Iranian amnesty.

“We have an agreement with the Kurdistan Region that we will not conduct military operations against Iran from its territory. Our struggle against Iran takes place inside Iran, in Eastern Kurdistan,” Nadri told VOA, referring to predominantly Kurdish areas of western Iran.
He said his party had respected Iraqi sovereignty and helped defend the region against the Islamic State and Iran-backed armed groups, including the Popular Mobilization Forces.
“Iran is not in a position to grant us amnesty,” Nadri said. “Our homeland has been occupied. We will return when our homeland is liberated and the enemy has withdrawn.”

Iran has repeatedly over many years launched missile, and drone strikes targeting Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in northern Iraq that have been fighting for Kurdish regional autonomy or independence in Iran. The attacks surged following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East as Iran launched retaliatory attacks against neighboring countries.
The Iranian Kurdish armed opposition Komala party said Monday that two missiles struck the entrance to one of its bases in the Balisan Valley in Iraq's Kurdistan Region.
Idris Kolahdozi, a member of the party's Central Committee and its head of relations in Sulaimaniyah, told VOA that the attack caused no casualties or property damage.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of who carried out the attack.

Iraqi Foreign Minister Hussein said the latest round of negotiations between Iraq, Iran and the Kurdistan Regional Government that started in October in Baghdad are continuing and that several options were under consideration.
In an interview with France 24, Hussein said the parties had reached a degree of understanding about how to address the opposition groups’ presence in Iraq.
He raised a possible amnesty deal that could allow Iranian Kurdish opposition members to return to Iran, provided they received credible guarantees for their personal safety.

Earlier this month, Iraqi government spokesperson Haider Aboudi told VOA that discussions had reached an “advanced stage” and that Baghdad hoped to resolve the issue soon, though no final deal has been publicly disclosed.
Aboudi emphasized that Iraq was determined to prevent its territory from being used to attack neighboring countries.
KRG spokesperson Peshawa Hawramani similarly told VOA that the regional government would not allow its territory to be used to harm neighboring states.

The negotiations come amid continued Iranian pressure on Baghdad and Erbil to remove Iranian Kurdish opposition groups from Iraqi territory. Tehran has repeatedly accused the groups of threatening its security, allegations the opposition parties deny.
Last month, KDPI spokesperson Khalid Azizi told VOA that his party had largely complied with Iraqi requests to withdraw from areas near the Iranian border.
He said the party had engaged in discussions with Iraqi and Kurdish authorities, with United Nations involvement, over the region's security for several years.

items.title: Labor policy backflip will allow more backpackers to work in regional Australia
paragraphs: The federal government has backpedalled on its plan to cut backpacker numbers, arguing the change is the “best possible outcome” for regional industries who had criticised the crackdown because they rely on travellers for labour.
On Tuesday, the Albanese government announced it would lift the proposed cap on third-year working holiday visas, boost regional work requirements and delay the start of a new ballot system.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, had announced in a major speech in September plans to cap the number of third-year backpackers to 5,000 from the current level of about 31,000.

Burke said on Tuesday that the cap would now instead be set at 25,000 places. The home affairs minister claimed despite the increase, the net overseas migration (Nom) target would not change, due to a go-slow on approving UK backpacker visas.

“From the day after the [September] speech, myself, the assistant ministers and the department started consultation with industry to work through what’s the best landing place to deliver the total numbers we’re talking about, but to do it in a way that works best for industry,” Burke told reporters.

“There was some slower processing generally happening before the announcement I made, and we have continued the slower processing with UK only since then. That’s provided the space that allowed me to go to the 5,000 to 25,000.”
The major reforms to working holiday visas unveiled in September included a ballot for backpackers seeking to stay a second or third year which would require them to work in the regions.

Under the original proposal, 45,000 backpackers would be allowed to remain for a second year and would be required to work at least three months in a regional area, and just 5,000 places would be allocated for workers for a third year.

The ballot, due to come into effect in November, will now be delayed until early next year. From 1 March 2027, backpackers will be required to work in regional areas for four months, instead of three. (The changes won’t apply to travellers who finish their current regional work by the end of February.)
Burke said the government would introduce a new “guarantee” for backpackers granted second- and third-year visas as part of the ballot process.

“From December, people will be able to apply for the guarantee. And from January, every month we’ll be issuing these guarantees. If you receive the guarantee and you do the regional work … then you’ve got the guarantee for the next year,” Burke said. “We’ll be issuing those every month.”
The minister said the extra requirement was “the best possible outcome” for regional areas.
Making backpackers do 120 days of regional work instead of 88 meant that even with the reduction in visa numbers there was a boost in the overall workforce, Burke said.
The changes followed months of consultation with industry, regional and agricultural groups who warned of worker shortages.
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, accused Burke of “creating a migration mess” and said the government should axe the visa ballot altogether.
“Working holiday visas are an important part of our migration mix,” Taylor said.
“We want to see more of it in regional areas. That’s critically important. But they’ve created a complete mess with this raffle.”

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said the initial policy announcement had damaged the confidence of small businesses and farmers in regional areas. He questioned how the changes would not increase net overseas migration numbers.

“Having slightly increased these backpacker number caps in this announcement today, the question has got to go to the government, surely the [net] overseas migration figure is now going up further,” Canavan said.
The government has set a net overseas migration target for 2026-27 of 245,000, and plans to reduce that to 225,000 in 2027-28.

Workers from the UK are exempt from the caps under a free trade agreement signed in 2021. Sources say the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is in discussions with his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, to force British backpackers to also do regional work going forward.
Burke said he was optimistic about negotiations.
“The conversations … have been going very well. But until every detail is landed on, I’m not going to get ahead of an announcement,” he said.
“The United Kingdom have a good understanding of the issues that we need to resolve, so I’m not going to put a timeline on it. But I will say I’m very optimistic.”
The Accommodation Australia chief executive, James Goodwin, said Tuesday’s backflip showed the government had listened to concerns from the sector.

“These are sensible and welcome changes that recognise the important contribution working holidaymakers make,” Goodwin said. “Minister Burke has listened to industry concerns and responded with changes that will make a meaningful difference.”
The government has felt pressure to reduce Nom, which has become a contested debate.

In September, ahead of the government’s original announcement, One Nation proposed cutting migration numbers by 750,000 over three years by drastically reducing international student and family visas. That policy has since disappeared from One Nation’s website.
The Coalition has also flagged a reduction in net overseas migration.

items.title: What's the story with Scotland boss Pocognoli - is it time to go?
paragraphs: A few short months ago, Craig Mulholland, the Scottish FA's chief football officer, and Ian Maxwell, the association's chief executive, spoke about the worldwide search for a new Scotland head coach.
The data, the metrics, the cosmic input from the analytics company whose input was received at Hampden as if written on tablets of stone.
The process all pointed to Sebastien Pocognoli being their guy. They paraded him around Hampden, told everybody that loads of clubs were on his tail but that they won the chase.
They may, or may not, have mentioned the word 'coup' but that was certainly what their body language was telling you.
For coup, read boo, the sound surely reverberating around the Tartan Army right now after Monday's 4-0 defeat by Switzerland.
Some nonsense has been written about Pocognoli being on twice the salary that Steve Clarke was on, but whatever they're paying him, there's no value in it so far.

Money is a factor here. Clarke's three qualifications brought a rich bounty into the SFA's coffers, many millions even after deductions. That cash gave the association a little more opportunity to do some of the things they want to do in grassroots football.

A world where Scotland miss out on major championships and the financial windfalls that come with qualification is not a place they want to revisit. The next Euros looks like a gimme - almost harder not to qualify than qualify - but the sense of drift in this team is alarming and can't go on much longer.
Mulholland, Maxwell and let's throw SFA president Mike Mulraney into the mix, should be feeling mightily nervous.

Most people understood that Pocognoli needed time, but implicit in that understanding was a need to see something developing under him, a burgeoning style of play, some positives here and there, a few signs that even though things might not be great today or tomorrow, they're inching in the right direction.

There's been none of that. Decent players look lost. Pocognoli's system has made Scotland a disjointed soft touch. Structural discipline collapses too often. Players charge forward and leave space in behind. He wants hard pressing and maximum intensity, but his players don't look capable of providing it.
In six games they have scored five goals - two from the penalty spot. Promises of jam tomorrow are not cutting it. People can see a team on the slide.
In Switzerland, there was a drubbing that piles the heat on the Belgian, on the people who appointed him and on the players, too.
'You do not have time in international football'

If the chaos on the field wasn't a bad enough look for Pocognoli, then some of the words said in the wake of this objectionable 4-0 pummelling to a Switzerland B side playing in third gear only made things worse.
Andy Robertson, on the night he became Scotland's most capped player in history, delivered a damning riff that sounded strongly like a commentary on this coaching regime and this set of players.
In his stead, John McGinn did much the same thing. "You don't get time" was the gist. Who doesn't get time?

Robertson and McGinn didn't lay it on the line, but their thoughts resembled distress flares. These Scotland players can be overhyped, but they are better than some of the nonsense they dished up in St Gallen.
More than one former Scotland international reckoned they saw players not exactly busting a gut out there. These guys know the tell-tale signs.
Some private conversations between the SFA hierarchy and the senior operators in this team need to take place. What were they suggesting in the post-match? What are they really thinking?
An honesty session behind closed doors needs to take place long before the qualification campaign for the next Euros begins in March.
Pocognoli comes across as a good person: open, communicative, passionate and hard-working.

He also appears stubborn in the way he sets up his team, a system that is so easily exploited by more experienced coaches, people like Switzerland boss Murat Yakin, who was missing a battalion of heavy hitters and yet still won this game at a canter.
Yakin started six players who had six caps or fewer to their name - three of them scored.
McGinn said later that Scotland were in this movie before in the early days of Clarke's tenure, mentioning the 4-0 loss to Russia in 2019 - four goals conceded in 27 minutes.

The difference between Clarke and Pocognoli is obvious. Clarke had vast experience and the nous to fix the problems. Pocognoli is a young coach with no such back story, no such track record in turning bad situations into good.
Pocognoli said later that people should look beyond the result, to the "attitude of the players" who were at times "brilliant, brave and on the front foot".

He argued that 4-0 wasn't a true reflection of the game, referring to the glaring misses by Lewis Ferguson and Scott McTominay. Scotland were 3-0 down at the time. He didn't think the loss had anything to do with a system or a lack of confidence or a lack of belief.
Not many fans were buying what he was selling. Listening to some of his players, you doubted that they were buying it either.

After the home loss to Slovenia, Robertson said his team had been "out-played" and "out-fought." There were some other comments made after the desperately stodgy 2-1 win over North Macedonia on Friday. On Monday, it cranked up another level.

McGinn was asked if he felt Scotland were on the right path. "Impossible for me to say yes," he replied. It was hard to listen to what the players were trying to say and conclude that everybody's on the same page in this set-up.

Intransigence is not a good characteristic for any manager. In recent times we've seen a few bosses at big clubs who were wedded to their principles. Russell Martin and Wilfried Nancy didn't last long at Rangers and Celtic.
To repeat Robertson's line, you don't get time.

Clarke had an instinctive understanding of that and pragmatism was his way of taking his team forward, difficult yard by difficult yard. Rigid idealism is not a sensible way to operate, but Pocognoli has gone down that road in his first six games.
It's a dead-end down there. He needs to turn back and find another way while he still can. If he still can.
'Scotland have not played well in any game this campaign'

items.title: Met Office yellow warning in place as snow could disrupt Tuesday morning travel
paragraphs: A weather front is pushing north and east across the UK bringing a spell of rain to many areas. As this rain reaches northern England it will encounter a reservoir of colder and drier air.

Some of the rain will evaporate in this drier air, which will cool the atmosphere further by a process known as evaporative cooling - the same process involved in cooling your body down when you sweat.

Eventually rain will start to turn to snow, initially over higher hills in the Pennines, moving to lower hills with time. As the precipitation moves northwards and eastwards, the snow will spread to the Cumbrian hills and into Scotland's Southern Uplands.
The snow will come down in big, wet, chunky flakes which could stick to powerlines and tree branches.
The extra weight of the snow combined with wind gusts of 40-50mph over high ground could bring down tree branches and powerlines, bringing an additional risk of some localised power cuts.

items.title: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
paragraphs: The number of young people who are not in work, at school or in college is both an economic and moral crisis, a landmark report into the problem will say later.
The 241-page report, by ex-Labour minister Alan Milburn, will set out a raft of recommendations for the government to consider.

Ahead of its publication, four young people who are not in education, employment or training - those dubbed as "Neets" - tell us why they can't get a job and how the government could help them get one.
We meet Michael after his early work experience shift at a supermarket

Michael, 19, who lives with his dad in the Wirral, says he dropped out of college and spent a year at home after his social anxiety "got really bad". It is "very easy" to fall out of the system, he says, if there is little support available.
Michael's story is not unique. There has been a large rise in anxiety and mental health problems in young people.
About one in five Neets have a mental health condition, according to 2025 data, external from the Department for Education (DfE) - more than double the rate in 2012.

Having signed up for Universal Credit, Michael was put in touch with the Merseyside Youth Association to help him find a job. He says mentors there have helped him improve his mental health, which led to him dropping out of college during his A-levels. He says that left him trapped inside his bedroom.

He says jobs in his area are scarce and those that do come up tend to go to older people with more experience. Michael says he is trapped in the cycle of not having the experience needed to build more.
"Everything is experience, experience, experience - that's the one thing that I always used to hear when going for jobs on my own without the help," he says.
We followed Michael for a day, meeting him after his 05:00 start for a work experience shift at a local supermarket that the Merseyside Youth Association helped him get.
Michael says getting his dog Dave motivated him to get out of the house and speak to people more

Lots of Neets receive Universal Credit. For under-25s, the standard rate is £338.58 a month, external, which Michael gets. For some people who cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness, an additional £217.26 to £429.80 per month may be available.

Ahead of the publication of his full review, it was reported that Milburn would recommend young people should no longer be able to claim those additional health-related benefits, as part of a major overhaul of the welfare system.
Michael acknowledges some young people may be "taking advantage" of the benefits system, but says most "just want the money to get by so they can get a job".

More recently, he has been doing shifts at the Merseyside Youth Centre's on-site cafe to gain more much-needed experience. His hope is to be in a steady job earning money this time next year, with space to have his own art studio one day.
"From three months ago I'm a different person," he says. "I can do stuff, keep going."
University graduate Maariyah says she is getting turned away from voluntary opportunities
Maariyah, a 22-year-old history and politics graduate, finished her university course last summer. Her dream is to work in museums.
However, she is currently unemployed and looking for any paid job after working a temporary six-month contract for a housing association earlier this year.
She says she spends hours each day in her local library - where she feels more able to focus than she can at home - submitting at least 20 tailored job applications a week.
Those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualifications are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods - however, an estimated one in 10 Neets are university graduates.
Maariyah says she is applying for roles in retail and restaurants, alongside unpaid work experience opportunities in the heritage sector.

But she says she has also been rejected for voluntary roles because they had too many applicants, or because she does not have enough experience. "I'm actively going out of my way to do unpaid work, only to get rejected from these positions," she says.

Not hearing back from employers "happens so often now that's it's like second nature", she says, adding that she finds it frustrating that many of her applications are likely to be screened by AI before a real person sees them.
Maariyah says she tailors her CV and cover letter for over 20 job applications a week

On the day we meet, Maariyah heads to the job centre for her Universal Credit appointment after a library job application session. She says she has noticed an improvement in the support she gets there since she first received the benefit in 2025.
This time, she will be getting some mandatory hospitality training, which she says she is "really glad" to have.
She feels there is a growing sense of disillusionment among others her age. Being on benefits has become normalised because it is so hard to find a job, she adds.
It makes her feel that going to a good university, getting certain grades and doing extracurricular activities "doesn't make a difference in the end".

"I would like employers to give young people a chance to gain experience and take a chance on hard-working people who at the end of the day want a job so that they can contribute to our economy and contribute to their own lives."
Matthieu has had many voluntary opportunities, but wants to find paid work
Matthieu, 19, from Edgware in north-west London, is autistic and currently volunteers at a gardening club and a computer repair shop.
We meet him in Finsbury Park, where he is helping to mulch some newly planted trees. Working in nature is calming, he says.
He is looking for work with the support of the charity Ambitious About Autism and his mentor, Annie. He previously did a year-long supported internship with the Whittington hospital.

Matthieu says speaking to people face-to-face there helped his confidence and he enjoyed being part of the team. At his family home, Matthieu's mentor Annie tells us that not having maths and English GCSE qualifications is a barrier to finding employment.
Matthieu says he's more of a manual worker and wants to work in a factory, warehouse or doing deliveries, so that he can contribute financially for his family.
Matthieu enjoys volunteering outside in nature

Those with learning difficulties, including autism, make up an estimated 12% of Neets, DfE data, external shows. Milburn's interim report, external, which was published in the summer, said 45% of Neets reported having a disability. He said the situation for young disabled people was "devastating".
To make work accessible to him, Matthieu says he would need an employer to take their time with him. He says: "I don't learn that quickly." But he thinks it would be worth it.
"Honestly, you might be surprised what the people can do when you take the time with them and give them that chance," Matthieu says.

Many employers say they can not afford to do so following rises to National Insurance contributions and the minimum wage, which is increasing further as part of announcements made in October's Budget.
Some businesses have told the BBC they are struggling to provide new jobs for young people due to these changes, as well as other factors like rising energy bills.
Although finding work is hard, Matthieu says he remains hopeful because of the support from his internship and job coach.
Alex says there aren't many job opportunities in her area

Alex, 20, from St Helens, has been looking for work for a year. She struggles with anxiety and is looking for roles as a cleaner or in retail. She also shares caring responsibilities for her mum with her other family members.

We meet her at Spear, an employment and mindset coaching programme. Alex says her dream is to work with animals. She says she had been studying Level 3 animal management at college before dropping out last year because of her mental health.

"I was so burnt out," she says. "I was struggling to get out of bed, I couldn't do anything. I was dragging myself to college. I was like, 'No, I need to have a break for a bit and try and figure out what to do after that'."
Building up her resilience is something she now works on with a mentor, as well as job applications.

Alex says she is applying for "anything and everything" and wants to get off benefits. She is also currently receiving Universal Credit, which she says is "all the money that I've got until I get a job and I'm earning more".
Alex and her mentor, Grace, work on her CV during one-to-one sessions
When asked what she thinks about potential benefits cuts for young people out of work, Alex says not being able to access benefits would "make life so much worse".
And she says trying to find work in a place like St Helens is harder, because many businesses in the town centre have either "gone or moved or shut down".
"Lots of people think, 'well, young people just don't want to work,'" she says. "But we do. We so desperately want to work. Places don't want to hire us."
Milburn has already said the system isn't working for everyone, and that serious action is needed to avoid young Neets becoming a "lost generation".
Additional reporting by Branwen Jeffreys and Kate McGough

items.title: Aged 16-24 and looking for work? Use our look-up to find out which areas have the most jobs
paragraphs: ByTommy LumbyBusiness data journalist and Nick EdserBusiness reporter
If you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start.
Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say.
But how many jobs are there where you live and in which sectors are you most likely to find an opening?

There is no official measure of how many vacancies are suitable for young people, but across the whole economy there were 691,000 jobs available in the July to September period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021.
The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted.
Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years.
Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment.

In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008.
The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a recent peak of 291,300 in 2012.
Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job.
We have used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population.
The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education.
According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000.
Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils.
Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in.

The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna.
The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work.
Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships.
Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings.
Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts.
Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector.

Here are the average salaries for jobs in the sectors with the largest number of entry-level jobs, according to Adzuna. The highest average salary is £30,530 in engineering, while social care has the lowest at £25,880.

items.title: We couldn't afford a house alone, so we bought one with strangers
paragraphs: The Pullman family, on the left, and the Wilcox family, bought a home together soon after meeting
When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.
They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.
Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in.
"We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.
With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.
That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.
They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children.
In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.

The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.
Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".
Mums Ashley Pullman, left, and Elizabeth Wilcox say the two families get along

While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosal says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.
Gosal is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.
It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.

It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche".

"I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don' t know."
The Wilcoxes and the Pullmans pooled their resources to buy a detached Vancouver home
Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.
While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer.
"If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.
Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.

Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018. When she signed on the dotted line and moved in she didn't know one of the other two people.
While Sabrina says she isn't comfortable sharing the exact financial details, she says they decided to divide up the deposit and mortgage payments based on each of their levels of income.
She says any household disputes can be addressed early with open discussions. "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home."
They have regular house meetings where they discuss chores, financial issues, birthday celebrations, and any disagreements.
"It's great to see people be honest about something they may not be comfortable about and for us to find a solution to that problem," Sabrina says.
Sabrina Bowman says it is important to have open communication
In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out.
For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share.

Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says.
Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.
"I can't put a price on how it felt to watch the kids jump on the trampoline for the first time, or run in circles on our patch of green grass."

items.title: Hacker behind 2022 GTA VI leaks pleads guilty
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Arion Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group who leaked 90 videos of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022 and hacked other big companies, pleaded guilty on Monday, according to the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).

Kurtaj, who is now 21, hacked BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021, and starting in early November of that year, the company “noted a marked increase in unauthorised SIM swaps of their customers mobile phones.” He was charged for those offenses and moved to a hotel for his “own protection” in September 2022, but “breached his bail conditions to carry out further hacks on major companies using a mobile phone, the hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and a firestick,” including hacks on Rockstar Games, Uber, and Revolut, the CPS says.
He was sentenced to life in a secure hospital in December 2023 because of his autism, but in January, Kurtaj was deemed fit for trial and moved to prison, the BBC reports.
Kurtaj is set to be sentenced on November 23rd. GTA VI will be released on November 19th.
Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

items.title: The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
paragraphs: In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.
Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.
Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.

Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons, across 24 states in India.
He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.

"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.
These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.
The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.
Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.
Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.
An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.

With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.

The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.

Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.

Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.
Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.
It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.
On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.
"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.
In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.

The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.

It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.

This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42, external, a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.
Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.

"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.
"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."
Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.
"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.
"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.
The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission, external, but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.
Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.
Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.

"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.

From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.
"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.
"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.
