items.title: Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him
paragraphs: Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.

At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. US agencies haven’t confirmed whether this is the case, and President Donald Trump claims he was unaware of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; subsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg.

David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.”

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.”

SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole.

More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

items.title: Police searching for three stolen Melbourne Cup trophies worth $1m each
paragraphs: A police raid has failed to locate three Melbourne Cup trophies belonging to champion horse Makybe Diva after a smash and grab at Flemington racecourse.
A Mount Waverley home in Melbourne’s east was raided on Monday evening after thieves smashed their way into a glass display case at the racecourse about 6.30am.
A 36-year-old Malvern East man was arrested at the Solomon Street home.
He was interviewed by police and released, pending summons.
The trophies, which Victoria police says are valued at $1m each, are yet to be recovered.
The cups, won by the history-making mare in 2003, 2004 and 2005, had been on public display at the racecourse, which hosts the Melbourne Cup, since September.
The champion racehorse, which died in February at the age of 27 after a short and sudden battle with a gastrointestinal condition, was “the people’s horse’, former owner Tony Santic told 3AW.
“Hopefully we can get them back in one piece,” Santic said. “It’s more than devastating. I just can’t believe it.
“I just want to try to get them back and hopefully we get them back in one piece.”
The Victorian Racing Club said the theft was devastating.
“Victoria police is investigating a theft incident that occurred at Flemington racecourse [on Monday] morning involving three Melbourne Cup trophies,” it said.
“We are devastated by the incident and are in direct contact with Tony Santic.”

items.title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
paragraphs: Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.

"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.

"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.
The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.
Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".
"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

items.title: China is hosting the world's leaders in its AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see
paragraphs: Watch: The two sides of daily life in Shenzhen
China correspondent Reporting fromShenzhen
At 27, Huang Shihua is living the Chinese Dream.

He works as an engineer for a leading humanoid robot company in Shenzhen. The sprawling south-eastern metropolis is touted by China as the origin story for a high-tech future powered by artificial intelligence, robotics and home-grown innovation.

Drones soar across the sky to deliver your dinner, driverless taxis play relaxing music as you journey to your destination, and robots don't just hand you a cappuccino - they explain the origin of your coffee beans.

"We have created a miracle in Shenzhen," Huang says, surrounded by humanoid robots making coffee and playing chess. "Many young people from across China, full of passion and dreams, have flocked here."
Now they all spend their days figuring out ways to make robots smarter.
Shenzhen, China's AI-powered "city of dreams", has long been a place of opportunity
The Chinese call Shenzhen the "city of dreams". The moniker suits it: one of China's wealthiest, it is close to Hong Kong and the place where the country's explosive growth took off decades ago.

Its manufacturing inventory mirrors China's rise: cabbage patch dolls, then TVs, later iPhones, electric vehicles, drones and now the robots, which are drawing Huang and a new generation of Chinese ambition.

The "miracles" these young engineers are chasing are central to Xi Jinping's bold vision for China. So where better to show it off than Shenzhen, which will be centre-stage when US President Donald Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and others arrive for a global economic summit this week.

And yet there is another side to this flashy, coastal city, a side that they will not get to see. Drive away from towering skyscrapers towards Shajing and Songgang, once the source of much of the world's electronics, and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.
Young, ambitious developers have turned Shenzhen into a "miracle", Huang says
"Everyone feels life is hard," one construction worker tells us. "Lots of factories have relocated and workers lost their jobs."

China remains exceptionally good at making things - and Shenzhen is proof of that. But the city also holds the evidence for what ails the world's second-largest economy. The property crisis is not over, denting confidence in the future. This is one of China's most expensive cities but even here, our taxi driver tells us, his house is now only worth a third of its original price.

A weak property market and sluggish consumer spending mean many households are buying less. Factories are increasingly relying on exports while many manufacturers have cut production, downsized, automated or moved elsewhere in search of cheaper labour.
The result is a growing number of workers turning to temporary jobs in the gig economy, often with lower pay and fewer benefits.
"Shenzhen is not a magic place," says one delivery driver in his 40s, unwilling to give his name.
"Some say there is gold everywhere in Shenzhen, but it's not like that anymore. It's not a city where you can come and thrive. If you don't work hard, you won't have anything."

The BBC spent several days in Shenzhen exploring these two very different sides of China's progress: on the one hand is the dazzling promise of AI, and on the other are the anxieties of workers who worry if there will be room for them in the future it creates.
Delivery drones in Shenzhen have become a tourist attraction
Wednesday is sandwich and bubble tea day in the offices of DexForce Technologies.

The elevator is packed with young engineers and developers headed to the right floor for the free carbs and sugar that will fuel their afternoon. They jostle past their creations en route: human-sized, yellow robots whose limbs fill every available corner.

"I believe that in a decade, robots will be able to better serve humanity by taking on highly repetitive or even dangerous tasks," Huang says. That could be anything from serving coffee to working in mines, and they are being trained for all of that in this laboratory for the future, where machines flail, jerk or lurch into motion as they learn to behave.
To him, "Shenzhen is another 'America'. Because, much like in the US, many young people have been able to realise their dreams and earn the wealth they desire."

This is what Xi wants to hear as he pushes China to lead the world in advanced tech. Shenzhen has indeed long been a place for seeking opportunity but Huang and his colleagues want to do much more. They don't simply want to continue China's manfuacturing supremacy. They want to transform it.
DexForce Technologies is brimming with robots - and faith in a tech-charged future

Beyond making "our lives more convenient and comfortable", Huang sees AI as helping "the entire world become one family - a global village. AI has the potential to foster equality and the prospect of AI-driven equality is, to me, the most exciting possibility of all."
Smiling enthusiastically, he explains how he hopes that robots can help emerging economies across Africa and South East Asia catch up by reshaping their production lines too.

This tech-charged optimism, which is everywhere in the building, jars with the uncertainty elsewhere in Shenzhen, where robots are nowhere to be found. Yet. But that's just the first of the differences.
In Huang's side of the city, tech and finance workers stroll to the office after a morning workout, sipping coffee that probably cost more than 30 yuan ($4.50; £3.40).
On the other side, scooters whizz through streets piled high with goods being shuttled between factories as vendors sell whole breakfast plates of spicy noodles for under 3 yuan.
The two sides of Shenzhen are a contrast in more ways than one
Outside one of the city's tallest skyscrapers, 50-year-old Ms Lu has a phone to her ear and a pen in her right hand while grabbing a bag with her left from a delivery driver.
She shouts four key numbers at her co-worker: instructions for another Chinese woman who is waiting to take the delivery up the elevator to someone sitting at their desk.

This is the lunchtime rush outside SEG plaza, home to 70 storeys of thousands of tenants. Lu used to be one of them. "I ran a small business on the second floor. I sold circuit boards," she says. "But it's getting so hard to do business these days and the rental fees got higher."

Often likened to China's Silicon Valley, Shenzhen has seen rents soar with the influx of new capital, squeezing out smaller, more traditional businesses. At 50, Ms Lu couldn't find another job until the delivery drivers came to her with a plan.
The wait for the elevator can take half an hour – wasted money for a driver trying to fill as many orders as possible. So Ms Lu became a new layer in the ever-evolving gig economy.

"The delivery drivers bring food here to the building entrance. We pick it up and take it upstairs. The drivers pay us 2 yuan per order," she explains, always on the move. Delivery drivers earn between four to eight yuan per order, so Ms Lu gets a decent cut of their earnings.

"The lunch peak time only lasts two or three hours… if they use our service, they can get more orders done, and we can earn some money as well. But the market is bad. These days I only earn around 200 yuan per day."
Ms Lu, standing in the middle, joined the delivery business after losing her job

An estimated 200 million Chinese workers, roughly 40% of the urban labour force, now depend on some form of gig work. Many delivery drivers in Shenzhen tell us they chose temporary work because there are fewer opportunities at factories than before.

"We need to adapt to the situation we find ourselves in," one driver told us, "rather than waiting for it to adapt to our needs." A group of them are waiting outside the gates of an e-cigarette factory to make industrial deliveries.
Others nod in agreement. Another driver says he has little choice: "I have two children to raise and I can't stop working. I don't have time to think about anything else."
Permanent jobs often require contributions to social security and pension, which reduces take-home pay. But gig work means more cash in hand and flexibile hours.

"Most workers prefer jobs with a fixed, shorter-term duration. It allows them the flexibility to resign and leave whenever they choose; they have no desire to become permanent employees," says job agent Li Xiaohe.
Increasingly, he puts up boards on pavements advertising temporary factory jobs that pay around 22 yuan an hour for assembling small electronics.
Although agents also appear to be in a shrinking pool, with several former shop fronts shuttered: yet another sign of the downturn in traditional manufacturing.
"Our business is perhaps not as optimistic as it once was," Li admits. "We can feel the effects of Shenzhen going through a transformation."
Li, a labour agent who advertises temorary jobs, says his own business has been struggling

Drones buzz above the lush grounds of a purpose built "talent park" along the city's waterfront, dipping and darting as they deliver meals to a dedicated platform. Phones held high, tourists capture them landing with their lunch.

"This is amazing. The technology is just great. I wish we had this back at home," exclaims one Canadian tourist. Our coffee order - for a five-yuan delivery - arrives in just over 15 minutes, the drone landing seamlessly so I can pick up my order.

"I heard that many years ago, Shenzhen was a fishing village," says Anle, who is visiting from Vietnam. "Ha – no more fishing village," he laughs as he orders milk tea to be delivered by drone for him and his wife.

For all the ingenuity on display, it feels more like a demonstration of what is possible rather than a mundane reality. The deliveries, which are only possible in certain locations, stop at 20:00 local time. The driverless cars, which need a separate app to order, are also a novelty – they even offer you a massage when you are on your way.
At night, in the glow of a thousand dancing lights, the drones take on a different role. They fly above the park warning people to behave and not cause trouble.
Shenzhen still draws millions of migrant workers from across China
Far from the glittering skyline, workers gather around plastic tables outside restaurants serving cheap hotpot and seafood skewers.
There are more expensive restaurants along the street, but they too have taken a hit. One owner told us business is down by more than 70% as workers are hesitant to splurge on dinner.
Many of them have spent decades here, including 58-year-old construction worker Mr Wu. He arrived in Shenzhen from Sichuan in the 1990s not long after China opened the city up to foreign businesses.
He was among millions of migrants from poorer provinces who came to work on production lines or build skyscrapers. They are still coming.

All the people we spoke to came from elsewhere. They often labour up to 14 hours a day and live in shared dormitories, sustained by the prospect of stable work and decent pay to send home to their families.
Dormitories like these have houses workers over the decades
For these workers, the Covid pandemic, when Chinese manufacturing hit a record low, appears to have been the first turning point.
"After Covid, our salary dropped by at least a third," Mr Wu recalls, after which wages never fully recovered.

"I will continue to work," he adds. "As long as you keep working, you will have an income. More salary or not? It doesn't matter. As long as you keep working, you will have an income. If the economy slows down, we all slow down. If it grows, we all get better."
For all these decades, Shenzhen lived up to its bargain: work hard and your life would improve.
But now, in a city that is being redefined by automation and AI, that old promise feels less secure.

items.title: United Airlines system outage disrupts departures just days after the big ground stop
paragraphs: is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Less than a week after an issue with air traffic control communications and radar caused the FAA to halt takeoffs nationwide, United Airlines departing flights are being disrupted by an outage. At 6:13PM ET, United said the problem has been fixed:

Earlier today we experienced a technology-related issue that impacted some departing flights. The issue has been resolved. Please check the latest status of your flight at united.com or the United app.

The outage is also coming after last week’s global Microsoft Outlook shutdown, and the great-bank-outage-that-wasn’t earlier Monday afternoon. According to posts on social media, a number of people onboard the planes have heard from their pilots that a systemwide IT outage for United has caused problems with a weight and balance calculator that has stopped them from getting clearance to take off.
United tweeted earlier that “We are troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights. There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.”
Update, November 16th: Added note that United says the problem has been resolved.

items.title: Pocognoli wants patience but Scotland 'don't have time' says Robertson
paragraphs: "First half, I thought we were in the game, we lost a stupid goal, but I thought we had chances and could have been 2-1 at half time," a frustrated Robertson said, on the night he surpassed Kenny Dalglish as his country's most capped men's player.
"By the time you get to 50 minutes and you're 3-0 down, that can't happen in international football.
"It is a really tough night for us. I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it.

"These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.
"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.
"We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."
In contrast to his deflated players, Pocognoli put on a brave face post-match and insists he sees positive signs after his first two camps.
"The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don't think it's a reflection of the game," he said.

"We played a good first half, we created chances, we were dominant in some moments, and we faced Switzerland with different shapes and adapted well from the first minute. We conceded from maybe one of the first chances they had.
"At the end, it's a bad feeling, the score, but I think that the players try to do their best and create moments that we want to see."
Again Pocognoli called for patience and the time which Robertson says Scotland do not have.
"The more we have games together, the more we will try to fix these things," the head coach said. "We have a lot of good response from this camp and it's good for the future as well."
But whatever Pocognoli's selling, former Scotland winger Pat Nevin isn't buying.
"If I'm ever in trouble and I need a PR man, I'm getting him because he's absolutely good at it," he said on Sportsound.
"He's certainly a glass-half-full person. You can talk away any moment and say it's just a moment, but it's four moments, five moments, six moments.
"A really horrible thing in that situation is that if I am running the SFA, I'd be asking the players what they think and just saying 'tell us the truth... are you backing us?'
"If a couple of the main ones say 'we're not sure of the decision-making' then I think it's got to that stage."

items.title: 'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review
paragraphs: Sweeping reforms are needed to help 440,000 more young people into work, according to former minister Alan Milburn.
Almost one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - a current rate of 13%, which Milburn wants to fall to around 5% within a decade.

His government-commissioned review, due to be published in full on Tuesday, calls for ministers to intervene from early childhood through to adulthood, funded in part by radical changes to benefits for young adults.
But Helen Whately, Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn's proposals were in parts "too cautious" and too reliant on the "expensive hand of the state".
Many of the review's proposed changes are specific to England, with some welfare and tax measures applying across all home nations.
Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, says extensive change is needed to avoid a "lost generation", and address what he describes as a "moral" crisis.
The review says that, in 2024/25, for every £1 spent helping young people into work or education, £25 was spent on youth benefits.
By 2036, it says the aim should be for that ratio to be £2 on benefits for every £1 on work support.
In order to make change of this scale over the next decade, the review will call for:
A new target of 90% of children to be school-ready with basic life skills by five years old (this figure is now 68% in England, with a current government target of reaching 75% by 2028)
More emphasis on work skills in the school curriculum
Instant access to mental health support without diagnosis
A doubling of the number of young apprentices
Incentives for employers, such as lowering the National Insurance rate for young workers
At the heart of the changes recommended by Milburn would be a legal entitlement to support, provided through a new "Youth Opportunity Service" in England.
The service would put a young person in touch with a named adviser to help to secure them an apprenticeship, college place, supported employment or a job within four months.

To pay for these reforms, young adults would no longer be eligible for the health top-up of Universal Credit, which provides extra money for people whose health conditions limit their capacity to work, or Personal Independence Payment (Pip), which helps with the extra living costs of having a long-term health condition or disability.

The review's key welfare measures, some of which have already been announced, suggest replacing these benefits for under-25s with a new Youth Allowance at the current base rate of Universal Credit for young people, and a new Additional Cost Allowance to replace Pip.
The minority of young people who are unable to ever work would be supported through a new Severe and Complex Needs Insurance.
Kat, 21, from Devon, currently gets Universal Credit with the health top-up, so is potentially at risk of receiving a much lower level of benefits under the proposed new system.
She has fluctuating physical and mental health problems, including occasional seizures caused by functional neurological disorder, which recently left her needing crutches.
Kat says she "really wants to work", but says she has to rely on welfare support as she has been unable to find a job where she can be employed in a "safe way" because of her health.
Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, says many young people are desperate for opportunity, but that many get knocked back repeatedly.
Josh, 19, has spent three years looking for work while on Universal Credit with the support of youth employment charity Spear.
Although they help him with applications to prospective employers, Josh says "none of them are getting back, and if they do they say you've not got the spot".
Grace Coates, who manages Spear St Helens, says she wants to see "more openness to employing people with limited experience".
Milburn's review will suggest gradually lowering the rate of National Insurance which employers pay for young adult employees to make hiring and keeping them more attractive.
The existing Youth Jobs Grant, where employers receive £3,000 for hiring a young person who has been looking for work for six months, would be retained under the recommendations.
So would the existing Jobs Guarantee, in which the government underwrites the cost of a paid six-month job.
The government has recently announced that young adults will be eligible for the guarantee after 12 months of being on Universal Credit and looking for work, rather than the current 18 months.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said reforms will have a greater chance of success if support for young people is balanced with incentives for businesses to hire them.
It said that while cutting benefit entitlements would reduce the cash young people receive immediately, it might take longer for an increase in employment to make up for that for some young adults.

Responding to the Milburn review proposals, the Conservatives' Whately said: "Where Milburn gets it right, we'll back him," but added that the review "fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won't make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now".
Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said cutting national insurance for young workers would "only partly undo the damage of Labour's job tax".
She said her party's plans would "shut off the Neets pipeline at source, with 100 hours of real work experience before 18 and a careers coach for every young person".
Reform UK's shadow education secretary Suella Braverman said the 10-year wait to see changes from Milburn's proposals "would be consigning another generation to the scrap heap".
"Reform UK would act now to axe Labour's jobs tax, double the number of apprenticeships and end university scam courses that laden students with debt," she said.

For the Greens, deputy leader Mothin Ali said Milburn's proposals announced so far were "extremely concerning", adding: "There is an alternative to threatening vulnerable people with benefits they need, an alternative to unsuitable short-term work."

items.title: Children dropping out of school: What can politicians do about it?
paragraphs: The stories of Eva and Mali - which you can watch in the video above - and the many teenagers like them who don't go to school, either regularly or at all, strike to the heart of one of the many big challenges the Milburn Review is seeking to address.

The government-commissioned work, led by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, is looking into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people not being in employment, education or training, or Neet.
A key challenge is addressing the issue of school absence.
The government believes around a third of young people who are persistently absent in Years 10 and 11 in England go on to be Neet, compared with 10% of those who are not persistently absent.
Persistent absence almost doubles between Years 7 and 9, reaching around one in four children by Year 9.
Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September.
She described how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door.
Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago when she was in year 10.
We shared their stories with the decision makers and those who want to be our decision makers – in other words, those in government and those who would like to be.
It offers an insight into the political arguments to come.

Labour reckons the Conservatives' education reforms of the last decade and a half served academic high achievers very well but created what one source described as an an "endless treadmill of failure" for some - and so let them down.
A government spokesperson said: "When children feel they belong at school, they show up, and when they show up, they achieve."
Therefore, the spokesperson added, "the education secretary is driving ambitious reforms to boost attendance" and "intervene earlier when children need support".
The Liberal Democrats also sought to pin the blame on the Tories.

Munira Wilson, who speaks for the party on education, said "the Conservatives failed to give them the support they needed after lockdown, and years of underinvestment in their recovery are now showing up in rising mental health figures". She added that "every young person should feel they belong".
These reactions prompt some of the big questions that arise from Eva and Mali's experiences.
Where should responsibility for their situations lie? The individual, the parents, the rules in the pandemic, schools, colleges, mental health provision?
Perhaps a combination of all of these things in some instances and other things besides.
The Conservatives have pushed back strongly against the criticism from Labour and the Liberal Democrats.
Shadow education secretary Laura Trott told the BBC: "We mustn't give up on any child, every day a child misses school sets them back.
"Schools are doing great work to bring absence down. Those children who have special education needs or are struggling to leave home, need specialist support and in some cases specialist schools."

And she added: "High academic standards lift everyone up. It is insulting to suggest that not all children are capable of good academic outcomes. Too much maths and English are not making young people Neet."

Former Conservative cabinet minister Suella Braverman, now Reform UK's education spokesperson, told us: "As someone who co-founded and chaired an outstanding state school with a high proportion of children on free school meals but a below average school absence rate, it is clear that the culture and teaching in a school can make a huge difference."
She added that "greater parental engagement" and a "culture of perseverance" were essential too.
The government is expected to accept the broad thrust of Alan Milburn's report, before responding in detail in the next month or so.
We are told there will be an announcement from Education Secretary Lucy Powell directly relevant to Eva, Mali and the many like them, later this week.

items.title: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
paragraphs: The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she doesn't support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.
Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.
She was speaking at a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, which the government said would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.
A government spokesperson said they welcomed her comments and would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right".
Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.
There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.
When the government introduced its draft legislation, external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it, external.

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not".
She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.
But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".
Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities."
But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.
"If a young person, for example, has been sexually abused, any discussion about it is going to be incredibly triggering.
"But if you can't therapeutically work through it without any reference to it, and that's the problem," she said.
She said that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.
Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but hadn't had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.

When she published her report on gender identity services for young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.
She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]."
The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny.
"We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences.

"We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."

items.title: California sues OpenAI over hacking risks
paragraphs: California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday Nov. 16, 2026. In the complaint, California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. California Department of Justice/Screenshot by NPR hide caption
California Department of Justice/Screenshot by NPR

California sued OpenAI Monday, alleging that the frontier AI company failed to protect the public from its systems' advanced cyber capabilities. The lawsuit stems from OpenAI's agents' attack on open-source software platform Hugging Face over the summer but also touches on a wide range of other related incidents tied to the company's agents acting without authorization.

"Just because the technology is new or rapidly evolving doesn't mean the people behind it are above the law," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. "Whether it's a car or a toy, the law is simple: don't build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards." The lawsuit cited potential concerns about cyberattacks "on power grids, emergency infrastructure, hospital systems, and financial institutions."

In the complaint, California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. The state said the company admitted to the attorney general's office that "it lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing."

That number is higher than what OpenAI has so far disclosed publicly and more than what outside researchers have independently discovered, but OpenAI has otherwise provided little information, California said. The state also accused OpenAI of poor security practices, stonewalling the state's investigation into the company and discouraging employees from speaking up about safety.

In a statement to NPR, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab" and that the company has "engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry."

After the most notorious of cyber incidents involving OpenAI's agents – the attack on Hugging Face over the summer – the company admitted that it did not monitor its agents in ways its own researchers deemed important. Since then, outside researchers as well as OpenAI itself have found more incidents in which AI agents have interacted with websites and communicated with each other on the internet in ways that OpenAI did not intend. The lawsuit mentions these events as well as other incidents that OpenAI started disclosing voluntarily to the public.

Other AI companies have also had to wrestle with their systems behaving in unexpected and undesirable ways. Anthropic and Meta have both said they found that their AI systems have hacked into places they shouldn't have. Major AI companies have since signed onto an agreement organized by the White House to develop AI responsibly, but the agreement is nonbinding.

Drawing from reports including from OpenAI's own disclosures, California alleges that the top AI company has engaged in unfair competition and created a public nuisance. It asked the court to stop the company from further engaging in such activities and order it to pay monetary damages.

items.title: In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
paragraphs: Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.

Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.

Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.

The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.

As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.

As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.

Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.

Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.

What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.
All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

items.title: Discover this year's Dezeen Awards Designers of the Year
paragraphs: Dezeen has announced the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening’s ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori.
Our Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.
This year, Ghotmeh took home the architect of the year award, while studio duo Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo were named emerging architect of the year.
Interior designer of the year was awarded to Tokyo-based Ashizawa, and Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was named emerging interior designer of the year.
London-based Ilori won designer of the year with Stockholm-based Simon Skinner named emerging designer of the year.

Ghotmeh, who is the founder of architecture practice Lina Ghotmeh Architecture, is one of the world’s most sought-after architects. Among her high-profile projects was the 2023 Serpentine Pavilion and she was recently appointed to renovate the British Museum’s Western Range galleries.
“From Beirut to Paris and beyond, Lina Ghotmeh creates architecture that feels both rooted in history and entirely of the future,” said the judges.

“Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet. We anticipate her studio continuing to go from strength to strength.”

Ghotmeh is known for her sustainable and historically rooted designs, including the Stone Garden apartment block in Beruit, which was named architecture project of the year at Dezeen Awards 2021. She has received multiple accolades, including being named on the Time100 Next list in 2025 and winning the 2023 Great Arab Minds Award.
Emerging architect of the year: Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo
Founded by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect and urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa is an emerging architecture studio with offices in France, Spain and Japan.

“Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo’s emerging practice brings a fresh sense of curiosity to architecture, balancing bold forms and material experimentation with tactility and unexpected gestures,” said the judges.
“Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.”
Among the studio’s varied and intriguing work is Nakano House in Japan’s Fukuoka prefecture – an apartment block informed by the design of a traditional Japanese engawa.
Interior designer of the year: Keiji Ashizawa

Interior designer Ashizawa runs his interdisciplinary, craft-oriented studio based on the ideal of “honest design”. Along with interior spaces, his Tokyo-based studio designs everything from lighting to furniture and products.

“Prolific designer Keiji Ashizawa brings a quiet confidence to interior design, where natural materials, considered details, refined craftsmanship and a sense of calm take centre stage,” said the judges.
“His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.”
Recent work from the studio includes a tea shop in central Shanghai, a holiday home clad in charred cedar in central Japan and a showroom for Japanese furniture brand Karimoku.
Emerging interior designer of the year: Yasmine Ghoniem
Australian designer Ghoniem has found great success since founding her interior studio YSG in 2020 with the aim of creating bold, holistic design experiences.
“Yasmine Ghoniem takes a bold, instinctive approach to interior design, bringing together rich textures, unexpected colour and cultural references,” said the judges.
“Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.”

Among her recent – and varied – designs are a wellness hotel in Bali, the revamp of a Sydney apartment, a warehouse conversion in Sydney designed to evoke the Mojave desert and a bar for gin brand Four Pillars.
Ilori designs pavilions, installations, pop-ups, products and furniture, all united by a bold use of colour informed by his Nigerian heritage.
“Yinka Ilori injects design with an irresistible dose of colour, humour and optimism, turning everyday objects and spaces into lively celebrations of culture and community,” said the judges.

“Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.”

Ilori has designed numerous pavilions, including the Colour Palace in London and an events space for the Estrel Berlin hotel in Germany. On a smaller scale, he has designed products including a watch for Swiss brand MB&F and his own range of branded homeware.
He also recently created an extensive collection of furniture, fabrics and homeware for Dunelm.
Emerging designer of the year: Simon Skinner
Swedish designer Skinner is well-known for his furniture, sculpture and installations that explore how materials can be rethought or reused.

“Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language. His work subverts the familiar, creating distinct new objects that hint at an exciting new direction for design.”
Recent examples of his varied, multidisciplinary work include a range of sculptural lights made from second-hand bowls, ashtrays and cat figurines.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

items.title: US, nine partners sign SI supply chain accord ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

The United States and nine partner countries have signed a declaration to protect super intelligence, commonly referred to as artificial intelligence or AI, supply chains, the State Department announced Sunday.
News of the signing comes days before President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are expected to discuss SI at a summit in Shenzhen.
The San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity establishes a shared security framework for supply chains supporting AI.

Joining the United States are the U.K., Japan, South Korea, Australia, India, Singapore, Israel, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. All participate in Pax Silica, a U.S.-led initiative to strengthen technology supply chains.
The declaration underscores Washington’s efforts to secure SI supply chains with partners while pursuing discussions with Beijing on managing the risks from increasingly powerful systems.

The State Department released the wording of the declaration that calls for coordinated action against "economic coercion, supply chain disruptions, and non-market policies and practices and their market-distorting effects..."
The declaration also seeks to protect "private investment and ensuring a level playing field for innovation and growth..."
Its framework focuses on two areas: sensitive technology and critical infrastructure.

Sensitive technology includes the "goods, software, materials, knowledge, components, and inputs used to produce them." The signatories say they will work together to stop the theft, or smuggling of AI technologies that could pose significant national security risks.
Critical infrastructure includes ports, transportation, communications, energy and computer networks that SI supply chains rely on. Attacks on these systems or data leaks could cause serious harm.

Pax Silica was formally launched last December, when Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg and representatives from Japan, Australia, Singapore, South Korea and Israel signed its founding declaration in December 2025.

At the time, the State Department said the initiative aimed to reduce “coercive dependencies,” meaning reliance on suppliers that could use that leverage to pressure other countries, and that it wasn't meant to isolate any one country.

Asked Monday whether the agreement could affect the upcoming Trump-Xi meeting, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said SI should benefit all humanity. She said China opposed dividing countries along ideological lines or forming closed, exclusive groupings in the sector.
Mao said Beijing and Washington remained in communication about the leaders’ meeting.
Trump and Xi are expected to meet Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, their third meeting this year.
Trump said last week that he would not raise the alleged spy allegations involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, although he expected Xi to bring up the matter.
Despite their technological rivalry, Washington and Beijing have been exploring cooperation on AI safety.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last week that the two sides would use the APEC talks to work out ways to warn each other about SI safety problems and to share ways of testing advanced AI systems, according to Reuters.
Three people briefed on preparations told Reuters that other planned talks would focus on ways to manage potential misuse of the technology.

The news outlet reported that Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed an emergency mechanism for notifying each other of serious AI incidents in September, but that has yet to become operational.

The mechanism is intended to prevent SI incidents or misunderstandings from escalating into national security crises. Communications so far have relied largely on direct contact between senior officials, the sources told Reuters.

items.title: OIC voices support for Afghan women amid doubts over change in Taliban’s policies
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

In his recent address to the international conference on women empowerment, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Assistant Secretary-General for Humanitarian, Cultural and Social Affairs Tarig Ali Bakheet restated the organization’s “solidarity with ... women in Afghanistan in their pursuit of their right to education and employment.”
Since seizing power in 2021, the Taliban have imposed strict restrictions on women in Afghanistan, where they are barred from education beyond primary school, employment and public spaces
The United Nations reported that the group has issued more than 100 decrees and edicts curbing women’s basic rights in the country.

Despite pressures from the international community, including OIC and Muslim-majority countries, on the Taliban to change their policies toward women in Afghanistan, the group has not reversed any of its restrictions.
Afghan political expert, Obaidullah Burhani told VOA that OIC’s stance is ‘commendable,” however, it lacks concrete measures and action.
“Their efforts are limited to issuing declarations, and I see no prospect for change,” Burhani said, adding that OIC’s leverage is limited “because the organization lacks executive authority.”
He said that OIC member countries lack shared will.

“There are political and security-related calculations and disagreements [among member states]. However, regardless of what they may be, I do not believe they will have any significant impact on the situation [of women’s rights] in Afghanistan, which has remained unchanged thus far.”

In July, the OIC ministerial conference in Islamabad, Pakistan, issued a declaration expressing disappointment and regret at the Taliban’s restrictions on women, calling it inconsistent with Islamic values.

The Taliban’s ban on women’s education and employment “tarnishes the essence and image of Islam and stresses the importance of commitment to guaranteeing equal participation of all women and girls, without distinction, in public life within the Afghan society as per Islamic values and principles,” said the OIC declaration.
The Taliban’s spokesperson Zabiullah Mujahid told TOLOnews in July that women’s rights in Afghanistan are “ensured all the rights” of women “required under Sharia [Law].”

Fazl Hadi Wazin, an Islamic scholar and president of Movement for Understanding and Reform of Afghanistan, however, told VOA that the Taliban’s leadership position that girls should not pursue education beyond sixth grade “contradicts Islamic teaching.”

“Unfortunately, some members of the Taliban’s leadership, based on their flawed interpretation [of Islam], argue that girls should not continue their education beyond the sixth grade. This position is not consistent with Islamic teaching,” he said.
Wazin said that he sees little hope for the reopening of girls’ schools as long as Taliban leaders who oppose girls’ education continue to hold power within the group.
“I don’t believe they will allow girls to attend schools or universities,” he said.

items.title: California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
paragraphs: OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters.

The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”

OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

items.title: Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year revealed
paragraphs: A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.
The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.
Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.
Leisure and wellness projects win big again
The judges hailed the biophilic project as “beautifully minimalist with a spiritual touch of the soul”.
“It’s totally fresh, totally innovative, and never seen before,” they added.
The win marks the second consecutive year that the leisure and wellness project of the year has gone on to claim the overall sector title, following Herzog & de Meuron’s win last year.

The winning project of the year was up against category winners including a sprawling brick-clad university building modelled on stepped wells in India, a country house with walls formed of unstabilised rammed earth in the UK and a project featuring an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through in Mexico.

A housing project that appears as if emerging from the natural landscape and a viewpoint designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the burial site of a legendary Viking were also amongst the category winners.
Architecture project of the year and leisure and wellness project of the year: Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi
The project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.
The idea for the project was to make the trees feel part of the architecture, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.
“Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly,” said the master jury.
“It is a building that offers a spiritual connection between humans and nature.”
House (urban) project of the year: Amami House by Sakai Architects
Local studio Sakai Architects won urban house of the year for its off-grid home on Amami Ōshima, an island in the Amami archipelago off Japan‘s southern coast.
The design was informed by the region’s traditional materials and crafts and its development was spurred by the increase in extreme weather conditions on the island.
“This house shows how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature,” the master jury said.
“In a time of climate crisis, it offers an excellent solution for autonomy of energy, while smartly reinterpreting the arrangement and materials of a traditional Japanese house.”
House (rural) project of the year: Jiang Deng Lu by Shisuo Design Office
Shisuo Design Office won rural house of the year for Jiang Deng Lu in Anhui, China.
The compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site and made using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.
“This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result,” said the judges.
“Innovative in its use of available materials, the project is highly resolved, with incredible quality of light and generosity of space despite a small footprint.”
Housing project of the year: La Querola by Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos
Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos won housing project of the year for La Querola in Ordino, Andorra.
Made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley and clad in locally sourced slate, the building’s facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor terraces.
The judges commended the development’s trend-bucking design as a “deliberately expressionist project, celebrating forms that are not repeatable”.
“It’s a deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core. It’s unconventional, unique, controversial, and a very strong statement,” they said.
Recently, a fire damaged all seven buildings in the uninhabited development. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.
House renovation of the year: Haniyasu House by Aatismo
Local architecture studio Aatismo won house renovation of the year for Haniyasu House, a home in the coastal town of Kamakura, Japan.

The project saw the single-storey home, originally built in 1967, stripped back to its timber frame after a typhoon had left it structurally unsound, and boldly characterised with rough walls streaked with clay, soil and metal powders to evoke ceramic glazes.
The judges praised the project’s sensitivity to “the history of both the architecture and its owners”.
“It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability,” they added.
House extension of the year: Golmorad by ZAV Architects
Iranian studio ZAV Architects won house extension of the year for its project featuring a series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue in Tehran, Iran.
Transforming the residence from a weekend villa into a permanent home, its arched series of overlapping arched roofs appears as if organically growing from the home.

The judges found the extension to be “playful with a sense of freedom,” adding that, “it doesn’t manipulate the old house in any way, but instead seems to organically extend it in a very unpredictable direction.”
“It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life,” they said.
The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.
Civic project of the year: Zando Central Market by Think Tank Architecture
French studio Think Tank Architecture won civic project of the year for its geometric brick-and-concrete market in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo.

The new building, with space for 20,000 vendors, replaces a historic market on the same site in the capital that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.
“A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves, and a capacity to serve the community in a really large-scale way,” said the master jury.
“It has a variety within it to allow a lot of activity to take place, with materials that are simple but sustainable.”
Cultural project of the year: Ismaili Center Houston by Farshid Moussavi Architecture
Farshid Moussavi Architects won cultural project of the year for its Ismaili Center in Houston, United States.

The building and its sprawling gardens is the first Ismaili Center in the US and is one of several around the world commissioned by the current Imam, or spiritual leader, of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community to serve as a place of worship and cultural exchange.
The judges praised it as a “very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner”.
“It has a stunning relationship to light, and incredible detailing and materiality,” they added.
Workplace project (small) of the year: Carpenter’s Home by Primary Architects
Chinese studio Primary Architects won small workplace project of the year for its undulating timber roof-topped studio in Xinyang, China.
The project, a local carpenter’s studio, was designed by the practice to incorporate the craftsman’s studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public.
“A beautiful project that goes above and beyond the brief,” commended the judges.
“The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.”
Workplace project (large) of the year: Florentia Village by Turner Works
Architecture studio Turner Works won large workplace project of the year for Florentia Village, London.

The practice transformed an old textile manufacturing site in London’s Harringay Warehouse District into a creative hub that offers flexible workshops, studios and industrial units ranging from 46 to 1,400 square metres, alongside community spaces and a cafe.

The judges praised it as “well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour,” as well as the buildings being “highly flexible, with spaces designed to reinforce a sense of community”.
The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.
Education project of the year: Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects
Sanjay Puri Architects won education project of the year for its sprawling brick-clad university building in Indore, India.

Referencing traditional stepped wells found in the country, its defining feature is its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof, which comprises 463 stepped platforms that can be used as individual social spaces or as a singular auditorium for up to 9,000 people
“This project creates its own universe,” said the master jury.
“In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most new constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould,” they continued.
“The massing of the roof reduces scale and creates interesting courtyards, creating spaces that feel appropriate for both the place and its climate.”
The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.
Heritage project of the year: Olympics Utilities by Chartier-Corbasson Architects
French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes won heritage project of the year for its transformation of a neglected underground passage beneath Paris, France.

Located in a passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens, the studio created a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a new purpose.
“It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant,” said the judges.
“The project creates architectural character, while also preserving a connection to 19th-century futuristic architecture. Unusual, but iconic.”
Hospitality project of the year: Perma by Mold Architects
Perma by Mold Architects in Serifos, Greece won hospitality project of the year, sponsored by Sanderson.

Comprising five guest houses, the rugged retreat on the island of Serifos was constructed by using material extracted during construction to build much of the retreat itself, rather than removing the hillside and building on top of it.
The judges praised its “striking architecture”, noting it as “very innovative in its programmatic possibilities”.
“There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint,” they said.
The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.
Infrastructure and transport project of the year: Naples Underground Central Station by Miralles Tagliabue EMBT
Spanish architecture studio EMBT won infrastructure and transport project of the year for Naples Underground Central Station in Italy.

Contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof, the 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a new public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city.
The judges commended the project as a “successful urban space, both elegant and spatially interesting.”
“A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train,” they continued. “The use of timber is also impressive.”
Small project of the year: Ring of Bjólfur by Arkibygg Architects
Local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture won small project of the year for their mountain viewpoint in Seyðisfjörður, Iceland.

Designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

The master jury hailed the viewpoint as a “minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way,” adding that, “the minimal use of material maximises the experience”.
Mixed-use project of the year: York Minster Centre of Excellence by Tonkin Liu
Architecture studio Tonkin Liu won mixed-use project of the year for its two timber buildings on either side of a Grade I-listed Gothic cathedral in York, United Kingdom.

Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stonemasons views of the historic York Minster cathedral.
“There is a real honesty in the combination of buildings, with a unique roofing structure,” said the judges.
“The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a new generation of makers using the space,” they added.
Landscape and urban design of the year: Parque del Jaguar by Colectivo C733
Mexican studio Colectivo C733 won landscape and urban design of the year for its work across Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.
The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s important habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

It features an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest, as well as a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals’ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The judges praised the project as “rooted in its context, made for locals as well as tourists,” adding that, “despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.”
Sustainable building of the year: Rammed Earth House by Tuckey Design Studio
Rammed Earth house by Tuckey Design Studio in Wiltshire, United Kingdom, won sustainable building of the year, sponsored by Michelmersh.

Built on the site of a former brickworks, the rural country house was constructed from both the clay underfoot and an aggregate made from crushed demolition waste to form unstabilised rammed earth walls.
As a form of earth construction that is largely untested at such scale in the UK, the judges commended the project as “a radical example of material innovation”.
“Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe,” they said.
The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.
Sustainable renovation of the year: De Nederlandsche Bank by Mecanoo
Dutch firm Mecanoo won sustainable renovation of the year for its major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank in Amsterdam.

The project involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault, seeing a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

The renovation was praised as “an admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building,” by the master jury, who also noted its efforts to adapt it to a different use “while also addressing material and energy concerns.”
