items.title: Shisuo Design Office creates "surreal" rural house in China using salvaged steel
paragraphs: Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.
Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.
It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

“But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the new one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.
“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”
Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.
“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” said Shisuo Design Office.

“Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio said.

Externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio said deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.
It has a rectangular plan, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.
Inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

Interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.
According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.
“The most distinctive feature is a nine-metre-long horizontal window facing east, overlooking a grove of trees planted by the client’s late father,” said the studio.
“For the client, these trees are more than a landscape; they hold personal memories of his father. We wanted to bring the grove into everyday life, rather than simply frame it as a view.”
Jiang Deng Lu is shortlisted in the rural house category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Casa Plaj by Extrastudio and Hata-Mazanka Guesthouses by YOD Group.
Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

items.title: Eurovision organisers criticise Malaysian removal of LGBT+ footage in first Asian contest
paragraphs: Eurovision’s organisers have said they are “surprised and disappointed” that the first Eurovision Asia was altered when it was broadcast in Malaysia, apparently removing LGBTQ+ imagery and people from the show.

The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), the alliance of public broadcasters that owns Eurovision, said it would write to Voxovation, the company producing the Asian contest under licence, and ask it to establish with the Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why it happened.

Footage circulating online of the contest, which was won by the Philippines’ Carmelle, showed the first of two cuts during the voting in Saturday’s final in Bangkok, when the Philippines’ spokesperson, Vice Ganda, awarded the Philippine jury’s points.

Vice Ganda is gay and identifies as non-binary. The comedian is among the biggest stars on Philippine television, has fronted the country’s most watched daytime show, and has campaigned for LGBTQ+ acceptance at home.
Announcing a national jury’s points is one of the most visible roles in a Eurovision final. Each country’s spokesperson appears in turn to reveal how their jury has ranked the other entries.
While the international feed showed Vice Ganda announcing that the Philippine jury had given its 12 points, the maximum, to the Malaysian entrant, Aina Abdul, TV3 viewers saw only the scoreboard.
Separate footage shows part of the show’s opening number showcasing Thai culture, in which drag performers appeared on street food carts, replaced with a wide shot taken from rehearsals.
Eurovision fans accused the channel of “censorship”. The Guardian has not been able to review TV3’s broadcast independently as its livestream is no longer available online.
Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision song contest, said: “We are surprised and disappointed to learn that the broadcast of Eurovision song contest Asia was altered in Malaysia.
“We take this matter seriously and will be writing to Voxovation, the producers of the show, to seek clarification and ask them to establish with Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why this happened.
“This appears to be isolated to the Malaysian broadcast of the show, and all other transmissions were not altered.”

Voxovation said in a statement that it was aware of the concerns raised and was “looking into the matter with the broadcaster to establish the circumstances … We are working with the Malaysian broadcaster to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”
Neither the EBU nor Voxovation said whether the contest’s participation agreement required broadcasters to carry the show unedited or what the consequences would be if one did not.
The Guardian has asked Media Prima, Malaysia’s largest media group and TV3’s owner, for comment.

This is not the first time the wider Eurovision song contest has faced allegations of censorship. In May 2018 the EBU terminated its partnership with the Chinese streaming service Mango TV after it dropped the Irish and Albanian entries and blurred a rainbow flag in the audience, saying such censorship was not in line with its “values of universality and inclusivity”.

Asked before Saturday’s final how the EBU’s commitment to its values squared with the laws in Malaysia and Bangladesh, the other competing country where same-sex relations are criminalised, the EBU’s head of communications, Dave Goodman, said the contest’s values were “non-negotiable”.
Malaysia has some of the harshest anti-LGBTQ+ laws in Asia, with oral and anal sex being punishable by up to 20 years in prison.

Rights groups have warned of a hardening climate. In November last year, authorities raided a men-only spa in Kuala Lumpur and detained more than 200 men, though no charges followed. And in 2022, police raided an LGBTQ+ Halloween party in the capital and arrested 20 people.

In 2023, a festival appearance by the British band the 1975, whose singer criticised the country’s homophobic laws and kissed a male bandmate on stage, led to the event being cancelled and prompted tighter entry rules for foreign performers.
TV3 has faced pressure over LGBTQ+ visibility before. In February 2025, it apologised after male guests arrived at a red carpet event in clothing resembling women’s dress.

items.title: Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
paragraphs: Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.
At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand, push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.
He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.

The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal, which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Trump is under pressure to raise the matter with Xi when they hold a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Apec.

The US president has said he does not plan to bring up the subject; administration officials insist he will not do so and that the meeting will be dedicated to implementing a trade agreement between the two superpowers.
Huang persuaded the Trump administration to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China that had been imposed during Joe Biden’s presidency.

Mao Ning, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, told reporters on Monday that at the trilateral summit, Xi, Trump and Putin “will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance”.

Some analysts have characterised the meeting as a “big three” gathering echoing the 1945 Yalta meeting of Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin that in effect carved up postwar Europe, between a communist-ruled east and a democratic, capitalist west.

Such a prospect has alarmed Ukraine, which fears that Putin – who initially suggested the trilateral meeting – will use it to persuade Trump and Xi to agree to a settlement of the war with Russia on Moscow’s terms.

However, Trump has said Ukraine will not be up for debate at the meeting and that its main purpose will be to discuss ending the US’s war with Iran and “denuclearisation” – shorthand for a deal among the three powers to limit nuclear arms.

That is believed to be unpalatable to China, which has been increasing its nuclear arsenal, and has signalled an unwillingness to enter into reduction agreements until it is closer to parity with the US and Russia.

Analysts say the main beneficiary of the three-way meeting is likely to be Putin, whose standing will be boosted by being treated on an equal footing by two other leaders whose countries are, in reality, much more powerful.
Expectations of a substantial agreement are low.

Lyle Goldstein, an international affairs fellow and China specialist at Brown University in the US, said the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting would not have a substantive result. “There will be no ‘Yalta’, as many have feared,” he said.

Jonathan Czin, the Michael Armacost chair in foreign policy studies at the Brookings Institution, said Trump’s lame duck status would deter Xi and Putin from trying to reach long-term arrangements with the US.

“Both men know Trump’s time is expiring even more quickly than his leverage – and that he will be irrelevant in a mere 26 months [when his term expires],” Czin told an online Brookings forum. “Why would either man make a deal with a leader whose time and leverage are waning? They will only do it if they think they can pilfer more from Trump diplomatically than they will be able to gain from the next American president.”

Nevertheless, Goldstein – who took soundings on Chinese expectations for the summit in a visit to Shenzhen last week – predicted Trump would follow the pattern of previous presidents by turning increasingly to global affairs while he faces the prospect of his influence on the domestic front being curtailed after the Democrats’ victories in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

“The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,” he said. “That may cause him to be more active in foreign policy since he can act in that domain with fewer constraints. It would not surprise me if Trump is ready to go all-out to make some further splash in foreign policy.”

With the risks of reigniting the war with Iran high and the Russia-Ukraine war still resistant to a diplomatic resolution despite White House efforts, Goldstein suggested Trump could attempt “a dramatic foreign policy flourish in Asia”, such as an agreement with Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator with whom he has frequently boasted of having a close relationship. Kim is not expected to attend the Apec gathering, although there have been rumours he may appear.

items.title: How Playstation nailed its iconic startup screen
paragraphs: There’s a short ritual that plays out every time someone switches on a PlayStation. You press the power button and, before the dashboard appears, movement and sound take over, building through a sequence before the console hands you over to play. It lasts only seconds, but those seconds have a beginning, a build, a pause and a release. They are designed as an experience in their own right.

For more than thirty years, every generation of PlayStation has opened with its own version of this sequence. The motion, visual language and sound have changed but the decision to design that transition has remained. What could easily be functional downtime has instead become part of the PlayStation experience. It rivals the best motion in logo design, but it also has its own function as well.
All PlayStation Startups (PS1, PS2, PSX, PSP, PS3, PS Vita, PS4, PS5) - YouTube

That intent goes back to the beginning. When Manabu Sakamoto designed the original PlayStation logo, he wanted it to capture one of the console’s defining promises: 3D. The interlocking P and S created a sense of depth and space rather than simply sitting flat on a 2D screen. By spring 1994, that identity had been turned into an animation, handed to sound designer Takafumi Fujisawa as what the team called a “motion logo.”

Fujisawa was given little direction beyond that animation and had to set the tone himself, working within tight technical limits. He wanted the startup to feel like walking into a cinema. That particular hush where you sense something is about to begin.

A straight cut from power-on to interface would give you a change of state and nothing else. Motion gives those few seconds structure; sound and visual design give them character. They are all working together, but motion is what determines how the experience unfolds through time.

The startup’s primary job isn’t just to create an ‘atmosphere’, as it also helps organise the experience of entering the console itself. The sequence tells the player that something is happening, creates a sense of progression, and makes the eventual handoff into play feel deliberate.

On the original PlayStation, it took on a more practical role. The startup sound helped confirm that the hardware was running correctly and that the disc had been read. If it hadn’t, part of the sound was designed to loop to signal that something was wrong.
The important point is that the startup was not simply decoration sitting on top of a technical process. Motion, sound and visual design were part of how that process was communicated and felt.
That is where motion becomes especially useful. It can signal change, control pace, create anticipation and prepare someone for what comes next.

Over time, the original function of that startup changed. Hardware changed, interfaces changed, and the need to tell a player that a disc had been successfully read stopped mattering. Yet, PlayStation kept designing the transition.

Five generations on, those startups have looked, moved and sounded very different. What has survived through that time is the expectation that switching on any PlayStation from PS1 to PS5 deserves an authored beginning.

That consistency does not always come from repeating the same expression. It sometimes (and in this case) comes from recognising which moments are the most valuable. PlayStation could change the way those seconds looked and felt because the thing it had established beforehand went beyond the mere execution of it.

Brands spend enormous amounts of time designing the things people see, whether it be the best logos, typefaces, colours, layouts or interfaces. But experiences are also full of moments between those things.

When an app opens, or a payment completes, an audience waits for something to begin. These transitions are easy to treat as functional gaps, especially when the instinct is to get people to the next thing as quickly as possible. The point, though, is not to add friction; it is to recognise that these moments already exist, and that repeated transitions can become part of the brand experience when they are deliberately designed.

Motion matters disproportionately in those spaces because it works in the same material the moment is made of: time. It determines how one state becomes another, and how that change is experienced along the way. PlayStation was able to make that transition worth designing and returning to in its own right.

Andrew Vucko merges a lifelong interest in motion and design with a passion for brand building. As the founder of Vucko, he leads a global motion studio that transforms brands like Google, Meta, and Spotify through award-winning motion identities, systems, and guidelines.

items.title: Casa Mouda opens Lagos gallery to promote design in Nigeria
paragraphs: Papa Omotayo, Gemma Sfeir and Nifemi Marcus-Bello have helped design two spaces in Lagos for the local creative studio Casa Mouda to host exhibitions that promote design in West Africa.
Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.

AiMe Gallery was redesigned by Lagos-based architect Omotayo at the entrance to the hotel’s conference centre, while aiMe Concept was designed with interior designer Sfeir and designer Marcus-Bello in a storefront in the larger Eko Atlantic development.
Both spaces feature exposed concrete walls and columns with touches of warmth, including an earthen bar and screen in aiMe Gallery.
Casa Mouda founder Caline Chagoury Moudaber said that the spaces, together, were designed to highlight the work done by designers in Lagos.
“As we began to conceive our first chapter of Casa Mouda, we knew we needed to start by recognizing some of the people who had already built so much of its foundation,” said Chagoury Moudaber.
“There are incredible designers producing on the continent that have done extraordinary work, often taking on alone what usually takes an entire industry elsewhere.”
The inaugural exhibitions include designers from Lagos, but also those who have chosen to work in the city from abroad.

Among the latter group is American designer Germane Barnes, who showcased his wooden Corona Chair, which features inverted pyramidal legs, and his take on a peacock chair, both produced in Lagos in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Beyond his contribution to the interior layout, which includes permanent seating for the hospitality at aiMe Concept, Marcus-Bello showcased his LM stools and M2 shelves. The works showcase the production possible in Lagos, but also a more modern, minimalist angle for Marcus-Bello, who is known for his massive metal collectible design pieces.
“Nifemi Marcus-Bello has been quietly doing the legwork to set up real pathways for production for years,” said Chagoury Moudaber.
On the more craft-oriented side, the collection showcased works in bronze and wood by craftsman Jean Servais Somian, also produced in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Servais Somian’s work includes an armoire with gridded screen wooden doors, a console with stacked oval shelves, stools in wood with painted recesses that have a graphic appearance and textural cast bronze stools and side tables. It is an impressive array showcasing the craftsman’s range.
French studio Hall Haus showcased its metal basketball hoops and chairs, a blend of African aesthetics with Parisian urban ephemera, reflecting the cross-cultural background of the studio’s members.
Meanwhile, Moroccan designer Hajar Daide showcased a mix of delicate Nigerian woven wood techniques with lush blue Moroccan fabrics for her Friction Bench.

Atmosphere was top of mind for the designers, and Casa Mouda worked with US musician Malloy James to create custom speakers at the entryway for aiMe Gallery, while aiMe Concept features a listening station.
The spaces have also been set up to further promote craft in the region through display and retail, such as textiles, bags and other smaller items such as jewellery.

“The designers who have forged the way are sharing information on what they have learned; the ones new to this area of production are bringing new techniques and perspectives,” said Chagoury Moudaber.
“It has been an incredibly collaborative, generous, and inspiring process – and we are only just beginning.”
Other recent design showcases include the inaugural Walker Design Triennial in Minnesota and Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project, curated by Christian + Jade.

items.title: Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial
paragraphs: The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology. Here are our highlights from the event, including installations and exhibitions.
Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.
Rao said the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.
“Though I’m not an architect, I’m literally talking to students day in and day out about how they see the world, and how that translates into the practice,” Rao told Dezeen.
“Being an academic, you’re always asked to define yourself in terms of your discipline,” she continued. “It doesn’t make sense to limit yourself, especially when you are in the practice of life.”

“You’re learning from people about the ways in which they live – that’s what I do as an anthropologist, and I think that’s what a lot of architects do because they’re inspired to build for people and the places that they inhabit and thrive in.”
Read on for eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Artist Curry J Hackett created this draping shelter spanning the width of the Old Al Jubail Vegetable Market in homage to the Black community in Virginia’s Prince Edward County, which created improvised learning spaces when schools closed during the Civil Rights Movement.

Videos play in the former stalls at either end of the fabric enclosure, screening archival images of the period, as well as images of Rosenwald Schools – the community-building initiative that established thousands of schools for Black children in the South.

“Rather than integrate, schools closed for five years, and leading up to that, schools were dealing with a lot of overcrowding,” Hackett told Dezeen. “The county begrudgingly funded ‘tar paper shacks’, which were shoddy, demoralising structures, to ease overcrowding, and that’s what you’re seeing interpreted here,” he continued.

“Interspersed sonically and visually throughout the installation is a mashing up of the local story of my home town in Virginia with the regional story of the Rosenwald Schools in the South – their architectural rethinking of materials and retelling the history.”
Research and construction studio Abari showcased a tent-like structure made from a bamboo frame, which was limited in size due to difficulties with material regulations.
The structure is one module of a larger pavilion that was constructed in Nepal, designed as a travelling venue to host bamboo weaving workshops.

“We were not able to create an installation here in the UAE, partly because Abari’s work is based on building with bamboo, and the difficulty with this project was that the global supply chain and its regulations could not be met within the timeframe,” said Rao.

“What you see here is one repeatable module of a pavilion that is currently moving within different communities in Nepal – we improvised and decided Sharjah would travel to Nepal, and we’d just have a piece of it here in this exhibition.”
Drawing upon her fieldwork in Sharjah, Palestinian architect Samar Halloum designed a brick pavilion that was shaded overhead by a draping fabric canopy.
In reference to the historical public drinking-water structures in the Gulf region, Sabeel Negotiated features a water fountain and wooden stools for people to gather around.
According to Rao, the strikes by Iran on countries in the Middle East in February disrupted brick supply in the United Arab Emirates, so Halloum redesigned the pavilion with cloth-filled bricks.

“One of the shortages was bricks because they come from Saudi Arabia, and the factory stopped producing bricks,” said Rao. “There were some leftover bales of cloth from another installation, so Halloum used those bales and cast them in resin, so you’ll see some of the bricks in the installation are actually made of cloth.”
History as Repair: Documenting Karachi by Kishwar Rizvi

This exhibition by art historian Kishwar Rizvi explores how colonised communities in Karachi, Pakistan, took ownership of their urban environment by adapting architectural styles, from European classicism to Mughal-inspired ornament.
Through maps, photographs, sketches and interviews, it aims to shine a light on an architectural history at risk of being forgotten.
The exhibition argues for the protection of colonial-era buildings in Karachi, which are under threat of demolition due to neglect.
Patch-Time by Hiba Bou Akar, Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb

The Patch-Time installation is a collaboration between researchers Hiba Bou Akar and Mohamad Hafeda and artist Nathalie Harb that explores the displacement of people in Lebanon, from the 1970s to the present day, through the materials used to protect and repair homes.

In workshops organised by Lebanese non-profit Ahla Fawda, displaced women crocheted tarpaulin, sand-bag cloth and sheeting into panels that form a canopy displayed in a courtyard at the triennial’s Al Qasimiyah School venue.
Underneath the canopy, a table made from breeze blocks, wood and a central mirror displays fabric artwork and the stories of women and children affected by war.

“We worked on two levels: one that is the collective, and one that is more of the individual, looking at how people shelter their home through war adversity and displacement,” said Harb. “We asked [the women] what their relationship to their home was, and in the pieces, you see how it changes from generation to generation with their relationship to material.”
After Night There is Nothing by Mohamad Nahleh and Ozayr Saloojee

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee designed a giant globe of the night sky and split it into three parts, which were scattered across different locations at the triennale.

The outer shells of the curved structures are wrapped in thatch, while the interiors feature vinyl surfaces with designs showing man-made military objects in the sky reimagined as creature-like constellations.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” said Nahleh. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures,” he continued. “We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us.”
Kuwaiti designer Badriyah Alsalem plotted 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun as cut-outs on the astronomical graph that forms a circular canopy over her pavilion, As the Sun Rests.

Forming patterns of shadow in the sand below, three of the suns were embroidered in red, depicting the sharaq rising sun, saqa’a noon sun and gharab setting sun, while markers on the ground show where these canopy highlights will fall on different dates during the triennial.
“If you look up, you see the static data visualisation, and if you look down, it is animated by the sun itself, so it becomes an analogue device to read this historical data,” said Alsalem.
Lalla Alwyia Khalwa by Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani
Situated on Sharjah’s Al Khan Open Beach, Lalla Alwyia Khalwa is an installation designed as a place for reflection away from the busy city, dedicated to the saint Lalla Alwyia Kasserine.

Dried plants form a grid of columns on a raised platform for visitors to walk through. Stone slabs on the floor mark places of pause, and a metal stool provides a reflective space to listen to the accompanying sound installation.
“We chose the beach because it is already a space for retreat, so this is a retreat inside a retreat,” said the design team, Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.
“We carved a series of spaces – one for prayer, one for sitting, and a courtyard to enjoy the sky.”

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

items.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
paragraphs: The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”
It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

items.title: These birds fly 17,000 miles every year. Climate change could make it harder
paragraphs: Pectoral sandpipers are among more than 12 million shorebirds that migrate to Alaska every year to breed. For years, scientists have been trying to understand how these unassuming birds make such monumental journeys. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

Pectoral sandpipers are ultra-marathoners. They fly more than 17,000 miles a year, crossing entire continents on their migration from Alaska to Argentina and back again. They don't soar or coast on the wind – they flap the entire way. And these elite athletes are only the size of a robin, weighing around three ounces.

The sandpipers are among more than 12 million shorebirds that migrate to Alaska every year to breed, spending the short summer season in open lands near water. For years, scientists have been trying to understand how these unassuming birds accomplish such monumental journeys from places like New Zealand, Asia, South America.

Rick Lanctot studies shorebirds with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. He marvels at the adaptations that allow the birds to make such long migrations. "All of the organs that they don't need during a nonstop migration get really tiny, like their digestive system shrinks," Lanctot says. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

"Shorebirds are not these little brown birds on the beach, but they're miraculous migrants that travel these huge distances by these crazy adaptations," says Rick Lanctot, a wildlife biologist with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

For 24 years, Lanctot and other researchers have tracked the return of shorebirds to northern Alaska. The data shows a concerning trend. Overall, almost half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are declining. Some have lost more than half of their population over the last 30 years.

Clockwise from top: A pectoral sandpiper, two red-necked phalarope, and a dunlin being tagged by a researcher are all examples of the 41 species of shorebirds that breed in Alaska. Nearly half of those species are declining. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

Migration, like any kind of travel, requires careful timing. Birds orchestrate their journeys to take advantage of the seasons, arriving when food is ample and the weather is ideal. But for many species, their itineraries are going increasingly awry. Habitats they count on, such as wetlands and grasslands, are disappearing. In a hotter climate, spring is arriving earlier, which affects when their food is available. It's like making a pit stop on a road trip and finding all the restaurants are closed.
The question is whether long-distance migrators, which already push the limits of survival, can adapt to a rapidly warming world.

"Shorebirds truly are sentinels about what is happening to the planet, because they're touching down in so many of the places across that planet," says Nathan Senner, who studies shorebirds at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. "If we can't listen to what they're telling us about the unpredictability of what we're currently doing to the planet, then we're not going to be able to respond to a lot of changes."

Morgan Ziegenhorn walks across open tundra searching for pectoral sandpipers as part of a team that attaches tiny GPS transmitters to the birds to better understand their migratory patterns. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

Lanctot gently holds a brown and white pectoral sandpiper in his hands as field technician Braden Meyer attaches what looks like a tiny backpack. This tracking tag will log the bird's locations as it flies thousands of miles.

Nearby, male pectoral sandpipers call out, searching for females and attempting to ward off other males. Some have already found places to nest, spread out among the low-lying plants of the Arctic tundra. The sun is still well above the horizon at midnight, since summer days last for 24 hours in Utqiaġvik, the northernmost city in the U.S., formerly known as Barrow.
The female Lanctot holds recently arrived from Argentina, after a pit stop in the Central U.S. to eat. Flying here used all her energy reserves.
"When we catch birds when they first show up, they're really skinny," Lanctot says. "You can feel the keel or the breastbone really prominently. They have hardly any fat on them."

His team secures the backpack tracking tag with stretchy loops around the bird's legs. It will collect her GPS position every 15 minutes, storing the data until the bird flies by any cell tower on her journey, where it's uploaded. Lanctot's team also uses tiny tags that attach to a bird's leg like an anklet, which weigh about as much as a grain of rice and were originally designed for butterflies.
From top: Two pectoral sandpipers circle the sky above the tundra, where researchers like Fernando Faria are studying the species along with other shorebirds. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

Tracking technology has revealed that shorebirds undertake far more arduous journeys than once thought. While scientists have studied the migrations of larger animals for decades, tracking tags have only become light and compact enough for small birds in the last 15 years. Since then, new migratory records have been broken.

One bird, a bar-tailed godwit, flew more than 8,000 miles for 11 days straight without stopping from Alaska to Australia. Researchers are still figuring out how these birds navigate an entire ocean. They also seem to take advantage of weather patterns, waiting for the optimal winds.
"That's why I still haven't retired, frankly," Lanctot says. "Because there's always a new tag or something coming out that lets you learn things you couldn't learn otherwise."

Rick Lanctot and Braden Meyer secure a backpack tracking tag to a pectoral sandpiper. It will collect the bird's GPS position every 15 minutes, uploading the data as the bird passes cell towers along its migration route. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

To fly thousands of miles, shorebirds must drastically reshape their body. Some double their body weight to store enough fat to fuel them on the journey. Some internal organs, like the digestive system, even shrink before takeoff, since they're not needed during a nonstop flight.

It's why the roughly six weeks pectoral sandpipers spend in the Arctic are crucial. The birds must eat enough to build their fat reserves for the next migration, while laying eggs and raising chicks. Those chicks only have about a month after hatching to eat and grow large enough to join that migration.

The numbers of shorebirds, like pectoral sandpipers, migrating to the Arctic have been declining over the last few decades. It's noticeable around Utqiaġvik, including within the community that's lived with them for centuries.
Robin Mongoyak grew up in Utqiaġvik and is now a wildlife guide. He says the seasonal patterns the Inupiat people have known for centuries are changing. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

"Birds have always been very special to the Inupiat people," Robin Mongoyak says, walking on the coastline where the Chukchi Sea meets the Beaufort Sea. "They give us something to always look forward to after a long, cold winter. The Inupiat people have always thought of it as a quvianaq time – a very wonderful time when the birds start flocking in."

Mongoyak is a wildlife guide who grew up in Utqiaġvik. He says each bird species has a different cultural meaning, telling a story of the world around them. That environment is shifting rapidly. Mongoyak remembers when sea ice lasted multiple years. Now, he says that's becoming rare and the ice is breaking up earlier in the spring. Temperatures in the Arctic have risen four times faster than the rest of the globe.
"The climate is getting warmer," Mongoyak says. "I don't see as many birds as I used to like seeing. It's really changed a lot in the last 35 years, at least."

Amanda Koltz and Julia Berliner of the University of Texas at Austin walk across the permafrost to study insects, the primary diet of shorebirds. They sample the insects to measure crucial nutrients like calcium, which birds need to produce eggs. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption
To understand the decline in Arctic birds, researchers are studying how warmer temperatures affect their food – insects.

"Whenever there's a sunny day, there's going to be clouds of non-biting midges," says Julia Berliner, a graduate student at the University of Texas at Austin, looking across the tundra. She holds up a bug vacuum, a modified leaf vacuum from the hardware store, that sucks insects into a net to collect a sample.

These small flying insects only emerge briefly during the short Arctic summer. Normally, the ground is frozen solid, but as the weather warms up, the top few inches of permafrost thaws, and flies and spiders emerge for their short life cycles.

"Insects and spiders are really tied to the weather," says Amanda Koltz, an assistant professor of integrative biology at the University of Texas at Austin. "So it could be that one week, there aren't any prey flying around, and then next week, there might be tons of flies flying around. And so that really changes the menu from week to week."

Shorebirds time their trip to this buffet of bugs, ideally hatching their chicks when the insect population peaks. But when spring arrives earlier with warming temperatures, the insects also emerge earlier. That puts the shorebirds out of sync with insects, which means the birds could miss their peak food supply, what's known as mismatch.
If insect populations shift their timing, it could also shift the nutritional menu, another way climate change could impact Arctic bird populations. Amanda Koltz; Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

Missing the peak food supply seems to have the biggest impact on shorebird chicks. Research shows that when chicks hatch late, fewer of them survive. Koltz says because different insects emerge at different times, what the birds can eat also matters.

"We need to know how much food they have available, but also what's the quality of that food?" she says. "If they eat a spider and beetle, the spider and the beetle have different nutrients in them, just the same as if you ate a pepper or a banana versus a potato chip."

Koltz and Berliner are sampling insects to measure crucial nutrients like calcium, which birds need to produce eggs. If insect populations shift their timing, it could also shift the nutritional menu, another way climate change could impact Arctic bird populations.
Julia Berliner collects insect samples in shorebird nesting grounds. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

Researchers are trying to figure out whether migratory birds have the ability to adapt to a warming Arctic. When spring arrives early, some shorebirds can speed up their nesting and lay eggs slightly earlier than normal, but not enough to keep up with the changes.

Birds that migrate long distances can also shift the timing of their migrations by a few days, but scientists are still studying how birds make those decisions, whether they use environmental cues or learned behaviors. Some cues may not help them adapt. They may be relying on signs in environments thousands of miles away from the Arctic, or in some cases, on signals that don't change, like when days get longer in the spring.

Red phalaropes are strong swimmers, often seen spinning in circles in shallow water. This helps them feed by creating a small whirlpool, which brings plankton and small crustaceans to the surface. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption

Habitat loss, largely from development, is also driving the decline of many shorebirds, particularly the wetlands and grasslands they use as rest stops along their journey. Drought is also affecting these places and is only intensifying with climate change.

Many migratory birds in the U.S. use agricultural fields and ponds instead, which may be useful habitat for only short periods of time. In a handful of places, conservation efforts are underway to boost that habitat, such as paying farmers in California to keep their rice fields flooded for longer periods so birds can use them while migrating.

"Shorebirds are actually frequently quite well-adapted to finding where patches of habitat are, but our current environmental state is that we've really messed with the predictability of a lot of landscapes," Senner says. "That's what starts to make it really difficult for some of these species."
Rick Lanctot and Tara Rodkey search for the nests of dunlin, hidden in the low grasses of the summer tundra. Ryan Kellman/NPR hide caption
Senner says if shorebirds keep declining, extinction is a possibility for many species. Now, the race is on to understand how much these birds can adapt to a changing world.

"We need to figure out: what are those tactics and then can we manage environments to maximize the likelihood that those tactics will be successful?" Senner says. "Because no one species can be ready for all of the types of changes that could possibly come their way."
Reporting for this story was supported by a Braided River Overlooked and Untold Alaska Journalism Grant.

items.title: NPR's Student Podcast Challenge is back for 2027
paragraphs: Students and teachers, it's time to turn on your microphones and start recording – in January, the NPR Student Podcast Challenge returns for its ninth year.
Since its launch in 2018, our annual audio storytelling competition for students in grades four through 12 has introduced more than 90,000 students to the world of podcasting.
During that time we've heard from students, teachers, parents and educators around the country about how they've enjoyed participating – and how much they've learned along the way.

"I can't tell you how many of my students come back to tell me this project was the most meaningful thing they did while in middle school," says Laura Frisbie, an advanced learning teacher at Minnetonka Middle School West, in Excelsior, Minn. "What a powerful way for students to use their voices in an authentic way and share a message that is important to them."

For teachers coming to the competition for the first time, maybe looking to shake things up in your classroom and try something new, we've got tons of resources available to help you get started. And for our returning educators, there's plenty there to draw on to help your students get better.
The 2027 competition will open Jan. 4, to students in grades four through 12. You'll have until May 30 to submit. Grand prize winners will be announced after summer break in September.
Our NPR education team will listen to every single one (more than 22,000 podcasts so far!) and narrow them down to a list of finalists and honorable mentions.

From those entries, our judges will select the grand-prize winners: one for grades five through eight, and another in grades nine through 12. Since 2024, we've also opened our contest to fourth-graders, and we choose winners and honorable mentions from that category as well.

"The Student Podcast Challenge gives kids an opportunity to shine and tell their own stories," says Ameya Desai, a middle school student in San Jose, Calif., who was our first-ever two-time winner. "Every kid should podcast about something they feel strongly about, something that's personal to them, something they have ties to."
Over the years, we've found that the best podcasts are the ones where students bring a particular passion for the story they want to tell.
For example, here are some of our favorite entries from last year:
These fifth graders in Hewlett, N.Y., for the celebration of the USA's 250th birthday, asked each other: "What do you really know about our country?"
An Iowa middle schooler told the story of her grandfather's dementia, and her struggle to understand how the disease took him from her.

A group of high school students explored a scientific mystery linked to a gas leak in their town of Glasford, Ill. And a student in Los Altos, Calif., told the story of how a football coach's courage and dedication defied the odds and changed the lives of students.

To learn more about making a podcast, you can start by reading the rest of this announcement post, and check out our student podcasting resources page. And subscribe to our newsletter for updates from the contest team.
It's worth noting that several of our finalists and past winners (including this year's middle school and high school grand prize winners) were first-time podcasters, so you can do it too!
And here are two important rules to keep in mind:

A special note here: Parents and educators, step away from the microphone! Please, no podcasts produced or edited by adults. The entries should be original work by students (see FAQ section below). Each year, we've had to disqualify some entries for clearly breaking this rule.
And, students, please keep it clean! No offensive language will be allowed.
As noted above, students do need to work with a teacher, educator or family member — who is 18 years or older — to fill out the submission form to enter the contest.

Our judges will select a middle school and high school grand prize winner. The grand prize includes a certificate, a trophy and a visit from the NPR education team. The team will interview the winner and their teacher for a story to appear on an NPR program, such as Morning Edition or All Things Considered.

In previous years, many podcasts created by our other finalists and honorable mention recipients, including some of our fourth graders, have aired on various NPR programs and podcasts. They've also received additional recognition from their schools or school districts, and many winners have been interviewed by local media.
In other words, it's a great opportunity to share your story and get a lot of people to listen to it.
Before you hit the record button, check out our podcasting resources. We have a starting out guide for student podcasters and a curriculum guide for educators.

In them, we cover everything from how to tell a good story, how to sound like yourself on mic to how to use music in your podcast, among other topics. Even, and we're serious about this: how making a pillow fort can make you sound better!

There are other good resources out there too: Check out this audio storytelling toolkit and recording tutorial from PBS News Student Reporting Labs. Or The Student Podcast Playbook, a four-week podcasting curriculum created by our friends at The Bell.

You can find more tips and tricks on The Students' Podcast, which our team created to help you make a good podcast. We also encourage you to get a feel for what we're looking for by listening to last year's high school winner and middle school winner, and previous years' winning entries.
Here are a few questions we get over and over again each year. For any other questions, don't hesitate to reach out to us at studentpodcastchallenge@npr.org.
What's an appropriate way teachers and adults can be involved?

All eligible contest entries must be written, recorded and produced by students. We welcome teachers and educators to incorporate podcasting into their class curriculum and walk students through the basics of audio recording and editing. And as a part of this process, we understand that students may be getting feedback from the adults involved. Bottom line, we ask the adults to provide coaching and guidance, but to make sure that the podcasts submitted are original work by the students.

And, of course, that goes for the use of AI in your podcasts as well! Here's NPR's policy on the use of artificial intelligence for our journalists. While students these days may be using AI tools in gathering information or conducting research, we've added a box on our application asking you to acknowledge that you didn't use AI in the writing or performance of your podcast.
Am I allowed to use this song or sound effect in my podcast?
Here's an excerpt from our rules page that discusses music and copyrighted audio:

"Pre-recorded music may not be used. Entrants may include live performances of public domain songs or non-copyrightable rhythm elements if it is relevant to the story. For avoidance of doubt, for the purposes of these Official Rules, "public domain" does not mean "publicly available"; it means that copyright has expired and the material is no longer under copyright protection. We encourage Entrants to err on the side of excluding music if the Entrant is not sure whether the music is copyrighted or not."
You can use your own audio, interviews, field recordings or natural sound, music or sound effects you recorded for the podcast. We advise not using audio if the student isn't sure about copyright.
On our entry form, we ask you to confirm that any music in your podcast is either copyright free, or self-produced.

Yes! You can submit as many entries as you'd like. Just make sure that each of your podcast entries are (1) between three and eight minutes in length and (2) don't use copyrighted audio. We wouldn't want any of your work to be disqualified.

And we really do listen to every single entry. So whether it's you and your friend's podcast, a class assignment or a passion project you're finally putting together, we're excited to hear from you and listen to whatever you got for us.
And, as we said above, for more tips, advice and the latest updates on this year's contest, make sure to sign up for our newsletter. Students, we can't wait to hear your stories. Good luck!

items.title: B2 Architecture turns North Korean defector testimonies into Prague exhibition
paragraphs: B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea.

The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments. The first features a grid of red-painted timber beams, with large sheets of red and pink fabric suspended between the frames to create semi-transparent walls.
The structure forms a maze that visitors can explore, with glimpses of other rooms and activities visible through the fabric.
Illustrated panels, games and interactive activities are fitted into the structure, while photographs by photographer Michal Huniewicz show North Korea as it is presented to the outside world.
Children are encouraged to navigate the maze independently and stop to draw, write and complete activities as they move through the installation.

The displays are based on Tota lítá, a children’s book by North Korean studies scholar and writer Nina Špitálníková, which explains the principles of totalitarianism in language that is accessible to younger readers.
“Children are often given very little space within exhibition formats,” B2 Architecture told Dezeen. “This project consciously challenges that convention.”
The atmosphere changes as visitors pass between two walls displaying photographs of the border between North Korea and China by photographer Tim Franco.

Beyond this threshold, the playful red maze gives way to a dark gallery. This contains black display structures with portraits and personal accounts of people who escaped North Korea, alongside stories of those who did not survive its regime.
Tall, translucent fabric panels printed with shadowy human figures were arranged throughout the space, creating silhouettes that overlap with the portraits displayed behind them.
In a central room, a monumental statue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un stands on a raised plinth, surrounded by spotlights and theatrical mist.
The temporary installation was constructed using lightweight, modular timber beams and stretched textiles, allowing it to be assembled and dismantled efficiently.
The timber structure was retained for use in another project, while the textiles and flooring were passed on to several theatres for reuse.
Prague-based B2 Architecture was founded by architect Barbara Bencová in 2012 and works across residential and commercial architecture, interiors and public spaces.

Other projects by the studio featured on Dezeen include the DDB Prague office, which features an anamorphic optical illusion that makes the advertising agency’s logo appear complete from a particular viewpoint.

items.title: Why Dispatch's creators said no to '10,000 endings'
paragraphs: Every interactive story faces the same temptation: give the player more. More branches, more endings, more ways to bend the script until it snaps. Dispatch, AdHoc Studio's episodic superhero workplace comedy, went the other way. It stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as former hero Robert Robertson, who now sends a team of reformed villains out on call-outs.

As the breakout indie game celebrates its one-year anniversary with the Dispatch Deluxe Edition, which lets you play the storyboard art, I caught up with the team. We've heard how Four video tracks and a doughnut shop got it started and how AdHoc made Dispatch feel like an animated TV series, so now I want to know how a choice-driven game gets that far by holding choices back. We put the question to AdHoc co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO and both co-creative directors.

AdHoc starts with the belief that most developers get the equation backwards. "When folks set out to make an interactive narrative game, they incorrectly assume that it's all about the branching narrative that makes it exciting," Herman says. "We believe it's about the quality of that narrative at the core, and then you have to branch that quality narrative."

That's easy to say and hard to do, he admits, and harder still when you have to write multiple good stories at once, which is what the team signed up for. So the development team works from the story's spine and its characters, then figure out what choice space could believably exist alongside them.

Robert Robertson arrives with a backstory and a personality, so options that betray him are off the table. Herman sees that as a gift: it "eliminates blue sky" and lets the team concentrate on a believable character. It's also why he's wary when people ask for thousands of endings. Would 10,000 of them really be as compelling as a six or seven that the team has made as satisfying as possible?

Lenart describes the whole process as "almost an exercise in restraint at times". Picture 10 developers in a room discussing a scene where a character is aggressive towards you. A couple of them will say they wish you could just punch him. "The thing we have to filter that through is, 'Would Robert conceivably punch him in this situation?'" says Lenart. "A lot of times the answer is no."

It isn't a flat ban. If everyone agrees that punching him would be thrilling but there's no motivation for it, Herman says the conversation becomes how to make it a viable choice. Lenart says you go back into the scene and the story and set it up "so that that choice feels like it's a payoff to something that exists".

Skip that groundwork and the cost is steep. "The more you do that, the more you start diluting your character and then they kind of become a little bit faceless," Lenart warns. Herman puts it more bluntly: the story starts to feel like "a narrative toy" and less like one with believable characters.

So how do you make a choice feel weighty without animating an entirely new story? Lenart says, "A lot of the magic in these types of games is the story that people are telling in their heads". The most effective choices, he says, are the ones where "you're affecting how another character in the story thinks about you".

Treat someone a certain way in front of the group, and players will assume that character's later behaviour is motivated by it. Every glance in a later scene gets read as payback for what you said earlier, which Lenart compares to real life. AdHoc builds on that expectation on purpose.

Herman calls it "the grease between the major cogs of choices". Players carry a decision forward for an hour or so, until the grease runs out and they need an injection of new stuff. If a scene doesn't land that way, he says, "it's probably because something's broken". Contrivance, or a sense of being guided, are the signs to go back and fix.

There's a hard budget reason for the discipline too. "It's also just so expensive to do it the way we're doing it," says Herman, with a vision for cinematic quality and animation that makes 30 different endings impossible.

Lenart gives an example of a branch the team could have offered. Imagine letting players choose at the start whether Robert works as a dispatcher or makes a new suit and heads off to be a hero in another city. It sounds great on a flowchart, but "you'd end up animating an entirely different game", with two separate stories, and Robert's arc would stop being about redemption.

Herman is generous about other approaches. He points to Slay the Princess, The Stanley Parable, and Detroit: Become Human as games where their branchiness and reactivity are major selling points. "Interactive narrative games are not one thing," he says. "The beauty of the medium is that everyone finds ways to express it in different ways."

Where does the line fall between what the player controls and what stays with the writers and developers? Lenart says it comes down to how much agency AdHoc is willing to hand over in order to tell a story it believes in. The more it gives up, the greater the risk of versions that aren't great. "Our goal was always to make it so that any path you play through is compelling and satisfying."
There's a cost, and AdHoc accepts it. Herman says some players will end up on a path that isn't their preference, and with stories it gets personal: "this isn't how I wanted it to go."

Lenart has seen the other side of the argument. On earlier games, multiple endings were mandated as a studio priority, and the takeaway was that "some of them worked". Some people had good playthroughs, others got endings they weren't satisfied with, and some were upset they didn't get the endings their friends did.

He doesn't count loose ends as a failure, either. "Not every story or movie you watch ends with you thinking everything is perfect and wrapped up," he says, and the threads people talk about afterwards are part of the experience. But "it can get out of hand if you don't keep it under control".

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: It's not just the U.S., the movement against data centers is global
paragraphs: Activists protesting data centers in their backyards are teaming up to learn tactics from allies around the world. "We are coordinated and we are together," said one Spanish activist.

The opposition to data centers that American voters expressed in the midterms is a worldwide phenomenon. Voters around the U.S. have made it harder for communities to build big projects tied to artificial intelligence. And in other countries, local groups are joining forces to slow the AI buildout. NPR's Ruth Sherlock reports.
UNIDENTIFIED DEMONSTRATORS: (Chanting in Spanish).
RUTH SHERLOCK, BYLINE: In Zaragoza in northeastern Spain, demonstrators fill an avenue.
UNIDENTIFIED DEMONSTRATORS: (Chanting in Spanish).
SHERLOCK: They're protesting against a data center Microsoft wants to build beside a much-loved local forest.
MONICA GRACIA: AI is causing a lot of problems.
SHERLOCK: Monica Gracia says she was inspired to join by the loud opposition to data centers in the United States.
GRACIA: I think that's one of the reasons why this place is so full of people.

SHERLOCK: While many environmental problems are local, most of the push to build data centers around the world comes from U.S. tech giants. So opponents who are fighting their construction are teaming up, says Spanish activist Aurora Gomez. She founded Tu Nube Seca Mi Rio - Your Cloud Dries My River.
AURORA GOMEZ: We have connection with, of course, USA, Africa, Australia and even some parts of Asia. We are coordinated, and we are together.
SHERLOCK: She says Spanish groups were inspired by activists in the U.K. to crowdfund money for legal bills.
LUIS GARCIA: We are exercising our rights.
SHERLOCK: Luis Garcia is from Ecologistas en Accion. He's part of a court case to stop his local government from allowing a giant expansion of Amazon data centers.
GARCIA: We know they have way more means than we do. But the crowdfunding proves we have gathered a lot of support from so many people - individuals, organizations.

SHERLOCK: There's evidence these tactics are working. The European Data Centre Monitor that tracks this opposition says more than 70 European projects were rejected or restricted in the first four months of this year alone.

SHERLOCK: This movement is both global and hyperlocal. In the main square of the tiny village of Quart on the rural plains of Spain's Aragon region, colorful bunting flaps in the wind from a recent celebration by the town's tight-knit community.
SHERLOCK: Also strung up on the wall here is a giant banner - we drink water, not data centers.
SHERLOCK: It's a slogan to protest a giant data center being built at the edge of the village. Resident Carlos Olivan describes it as a seven-headed monster.
SHERLOCK: So Olivan and the villages are getting organized.
SHERLOCK: "We're trying in a very small group to make visible the scale of what's happening so people understand, empathize and mobilize," says Olivan. They began with a referendum in the village.
SHERLOCK: "Ninety-five percent of people were against this," he says. They'll use the referendum results to pressure authorities to try to stop the project.
SHERLOCK: Laura Cosculluela says she got involved in the opposition after seeing what happened in other countries.
LAURA COSCULLUELA: We have a lot of data from the U.S., especially, which is the place where it's been going on for longer and where there are more data centers, so it's the most reliable source.
UNIDENTIFIED ANNOUNCER: (Speaking Spanish).
SHERLOCK: Back at the protest in downtown Zaragoza in Aragon, local activist Maria Pena Calvo says action matters even if it feels small.

SHERLOCK: "Because putting sticks in the wheels, putting stones in their path, can make some companies simply give up or go elsewhere. It's down to citizens," Pena Calvo says, "to defend every inch of their land."
Ruth Sherlock, NPR News, Zaragoza, Spain.

items.title: Albanese treads tightrope in upcoming Trump meeting, wanting Indo-Pacific engagement and end to Iran and Ukraine wars
paragraphs: Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the two leaders meet on Tuesday, arguing for a speedy resolution to the wars in Iran and Ukraine while urging the US to engage in the Indo-Pacific.

The Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines’ capital of Manila will be Trump’s first, in either of his presidencies. The US president, fresh from a crushing midterms result, will take centre stage in gatherings of Asian leaders and prepare for historic three-way talks with Xi Jinping of China and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week.

Underlying the diplomatic swing are efforts by the federal government to avoid angering China, as the Quad leaders gather for the first time since 2024 – and after Australia joined countries, including the US and Japan, in an agreement for new protections around key AI technologies.

Designed to firm up supply chains for chips and critical minerals components, the San Francisco Declaration was crafted to promote cooperation in the face of China’s efforts to control areas of AI development.

Part of the Pax Silica international accord, officials said the agreement would help ensure Trump worked with partners to set standards in AI, rather than relying on others for leadership. Signatories include the UK, India, Israel, South Korea and Singapore.
Albanese told the Asean-Australia summit on Monday that the region needed friendship, mutual trust, and optimism to prosper.
“At a time of global instability, the cooperation we demonstrate here will help us to confront the challenges we share at home and in our region,” he said.

Federal government sources told Guardian Australia the intense international efforts, including Albanese’s attendance at the Apec leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China at the end of the week, was about maintaining engagement with Trump in the final two years of his presidency and stopping the US from withdrawing from global leadership.
Asia Society senior fellow Premesha Saha said the Quad talks would focus on critical minerals, maritime security and energy security.

“For Australia, keeping the United States engaged in the Indo-Pacific is a core strategic interest, and the Quad is one of the few settings where the president is tied into a regional agenda alongside three close partners,” Saha said.
“After a year in which Washington has been engaged elsewhere and has opened its own channel with Beijing, getting Trump to a Quad leaders’ meeting in the region matters to Australia.”
Saha said Albanese’s objectives included keeping Washington engaged in the region and building a Quad capable of delivering results, even during shifts in US policy and interest.
“Beijing will criticise it, as it always does, and will cast it as bloc politics. But I will be cautious about overstating how much this will anger China,” she said.
“The Quad isn’t a military alliance, and Washington has gone out of its way to say it isn’t an anti-China coalition.”
Jennifer Parker, a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, said criticism of Albanese’s involvement in the annual international summit season was shortsighted.
“Our relationships in the region are essential to our security in an increasingly chaotic world, and our security is the backbone of our national prosperity,” she said.
“It is important for Australia to be seen on the international stage and advocate for our national interests.”
Parker disagreed that Australia was working to keep the US engaged in the Asia Pacific region.
“The US has enduring interests here, both economically and strategically. But sometimes it pays for Australia to remind them of that,” she said.
Albanese announced a new Asean-Australia digital economy program on Monday, to support AI safety and intelligence standards and digital trade standards.
He said humans must remain in control of AI, shaping the technology “rather than let it shape us”.
Albanese also held one-on-one talks with the Philippines president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

He told his Laos counterpart, Saleumxay Kommasith, that Australia remained very concerned about the deaths of backpackers Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol at a hostel in Vientiane in 2024.
Albanese said Australia remained concerned about the seriousness of charges over the deaths. Investigators said they did not have enough evidence to do more because autopsies were not carried out.
Albanese called the case a “tragedy” and said it remained a serious issue in Australia.
Kommasith said the Laos government had attached importance to the case and officials were “trying our best to put an end to this by bringing those perpetrators into justice”.

items.title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
paragraphs: The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.

Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.

India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. A low-pressure system formed during the early hours of Friday before developing into a depression on Sunday. The department’s forecast is for the depression to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday before gradually drifting north-west towards eastern India, with the expectation it will make landfall on Thursday. If the storm were to develop it would become the third of the season and be named Akvan. There is a “watch” level warning for much of the eastern coast on Wednesday and Thursday, with parts of the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states on an “alert” level.

items.title: Pepper & Well designs bathroom that mimics concrete architecture of Paul Couch house
paragraphs: Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing Lumeah, a new en-suite for a house by celebrated architect Paul Couch.
Located in Macedon, central Victoria, the linear single-storey house was completed in 2006 by the late Couch, who passed away earlier this year.
When new owners bought the property in 2018, they felt the layout and finishes of the main bathroom didn’t meet the standards of the rest of the house.
They asked Pepper & Well to upgrade it and make it more accessible.
“There was an opportunity to make the space more comfortable and practical as they aged,” said lead architect Andy Dal Pozzo.
The previous layout included a WC, an enclosed shower and a step-in plunge pool, all within a space just 3.5 metres long.
Pepper & Well’s scheme removed the plunge, allowing space for a larger WC and for an open shower to be built in place of the old frosted-glass enclosure.
The defining move was the addition of a cast-concrete element that partitions the toilet and shower areas.
This incorporates an informal bench, allowing for seated showers if preferred.
The geometry of this element clearly references the house’s exposed concrete structure, a rhythmic arrangement of concrete beams over concrete walls.
“Our approach began with understanding the logic of Paul’s work,” explained Dal Pozzo.
“We wanted the renovation to share the original architecture’s material honesty and clarity, while remaining recognisable as a new contribution,” he said.
A change in floor surface marks the junction between old and new.
While most of the room features the bluestone flooring installed 20 years ago, the toilet and shower have a surface of crazy-paved slate.
The stone is the same Mintaro Brown Back slate that Couch installed in the bathroom of his own house, Toolern Vale.
“Laid in crazy paving beside the retained bluestone, it introduces a distinct texture with a direct connection to Paul’s work,” said Dal Pozzo.
The rest of the room was left largely intact, including the solid timber doors and the vanity unit spanning the opposite wall.
There are subtle correlations between the two sides of the room, so as not to make the new insertion feel disparate. For instance, a glass screen matches the height of the mirror opposite.
The shower also includes a stainless-steel handrail that doubles as a towel rail, matching the rest of the bathroom fixtures.
“The scale of the commission demanded close attention to every decision, from the arrangement of the room to the meeting of two stones,” added Dal Pozzo.

“By revealing the original fabric, retaining what worked and introducing a few carefully resolved elements, we sought to give the clients a bathroom that would serve them into the future and continue the architectural story of their home.”
Lumeah is shortlisted for bathroom of the year in Dezeen Awards 2026.
Other projects in this category include Kan Atelier’s design for the William King Apartment, a residence in a 1950s block in Athens, which won the public vote.
