items.title: Elon Musk joins 165,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
paragraphs: Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses have called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation.
An open letter, which has more than 165,000 signatories, demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded, after reports he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.
On Friday, two big shareholders, the investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.

In Washington, however, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next CEO. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News.

Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing, Alice Huang.
The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to China – but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.
“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”.
Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days.
US lawmakers have said that Donald Trump’s administration must also must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before the House select committee on China, as well as the foreign affairs and the intelligence committees. The dates of the appearances, likely to be behind closed doors, have not been confirmed.
On Monday, Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where Alice Haung was an executive until she left in 2025, said it is a “legitimate and lawful business”.
In the past three years, the company was one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, buying nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) in AI chips and advanced hardware.

Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, the founder and CEO of the video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, the president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator.

Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”.
More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce.

The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”.

But the company – which will report on its quarterly earnings on Tuesday – has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

items.title: UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham to say ahead of EU summit
paragraphs: The prime minister is expected to argue that the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the European Union in a speech ahead of a UK-EU summit later this week.

Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet on Monday, Andy Burnham will compare the UK's Brexit deal to the "emperor's new clothes" - saying "a needlessly hard Brexit" created barriers for businesses and the promise to "take back control" was not delivered.
He is due to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility with the bloc at Friday's summit, the substance of those deals set by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.
The Conservatives have said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".

Burnham is expected to say on Monday: "It's like the emperor's new clothes – where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on.
"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained."
The prime minister says he wants to reset Britain's relationship with the EU - and his argument is not that Brexit was wrong, but the way it happened was.
Ahead of Friday's UK-EU summit, Burnham will set out three tests for any agreement.
Firstly, that it must be consistent with Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledge that there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement".

He will also say any deal must pass the "Makerfield test" of providing tangible improvements to people's everyday lives, and deliver an arrangement which improves the original Brexit deal and is closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.
He will say the prospect of a new deal is a "win-win" and illustrates a "new approach".
"Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive - showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges."

But the prime minister has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election, although he has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.
This week's summit will see the UK seek to agree further changes to former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's deal, struck in May 2025, covering fishing, trade and other areas.
The UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports ahead of the meeting.
Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.

Deputy Conservative leader Alex Burghart said that "instead of tackling the spiralling welfare bill, fixing our economy, and properly funding our defence, Burnham is preparing to hand Brussels more money in an effort to distract from the mess his party has gotten us into".

The Liberal Democrats said earlier this month that the draft deal on food exports was a "patch, not a fix" and that the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".

Reform UK has said one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules", and argued that any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.
The Green Party of England and Wales has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".

items.title: Yellow weather warnings issued for snow and ice as temperatures plummet
paragraphs: A spell of cold and wintry weather is set to grip northern areas of the UK early this week, bringing the threat of ice and hill snow.
A yellow weather warning for ice is in effect until 10:00 GMT on Monday after Arctic air pushing across the UK on Sunday night caused temperatures to plummet.
Cold health alerts for parts northern England also remain in force from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 21:00 GMT on Thursday.

Some snow is forecast over the hills and mountains in the north over the coming days but the wintry chill will be fairly short-lived in the south, where temperatures will rebound to above average by midweek.
Injuries from slips and falls on icy surfaces are possible as well as difficult driving conditions on Monday morning
Monday morning will start on a chilly note for all parts, although the coldest conditions will be across the northern half of the UK.

Whilst temperatures in the south will generally be a few degrees above freezing, northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland will wake up to a sharp frost with some wintry flurries over the hills.
A Met Office weather warning for ice is in place until 10:00 GMT on Monday for northern and eastern Scotland as well as part of Cumbria, Northumberland and Durham.
In these regions, showers of rain, sleet or hill snow are likely to fall onto sub-zero surfaces, bringing a risk of icy stretches on untreated roads, pavements and cycle paths.
Cold health alerts, issued by the UKHSA, are also in force across north-west England, north-east England, Yorkshire and the Humber until 21:00 GMT on Thursday.
These alerts are only issued in England and are aimed at health and social care professionals.
Though Monday will be dry and bright for many places, wintry showers will affect some eastern parts of England and Scotland, with these falling as sleet or snow over high ground.
Afternoon maximum temperatures will be a chilly 4-8C in most places - a few degrees below the seasonal average.
Later in the day, the next front will approach from the south-west bringing milder air and some heavy and persistent rain.
As this band of rain then moves northwards overnight into Tuesday, a further spell of hill snow may develop.

A yellow weather warning for snow is set to come into effect on Tuesday from midnight until 12:00 GMT, covering the Midlands, north-east and north-west England, Yorkshire and the Humber and parts of south-west Scotland.
Where snow does accumulate, depths of 1-5cm are likely, although some locations above 300-400m could see 5-15cm.
Some roads and railways are likely to be affected, resulting in longer travel times by road, bus and train services. Power cuts are also possible.
Further south, Tuesday will be a very different day with blustery conditions and some heavy showers.
This battleground of colder, drier conditions in the north and milder, wetter weather in the south will continue into the middle of the week.
You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app.

items.title: Tourette's film I Swear wins three Scottish Baftas
paragraphs: I Swear's director, Kirk Jones, thanked the town of Galashiels and Tourette's groups in Scotland for supporting the film as he picked up the first of three awards.
He also paid tribute to John Davidson for sharing his story.

"I know it's been a long and difficult journey," he said. "Thank you for having the strength to continue that journey and for stressing the importance of acceptance and empathy at a time when the world desperately needs it."
He added: "My big hope was that it would help people understand those with Tourette's.

"What I didn't realise was that there's a much wider community of people with neurodiverse conditions who have connected with the film and feel for the first time there's a representation of a condition which is often hidden."
For Davidson, Sunday's wins are the celebration he was hoping for at the Baftas earlier this year.
"Tonight's not really about me, although it is my story," he said.
"It's about celebrating the actors and a beautiful film. I was blown away when I first saw it. I've never watched it since because it makes me cry.
"So I'm chuffed to bits that it's won tonight."
Outlander, which concluded earlier this year after 12 years and eight seasons, won the Outstanding Contribution to Television award.
Culture Secretary Mairi McAllan, who presented the award, said the show had "changed Scotland forever".

She said the Outlander effect had "transformed screen tourism to Scotland, encouraging people to follow in the footsteps of Jamie and Claire, exploring our landscapes, our castles, towns and villages hoping themselves to fall through the stones and into the arms of an 18th Century Highlander".
Accepting the award alongside his fellow stars, Outlander actor Sam Heughan said it was "hard to put into words the impact the show has had".
Bafta Scotland said Outlander also had an "undeniable" impact on Scotland's screen industry, providing opportunities for local talent to develop and flourish.
The Traitors star Stephen Libby, who comes from the Isle of Lewis, won the Audience Award for Favourite On Screen Scot.
The cyber security consultant thanked his parents for letting him be himself, and his partner for his support.
Libby also thanked the BBC and The Traitors for giving him "the opportunity of a lifetime to be on the craziest show".

items.title: ‘It’s like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling’: the Book of Miracles may fetch £1m at auction
paragraphs: In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In another, blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. In a third scene, dated 1552, monstrous hailstones batter the Dutch city of Dordrecht during a storm so fierce people feared Judgment Day had come.

Created during the mid-16th century, when earthquakes, storms, floods and other extreme weather events were often interpreted as ominous warnings from God, the Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and meteorological phenomena.
It is the only known copy. To this day, no one is sure why it was created.

Now, public institutions will have their first chance to bid for the Book of Miracles since scholars learned it existed. It is expected to fetch between £700,000 and £1m when it is auctioned in London on 10 December, as the star lot of the Christie’s valuable books and manuscripts sale.
Members of the public will also have a rare opportunity to see it in person for six days before it goes under the hammer.

For nearly half a millennium, scholars were unaware of its existence. Found in the library of a small baroque castle in southern Germany nearly 20 years ago, the manuscript, which from 1550s Augsburg, was put up for auction alongside the castle’s furniture, carpets and tankards in 2008 and sold for just over £100,000.
Shortly after the sale, the manuscript entered the private collection of Mickey Cartin, one of Connecticut’s biggest contemporary art collectors.
Eugenio Donadoni, Christie’s international specialist in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, said the book was an “exceptionally rare” German wonderbook.

“German wonderbooks functioned as the sensationalist mass media of their day,” he said. “They were used by Lutheran theologians such as Martin Luther and Philip Melanchthon to further their Protestant eschatology, but crucially – with all the depictions of comets, cosmological events, natural disasters, all verified by witnesses, with exact dates and geographic coordinates – they laid early foundations for empirical observation and reporting. They mark a shift from medieval to Enlightenment.”
He expects the sale will attract collectors of both historic and modern art because some of the scenes, which are painted in watercolour and gouache, are “super surrealist … almost Dalí-esque”.
“If it weren’t for the little captions, which are obviously 16th-century German, some of them look so vividly modern … it’s really jaw-dropping,” Donadoni said.
The scenes depicted include a plague of locusts arriving in Poland on a “terrible wind” in 1527 and the North Sea flooding the coast of Frisia – in what is now the Netherlands and Germany – in 1230.
Other pictures are of fiery comets and eclipses, while scholars think an illustration of “wondrous dragons” flying across the sky over Bavaria in 1533 depicts the northern lights.
Underneath each scene, a German picture caption describes what is happening and where and when the event took place.

“All of these events are portentous,” said Donadoni. “The artists of the Book of Miracles, relying on contemporary broadsheets, chronicles and histories, have condensed into pictorial form the concerns of an age that was gripped by an anxiety – and learned curiosity – about the future.”

The book records how uneasy people felt about climatic anomalies at a time of doctrinal disunity, when there was growing interest in documenting and cataloguing visible, tangible scientific phenomena, he said.
“It’s really fascinating … it is a window into how Europeans were dealing with the impending end of the world, political uncertainty and extreme – and strange – weather events.”

The five suns over Leipzig, for example, is thought to depict the optical illusion of a parhelion, more commonly known as a sun dog. “You see in the sky various different rings of light and it looks like suns,” Donadoni said.

“Blood rain” occurs when high concentrations of red-coloured dust particles, usually from the Sahara, mix with water droplets in rain clouds. “Many of these things have actual rational scientific explanations to them,” Donadoni said.

He said he imagined that leafing through the pages of the book in the 1550s was similar to bingeing on bad news on social media today: “I think it could be a little like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling.”
In this way, the book straddles a momentous turning point in history. “We’re right at that period where the superstition of the middle ages turns into the age of scientific discovery,” Donadoni said.

Till-Holger Borchert, the director of the Suermondt Ludwig Museum in Aachen, has studied the manuscript and said the first time he saw it, his reaction was: “Wow”. “It’s one of a kind,” he said. “It grabs you by your heart or your soul or your belly.”
He said he thought £1m was a “very conservative estimate” of its value. “It [the final price] could possibly be much more,” he said.

A facsimile of the manuscript was published in 2013 that got people “really excited” about it, Borchert added, and since then the Book of Miracles has become “a kind of icon for people who are interested in apocalyptic things”. It would be wrong to value it merely as an historical document: “It’s more than that. It speaks to us, to our generation.”

items.title: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
paragraphs: Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.

It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU.

Burnham is due to meet European leaders at a summit this week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

Speaking at the lord mayor’s banquet in the City of London, Burnham is expected to argue that Boris Johnson’s promise to take back control was not delivered, and that the country was left with a needlessly hard Brexit that created barriers for businesses and damaged its economic potential.

“It’s like the Emperor’s New Clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on,” Burnham will say. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.”
Burnham is to say he will sign an agreement with the EU, so long as it:
Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines.
It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.
And it passes the so-called “Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.

“This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say. “It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges – but being constructive and positive, showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.”
However, the EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told the BBC on Sunday that the UK could have a “voice in the room” under a new deal with the bloc, but no vote on EU food policies.

He added there could well be an “exit clause” in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment, explaining that the EU was “worried” about the possibility of a future Reform or Conservative government undoing the agreement.
The BBC understands the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place after Brexit.
Meanwhile, Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister who resigned over Partygate in 2022, has said Britain would “absolutely” vote for Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.
He told the Telegraph: “It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority.
“He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

items.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
paragraphs: Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out.

It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.

The laptop’s solid aluminium body, look and feel are identical to its predecessors, using the design first introduced in 2021. With five generations of the machine having been and gone, it is a bit of a known quantity, but the 120Hz miniLED screen is still brilliant, as are the first-class keyboard and trackpad. The port selection is also solid and the MagSafe charging cable remains a delight.

The M6 model only comes with the smaller 14.2in screen, which is still the sweet spot for portability and productivity. It reaches a sustained 1,000nits brightness for standard content and working – double that of the MacBook Air – and hits 1,600nits to make HDR content pop. It is only really beaten by the OLED screen on the new MacBook Pro design, which costs considerably more.
Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz)
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones

The M6 is Apple’s latest generation chip and was first used in the Mac mini to great effect. Compared with the M5 generation of chips, including the current MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro is about 11% faster for day-to-day usage and 24% for more intensive multi-core tasks. The extra performance wasn’t that noticeable in day-to-day tasks, but just like the M5 version, it absolutely flies during use.

However, it also has up to 57% faster graphics performance, beating many of Apple’s older M-Pro chips. That makes the M6 quite a leap from older machines with more than enough power for many creative work tasks.

The MacBook Pro also has fantastic battery life, lasting about three days of light work between charges using the browser, messaging, notes and word processing apps. That makes it one of the longest-lasting laptops for general use, but even for more intensive work, developing and editing photos, the battery still lasted about two days.

The MacBook Pro is made of 45% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.
The MacBook Pro M6 costs from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199).

For comparison, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 14in OLED MacBook Pro costs from £2,899, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.
The M6 MacBook Pro is a potent machine for general use that is let down by its high price, mostly thanks to the scourge of RAMageddon.
But it is also likely one of the last iterations of its design, having been superseded by the new thinner, lighter and OLED-equipped MacBook Pro.
The M6 is a great laptop with fantastically long battery life and a quality screen, keyboard and trackpad, built on the foundations of the many great MacBook Pros over the last five years.

But at £1,999 or equivalent it is also a difficult pill to swallow, primarily aimed at Apple buyers who want a nicer screen or more ports than a MacBook Air and are prepared to pay £700 more for it. For everyone else, there are better models available with more grunt or a cheaper price.

Pros: great performance from M6 chip, minimum of 16GB memory and 1TB storage, super-long battery life, great ProMotion screen, great Centre Stage camera, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, great speakers, Touch ID, top-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, very expensive, not a big upgrade on M5 version, no OLED screen, heavier than newer design.

items.title: Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
paragraphs: Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.

The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.

At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin, the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.

UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.

UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.

Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).

Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.
Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.

But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).

Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”

The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.
Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?

Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.

There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.

The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.

And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”
On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?

In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.

Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.
A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.

It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.
Conscious partnership: will the EU welcome future closeness this week?

I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back”? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?

The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”

But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.
It’s not you, it’s me: what else is Europe worrying about?

The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right, street protests, hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026.
“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.

There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.

Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”
Tuesday | The work and pensions secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.

Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.
Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place.
With a stellar range of interviews, Nadia Khomami is excellent on 2000s pop culture, and how openly horrible it was to women. Poppy Noor, newsletters team
Emma Beddington’s piece on why gen Xer seem to have worse mental and physical health than boomers is a must-read. Poppy

Amelia Gentleman’s report over the weekend on two very different rape trials and what happened in each of them is a difficult read – but enlightening about all of the ways culture has (and has not) changed since Russell Brand’s prominence. Poppy

Football | England risked throwing away a three-goal lead against Spain after Elliot Anderson was sent off, but held on for a thrilling 3-2 win in Madrid, which Thomas Tuchel hailed as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure.
Cricket | Tom Banton’s century led England to emphatic win, with 135 runs, in second ODI amid Australian soap opera.
Rugby union | Tries from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey gave Scotland a 15-12 win against Australia in the Nations Championship at Murrayfield
“PM vows early years interventions will tackle youth joblessness crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today.
The i Paper leads with “Pressure grows for new consent law to protect teenagers from adult predators”, Metro has “Rethink on the age of consent”, the Sun writes “Brand’s rant from prison”.

The Telegraph says “Johnson: Britain would back Brexit again”, the Express writes “Brexit U-turn means ‘more asylum seekers’”. The Times has “Zero-hours ban to cost billions”, the Mail has “£80,000 a day spent ferrying migrants around”, the Mirror’s splash is “Dying in the dark”, and the FT’s is “Nvidia scandal spurs drive to choke China’s AI chip supply”.
Grand Theft Auto VI: the cultural event of the decade?

This week, after a 13-year wait, gamers will finally get hold of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment of the most successful console computer game in history. How did a game of stealing cars and shooting strangers become such an enormous cultural phenomenon? The Guardian’s video games editor, Keza MacDonald, traces the history of games by Rockstar, GTA’s creator, and what its most successful product has told us about the US, the setting of all its games so far.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.

Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app. “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg,” said Burgmans. “That just makes me happy. I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

items.title: UK exposed to polycrisis of threats amid government ‘complacency’
paragraphs: Ministers are complacent in the face of fast-changing and increasingly interconnected threats to the UK, and must act quickly to increase national resilience to possibly very major crises, a parliamentary report has found.

While Labour recently launched a “Be Ready” campaign, advising households to have stocks of food and water, most of the public are unaware of the scale of potential threats from cyber-attacks, proxy acts of violence or strikes on underseas cables, as well as natural disasters such as extreme weather and flooding, it said.

Written by the Lords national resilience committee after months of expert hearings, the report calls for a new and coherent approach to resilience planning, including a dedicated cabinet minister and an annual statement to parliament by the prime minister to set out the extent of preparedness.
It also called for more flexible ways to communicate with the public, including a pause to plans to switch off the Freeview-style digital terrestrial TV signal, in case other systems are disrupted.

Another recommendation is for the government to send every household a booklet setting out how people can prepare for and respond to an emergency, following the model of countries such as Denmark and Sweden.

The report said the UK’s current plans were often out of date and over atomised, dealing with responses to a single emergency such as a loss of power or water supplies, or a cyber-attack, and not an increasingly plausible “polycrisis” of several disruptions blending into another, especially as AI “supercharges” the risk from cyber-attacks.

“In the face of potentially catastrophic risks and despite the recent launch of the Be Ready campaign, the government appears complacent and the UK is underprepared. We need to move fast to turn things around,” the committee warned.
“The government must not treat emerging threats as distant or hypothetical problems. Doing so risks leaving the UK exposed as vulnerabilities develop.”

Among the particular vulnerabilities highlighted are medicines and food, both of which are dependent on highly centralised and generally international supply chains, with few if any back-up options if these are disrupted.

The bulk of antibiotic medicines are now made in China or India, the report noted, with about 90% of the world’s 6-APA, the organic compound which is the basis of penicillin-types antibiotics, coming from China.
This is, it said, the result of years of price pressures and cost-based procurement, meaning there is now only one integrated penicillin facility in Europe, and none in the UK.

The same is true for other medical supplies, with one witness telling the committee that such was the reliance on overseas-made items such as scissors and medical staplers that disrupted could badly disrupt many everyday surgical operations.

With food, the committee was told that while people stockpiling several days of food and water, as recommended by Be Ready, was something, this did not cover the wider strategic risks to a hugely centralised food system.

This results in almost 95% of UK retail food being supplied by just nine companies from 131 distribution hubs, meaning that disruption to just a handful of firms could create very significant disruption.

Despite the increasing risk of multi-area crises, too much current emergency planning remains “organised in silos around individual risks, organisations and sectors, rather than the continued operation of essential national functions”, the report said, calling for this to change.

There was, it set out, a particular risk to digital communications, including through possible attacks on undersea cables. BT, which has a dominant role in this area, has access to just two cable repair ships, the report found – “one French-owned and generally unavailable, and one UK-based but 35 years old”.

Among its recommendations, the report said the Cabinet Office, which leads on resilience, should set out a national resilience strategy within six months, with proper funding and a more coherent assessment than the current national risk register, which lists 87 separate items.

It also called for resilience to be embedded in civilian life, with a national register of volunteers and civil reservists drawn up, and the possibility of an entitlement to paid leave for people taking resilience-based training.
Jean Coussins, the cross-bench peer who chairs the committee, said ministers should not be “squeamish” about setting out the risks.
She said: “Evidence shows that the public would be reassured, not alarmed, by candid information. People are more than willing to step up in an emergency, but less clear [as to] why and how.”
A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office said it would “carefully review” the specific recommendations, but that the government was already working at speed.

“From launching a national campaign to raise awareness of the simple steps households can take to stay safe in everyday emergencies, to delivering the largest home defence exercise in recent history next year, and investing over £1bn in pandemic security – our work on resilience goes further than successive governments have ever gone before.
“However, we know there is still more work to do to make the UK the most resilient country we can be, including working with and learning from our allies.”

items.title: Experts explore returning beavers to River Waveney
paragraphs: A river separating two counties could become home to beavers as work begins to explore where a colony could be introduced.
The River Waveney Trust is in conversation with Natural England and other agencies about potentially reintroducing the river-dwelling mammals along the River Waveney.
The 59-mile (95km) waterway rises in Redgrave and Lopham Fen in Suffolk and heads east, creating a border between Norfolk and Suffolk as it flows out into the River Yare at Great Yarmouth.
Ange Lamb, catchment resilience officer, said the upper reaches of the River Waveney and its tributaries could make ideal environments for beavers. If successful, beavers could return by 2029.
Known as river engineers, beavers were native to Britain but they were hunted to extinction by the end of the 16th century.
Conservationists want to reintroduce them to help boost the health of waterways through their ability to create wetland areas.
But there are concerns, particularly around dams being built in inappropriate places and their ability to destroy trees.

items.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
paragraphs: The Jackdaw platform is located 150 miles east of Aberdeen
Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.
Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.
It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.
The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.
Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers.
"It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security.
"It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear."
Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain".

She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions.
"Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities."
Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea".
She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades".
Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial?
Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.
The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.
The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.
The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field.

Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners.
This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw.
He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade".
A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made.
Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning
The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism".
He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."
Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.
Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".
The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.
Jackdaw's operators said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages
Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.
The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.
Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.
But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully.
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.

The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.
An inside look at Jackdaw, the UK’s newest and most contested gas platform.
When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.
However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.

In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined, external.

"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.
Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.
McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.
He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.
Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.
But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

items.title: Women pay to break things – level 1
paragraphs: Many women in the UK are visiting new places called rage rooms. In these rooms, people use hammers to break old TVs, plates, and boxes.

People go there because they feel very stressed, tired, or sad about life and work. Owners of these rooms say that most of their visitors are women. Doctors say that it is good to let out bad feelings in a safe space. Men can get angry during sports, but women must be quiet and calm.
Breaking things makes people feel happy and strong for a short time. But it cannot solve big life problems forever.
Difficult words: hammer (a hand tool which we use for breaking things), stressed (worried and upset), owner (a person who has something and it belongs to him or her).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Women pay to break things – level 2
paragraphs: Rage rooms are becoming very popular in the UK, especially for women. In these special rooms, people pay to break things like old TVs, plates, and glasses with big hammers.

About 75 percent of the customers are women who are trying to deal with work stress, busy family lives, or deep sadness after losing loved ones. Experts explain that society usually expects women to stay calm, so they don’t have many places to express anger.

Smashing things gives people a quick feeling of power and release. On the other hand, doctors say that while rage rooms are fun and help you feel better for a short time, breaking things doesn’t fix big emotional problems forever.
Difficult words: rage (uncontrollable anger), sadness (when you are sad), smash (to break something into pieces with great force).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Women pay to break things – level 3
paragraphs: Across the UK, a growing number of people, especially women, are turning to so-called rage rooms to destroy everyday items like flat-screen televisions and crockery with mallets and hammers.

Owners report that up to three-quarters of their customers are female. Many use the sessions to cope with everyday stress, child-rearing pressures, or deep emotional trauma such as bereavement. Psychologists note that societal expectations often force women to suppress anger, unlike sports events where men are traditionally permitted to shout freely. Inside a rage room, participants find a safe, controlled environment where they can express frustration without judgment.

While smashing objects provides an immediate surge of adrenaline and physical relief, experts caution that it doesn’t serve as a permanent therapeutic cure for long-term psychological problems. Instead, they view it as a helpful short-term release of energy, and advise individuals dealing with deep-seated emotional pain to seek professional long-term support.

Difficult words: bereavement (suffering the loss of a loved one through death), suppress (to forcibly hold back, control, or prevent the expression of a feeling), judgment (an opinion or decision formed after thought or legal process).
You can watch the video news lower on this page.
