The Vatican houses a collection of Indigenous treasures questionably ‘gifted’ to it
Head of Christ Crucified by the Master of Liesborn (Johann von Soest?), probably early 1480s-1490

The blood streams over Christ’s deathly white face in a vivid, almost Hammer horror contrast between gore and pallor. It flows in thick rivulets from the crown of thorns that has been mockingly forced on to his head. The initials INRI on a piece of paper fixed to the cross stand for “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” in Latin, and the cruel crown rams home the barb. Christ bears the laughter and the physical pain with patience and dignity, lowering his eyes in sorrow as he waits for his earthly body to die. The stark, simple shock of this image comes from an age in which Europeans were encouraged to identify with Christ, to imagine themselves suffering alongside him. At the same time this artist’s explicit focus on flowing blood may serve a theological function: the central moment of the medieval Mass was the miraculous transformation of bread and wine into the actual body and blood of Christ. According to the philosopher Thomas Aquinas this took place literally: the bread and wine kept their “accidental” appearance while changing their “essential” nature. This painting is part of an altarpiece from Germany, but not all Germans were convinced by such ideas. In the early 1500s Martin Luther would rebel against the miracle of transubstantiation, and against art like this which he regarded as idolatry. National Gallery, London

items.title: Political divide threatens Kurdish autonomy; US urges unity
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
Last week's withdrawal of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan from the Iraqi Kurdistan’s regional government has deepened the political standoff between the region's two main ruling parties.
The rise in tensions came after a disputed parliamentary session prompted the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) to announce its withdrawal from the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG).

The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), led by the Barzani family, and the PUK, led by the Talabani family, have dominated Kurdish politics for decades. Their rivalry led to a brutal armed conflict and separate administrations in the 1990s.
Some regional analysts warn that the latest tensions could lead to a renewed division of the Kurdistan region.

"If we divide this region ourselves, the entire world will abandon us,” Kamil Omar, a university professor in Sulaimaniyah, told VOA. “How long can they continue worrying about us when we cannot protect our own region, our people’s future and our nation’s strategic interests?”
The Kurdistan Region gained de facto autonomy following the 1991 Gulf War, with its federal status recognized in Iraq’s 2005 constitution.
“We have received political and military support and protection from international allies for the past 35 years," he added.

Speaking at Chatham House in London on Wednesday, U.S. special envoy for Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack urged Kurdish leaders to overcome their “family” and “tribal” divisions and strengthen cooperation with Baghdad.
“This is an Iraqi issue. This is an Iraqi decision. This is not an American decision,” Barrack said. “My advice, the president’s advice, is: Get over it.”
Masoud Haider, a KDP member and former Iraqi deputy finance minister, described Barrack’s remarks as a clear political message urging both parties to agree on forming a government.

“A strong Kurdistan Region with unified institutions contributes to Iraq’s strength and stability,” Haider told VOA. “This message calls on Kurdish political forces to put their differences aside and form a government based on cooperation and responsibility.”
Mahmoud Khoshnaw, a PUK member, described Barrack’s remarks as both a reflection of political realities and a warning.

“Any step that promotes stability and development strengthens the region, while any step that undermines stability, creates political divisions or marginalizes a political party weakens it,” Khoshnaw told VOA.
Speaking Thursday at the Sulaimani Forum, PUK leader Bafel Talabani described the dispute as “the single largest political crisis in the history of the Kurdistan Region.”
He rejected the legitimacy of the disputed parliamentary process and warned against further unilateral moves.
“We effectively have two administrations,” Talabani said, although he cautioned that discussing two separate governments was premature.
“Every escalation will be met with a well-planned escalation,” he warned, adding that dialogue remained possible.
Talabani rejected characterizing the dispute as a family feud, describing it instead as a longstanding rivalry between two political forces.
On Monday, KDP leader Masoud Barzani called for negotiations.
“I call on our brothers in the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan to sit down with the KDP, resolve the problems and bring an end to the Kurdistan Region’s political crisis,” Barzani said in a statement.
The KRG Council of Ministers, meeting Wednesday without PUK ministers, also urged them to return and address their concerns through cabinet discussions.
Talabani dismissed those appeals as political rhetoric intended to shift blame for the divisions onto the PUK.

items.title: Marlon Brando cool to Jensen Huang joke: how the black leather jacket became a meme
paragraphs: For nearly two decades a black leather jacket has been a key part of Jensen Huang’s look. Now it has become a punchline.

As the founder and chief executive of Nvidia resigned this week after reports of multiple affairs, his affinity for a leather jacket, an item of clothing typically associated with a man in midlife crisis mode, has become widely mocked.

The Cut ran a story suggesting a clear line between his penchant for a luxury leather jacket and his extramarital affairs. “Jensen Huang’s leather jackets confessed before he did” read the headline. Writing in the New York Times, the author Anand Giridharadas asked “is an expensive leather jacket on a middle-aged man the new symbol of a honeypot victim?”

Meanwhile, the internet is rife with memes, including an AI-generated image of a leather jacket flying at half mast outside Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX. There was also another fake image, this time of Huang in a studded leather jacket, that many people believed was real.

Elsewhere, there are plenty of divorced dad jokes doing the rounds. “Jensen leather jacket discourse reminds me of the time two years ago when I wore my beloved moto jacket to a party and my good friend said “great jacket, sorry you got divorced”, wrote one user on X.

Similar to Steve Jobs’s black rollneck and jeans or Mark Zuckerberg’s Latin-sloganed T-shirts, Huang’s black leather jacket has become a visual trademark. He likes to pair a leather jacket (always black) with a black T-shirt and black jeans.

In September, in an interview with CBS, Huang explained he had 30 to 40 leather jackets. He credited his wife, Lori Huang, with choosing them. They vary from motorcycle-inspired jackets with a tighter fit and plenty of zips to collarless croc-embossed jackets and clean-cut tailored versions. He has worn them to trade shows, to parties and to give keynote speeches at developer conferences. In 2021 he appeared on the cover of Time magazine in a black leather jacket from Tom Ford. In July, another Tom Ford jacket worn and signed by Huang sold at a charity auction at Sotheby’s for $960,000, more than 10 times its original price.
“The leather jacket is Huang’s way of borrowing some cool,” says Peter Bevan, a writer and stylist. Bevan points to the leather jacket’s “rebel history” as part of the appeal.

Marlon Brando led his biker gang wearing an asymmetric zip jacket in 1953’s The Wild One; James Dean zipped around off-screen in a similar style while following his Berlin era; David Bowie wore a black leather jacket on the cover of his Heroes album in 1977. Patrick Swayze in Dirty Dancing, John Travolta in Grease and Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones also made a leather jacket an enduring symbol of Hollywood style.
By choosing a black leather jacket rather than a corporate suit, it suggests that Huang is unconventional, a leader rather than a conformist.
“It’s basically Huang saying: ‘I’m not a regular billionaire boss, I’m a cool billionaire boss’,” Bevan says.

When asked by CBS in October why he wore a leather jacket day in, and day out, Huang said it helped him avoid decision fatigue. “Black is the absence of choice,” he said. “It’s nice to wear the same thing every day because no surprises. For everybody else, they probably have to make three or four decisions. I took that off my plate. The moment I wake up, I could be thinking about important things.”

It’s a look that has not gone unnoticed by his fellow tech giants. In 2024, Zuckerberg posted a photo of Huang swapping jackets. Later in the year, at a Siggraph conference in Colorado, Zuckerberg presented him with another jacket. “It’s black and leather and shearling,” Zuckerberg said describing the coat. “It’s a vibe. I mean, get this guy a chain.” In return, Huang gave him the black leather jacket he was wearing, explaining that Lori had bought it for him to commemorate that year’s conference. “This is worth more because it’s used,” Zuckerberg said as he slipped it on.

Bevan says that while Huang’s choice of designer jackets are “the kind that most fashion insiders would rate”, a box-fresh leather jacket “feels try hard” and as a result, “tips into midlife crisis territory fast”.
The biggest mistake men make when buying a leather jacket Bevan says is choosing one that is “too shiny, too new and too tight.”
The list of those who get it wrong is long – including Jeremy Clarkson, who likes to wear a black leather jacket with bootcut jeans.
For Bevan, the men who have mastered a leather jacket are those who “look like they’ve owned it for ever”.

Lenny Kravitz who, like Huang, is in his 60s, prefers a battered leather jacket. John Malkovich, who is a decade older, likes a brown oversized leather jacket, while the rapper A$AP Rocky, who is in his 30s, has made a bomber leather jacket his style staple.

For those without youth or “rock-star DNA” on their side, Bevan suggests ditching a leather jacket for a cotton Harrington style that he describes as “having the same cool but none of the leather-clad midlife baggage”.

As for Huang, he may have to reconsider his default wardrobe for next week. While he managed to pull off a leather jacket at tech conferences, it may be harder to pull off at a congressional testimony.

items.title: Trump loses control of Congress – level 1
paragraphs: The Democrats win a big election in the US. They now control Congress. President Donald Trump and his team lose many votes.

Now, people in both political parties are fighting about what to do next. Vice President JD Vance says that the war with Iran is a bad idea. Many people do not like Trump anymore because of that. Trump said that his immigration rules are too hard. But he still puts his immigration leader in a top job. At the same time, Democrats are trying to agree on new plans for the country.
Experts think that it will still be very hard for leaders in Washington to pass new laws and help people quickly.

Difficult words: vote (when a person formally chooses a person in an election), immigration rules (what people who come from other countries must and must not do), pass (to officially say yes to a new rule).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: A lipsmacking journey from kisses galore to tears of despair – How Do We Find Love? review
paragraphs: To quote 1980s soft rockers Foreigner, I want to know what love is. And I want the Sainsbury Centre to show me. This big winter series tackles love in all its guises – and for now comprises two shows, one about smooching called The Last Human Kiss, another about desire and heartbreak called Ecstasy and the Aftermath.

The problem is, love is probably the biggest topic in human history, let alone art history. Think of the endless novels and poems and films; think of how many songs have been written, how many paintings painted. Love is an endlessly vast topic and this show barely scratches its surface.

The first exhibition begins, like so much love, with a single kiss – a gaunt couple locking lips on a 15th-century Italian vase. They don’t look too thrilled about it but, hey, that’s the reality of love. Sometimes it’s not great. The show then takes you on a salivary journey through every possible kind of kiss: political, maternal, interracial, divine, familial.

Allegories of righteousness and peace give each other an awkward peck in a William Blake watercolour, the infant Christ and St John the Baptist hold each other close in an Anthony van Dyck painting. Then a priest kisses a nun in a Benetton ad, the USSR’s President Brezhnev kisses East German leader Honecker, Cupid kisses Psyche. And that’s before you even get to the bulk of the show with its snogs by Edvard Munch, Wolfgang Tillmans and – obviously – Rodin, whose carved marble canoodle dominates the middle of the exhibition. It’s enough to give you chapped lips.

What they want you to see is the vast complexity of kissing, to understand its different histories and implications. So they show it through a postcolonial lens, a religious lens, a political lens, and so on. But kisses are not some underexplored, subconscious thing – they’re universal. We think about our kisses, we remember them, treasure them, long for them. The whole thing just feels obvious, like someone telling you the plot of a movie you’ve already seen.

There are works that deal with love more widely – including a Tracey Emin neon that says “The Heart has Its Reasons”, as if anyone on Earth needs to see another Tracey Emin neon. But they feature no actual kissing. The concept isn’t bad, and neither’s the execution, but in the end there are only so many images of people necking you can hack before you get mental jaw ache. It’s a whole exhibition of people locked in embraces, a whole show of painterly PDAs, and it wears thin.

The second exhibition, Ecstasy and the Aftermath, tackles the joy of new love, the despair of heartache, and everything in between. That’s where it really falls apart. There are some good works: a Somaya Critchlow nude, a set of deeply romantic and poetic Judy Chicago prints, a Jane Hayes Greenwood painting of leaking, breast-like plant forms, the Marina Abramović and Ulay video of him on the verge of unleashing an arrow into her heart. But the theme is so broad it sends you spinning.

There are works about motherly love, romantic love, desire, the gaze, heartache, grief. There are photos of people dancing in queer nightclubs, because community is a form of love. There’s a Paloma Proudfoot ceramic of gossiping mates, because really liking your pals is love, too. There’s so much to explore, each of those themes could have been a whole exhibition in its own right, but it’s all just been squeezed into one room.

The only way this could have worked is if they’d narrowed the focus. Or if they’d deleted all the wall texts, got rid of the faltering conceptual themes and restrictions and just whacked together a bunch of artworks about desire, adoration, romance, heartache and snogging and let you make your own way through it.
But if you want to know what love is, these two shows do actually provide a pretty good answer. Sometimes it’s beautiful, sometimes it’s joyful, but more often than not, it’s a bit of a mess.

items.title: You know that butter bot from Rick and Morty? You can buy that now
paragraphs: Struggling to find a Christmas or Black Friday prezzie for the person who owns every novelty mug on Earth? Why not gift a palm-sized robot programmed to endure a relentless existential crisis on your desk?! Ladies and gentlemen – here is the Butter Bot.

Following a successful 2024 Kickstarter and two years of intensive engineering, creative tech studio CircuitMess is finally shipping its officially licensed Rick and Morty Butter Bot. And yes, theoretically, it will be able to pass you the butter. Better yet, it rolls around on rubber caterpillar tracks delivering deadpan commentary about the futility of its own existence. Yes please!
However, even though this grumpy little companion looks like the product of some of the best 3D printers out there, it will set you back $349. Yeah, it's for the ultra-fans only.

Inspired by a two-second gag from the intro of an Rick and Morty episode, Butter Bot started life as a cult Kickstarter project backed by 2,715 eager fans ($441,349 pledged). CircuitMess spent two years, and three electronics revisions plus custom steel moulds, turning that animated gag into a real, palm-sized AI desk robot.

And yes, of course this includes AI. Under the hood, it packs an onboard AI camera, dual microphones, edge sensors, and a remote controller featuring a live first-person video feed. Because its voice, face, and object recognition run on-device, it should recognise its owner, identify random desk clutter, read out phone notifications, tell jokes, control your TV, and – crucially – ferry sticks of butter across the table (though how the hell this is done is currently a mystery to me).

Left alone, it roams your workspace, avoids table edges, and loudly questions its own purpose. Pick it up and it panics; shake it and it disapproves; press the controller’s 'Poke' button and you’ll visibly irritate it.

Tinkerers can also snap on six modular add-ons, including an air-quality sensor, motion-sensing intruder alarm, and LED light show. O you can reprogram its open-source brain from scratch using C++ or CircuitBlocks (I'll leave that to the people in the know).
Available worldwide now at circuitmess.com for $349, it’s a wonderfully over-engineered piece of pop-culture hardware that can turn existential dread into festive cheer. If you can afford it!

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. As Ecom Editor on Creative Bloq, when he's not reviewing the latest audiophile headphones or evaluating the best designed ergonomic office chairs, he’s testing laptops, TVs and monitors, all so he can find the best tech deals for Creative Bloq’s digital professional audience.

items.title: Summer heatwave put bin crews lives at risk, says council worker
paragraphs: Goddard, the council's streetscene service manager, said: "We had maybe five or six operational challenges that all came at the same time in a perfect storm this summer.
"Unfortunately, the heatwave was one of them and it was a contributing factor. We do have to prioritise staff safety above all else.
"My number one job every day is to make sure that everybody goes home safely and we take that really seriously within streetscene. That was only one of several contributing factors.
"That level of change is naturally going to cause a few bumps in the road, particularly with staff being asked to do a little bit more. There were some staffing issues during that period too."
Councillors praised Flintshire residents for largely embracing three-weekly residual waste collections and ensuring that the authority remained on-target to hit its statutory recycling rate.
"Three-weekly was very controversial at the time it came in," said Saltney councillor Richard Lloyd.
"It's quite clear to see now that the three-weekly black bin collection has been a good new factor. Recycling has improved at the kerbside."
Councillors said in the authority's meeting the change to three-weekly bin collections meant the council should still hit target despite the disruption.
The council also cut the amount of waste it sent to landfill or Parc Adfer by 6,467.49 tonnes between 2024 and 2026, and that improvement continued this year despite problems this summer.

items.title: Colette Kress becomes Nvidia's interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigns
paragraphs: Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang is out, and the company's chief financial officer Colette Kress is taking over as interim CEO. She'll have to guide the company through an exceptionally challenging time.

items.title: Perforated brick walls envelop giant market in Kinshasa by Think Tank Architecture
paragraphs: French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

Think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.
Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet’s, offices and a food court.
“The new market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot,” Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.
“However, the building’s footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context,” it continued.

“We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa.”

Zando Central Market has a rectangular plan measuring 245 metres in length and 150 metres in width. It contains 650 shops with space for 20,000 vendors, which is “more than 5 times its original capacity”, according to the studio.
At its heart is the central covered market, spanning two double-height levels, with three large entrances and outward views used to orient visitors.
It is surrounded by a three-storey building containing the other facilities. Landscaped patios punctuate the plan, carving out space for public squares and informal markets to take place.
“It’s an important part of our approach to keep the building open to the public, including the more modest,” said Think Tank Architecture.

The material palette for the project comprises brick and concrete, chosen to be in keeping with the local context and skills of the region’s construction workers. Demolition waste from the original market was used in the substructure.
“We are quite happy to say that this project reactivated three terracotta factories within a 60-kilometre distance from the market,” reflected the studio.
It uses a mushroom-slab structural system, in which the columns flare at their top, referencing the original market’s design.
Meanwhile, the perforated brick facades were designed to facilitate natural ventilation and provide shade from the sun.
In tandem with the thermal mass from the concrete, this helps cool the building, minimising the need for technical cooling equipment and keeping project costs low.

Interior finishes were also kept deliberately simple for cost reasons. However, the perforations of the facades help add flourish, evoking moucharabiehs – a type of projecting oriel window enclosed with wooden latticework, typically seen in traditional Islamic architecture.

Zando Central Market is on the eight-strong shortlist for the civic project category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Sydney Fish Market by 3XN and TCC DAKA Renewable Resource Recycling Center by KPF.
It is yet to officially open, as the second phase of the project – involving the renovation of the surrounding streets – needs to be completed to allow access.

“This phase of works is under the city’s supervision and is going slower,” said Think Tank Architecture. “We hope, and it’s in our client’s interest, that the market will be able to open by the end of this year.”

Other market architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the multi-level Tepoztlán Market in central Mexico by local studios Ramírez Suarez Arquitectos and Laboratorio Regional de Arquitectura, and an open-air market in Colombia designed by Tarq Studio to accommodate community gatherings.
Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC

items.title: Farewell, Cybertruck: why the winding down of the ‘Maga hat on wheels’ is a sign of the times
paragraphs: Three days after a historic blue tsunami changed America’s political landscape, Elon Musk announced Tesla would end production of its hulking Cybertruck next year.

Was it a coincidence? Maybe. Musk said the move was “to make room for increased Cybercab production”, referring to Tesla’s Robotaxi. But the combined circumstances felt highly appropriate: it was the end of an era.

Eccentric and overhyped, the Cybertruck became a kind of automotive stand-in for Musk himself amid his political ascent. Like so many of his projects, it was massively promoted, heavily delayed, and ultimately fell short: Musk once predicted he could sell 250,000 a year but ultimately sold 70,000 in three years, losing $1.9bn in the process, according to Quartz.

The design seemed to prioritize science fiction over robust engineering: the unveiling was in November 2019, when the film Blade Runner was set, as Musk proudly pointed out – but it didn’t arrive on the roads until four years later. At that unveiling event, Musk infamously showed off the Cybertruck’s durability by having a designer throw a ball at its window, which cracked. While Musk called it apocalypse-proof, it often seemed like the opposite: Cybertrucks suffered at least five vehicle fires, four of them deadly – making them deadlier than the notorious Ford Pinto, according to an analysis. They were subject to 11 recalls amid technical issues, including a loose pedal that could get stuck and cause unintentional acceleration. They routinely got stuck in the snow.

Like its creator, the Cybertruck was highly divisive. Many observers were repulsed by its bizarre, boxy appearance and its road-hogging size (a parallel parking nightmare). “It is the ugliest vehicle I think I have ever laid eyes on,” the automotive expert Mike Caudill told Fox Business. Others, however, were deeply devoted to their Cybertrucks. “I’ve got 6,000 miles on my Cybertruck; I’ve had zero issues,” Matt Holm, president of the Tesla Owners Club of Austin, told the Houston Chronicle.

Indeed, the Cybertruck had its strong points, according to experts. “People at Tesla were rightly proud of the engineering they put into it,” said Ezra Dyer, a senior editor and columnist at Car and Driver. But “a lot of the engineering problems they solved were self-imposed” – driven by the need to incorporate Musk’s super-epic design choices.
“Why is that important to you that it be bulletproof?” Jay Leno asked Musk during a test drive. “Because it’s badass and super cool,” the CEO replied.

All this, of course, coincided with Musk’s political rise in the Trump administration. The truck, as the Guardian’s Andrew Lawrence put it, became essentially “a Maga hat on wheels”, indicating its driver’s political beliefs – or at least the politics onlookers would ascribe to them. The archetypal Cybertruck driver was a guy, “probably with some kind of goatee, likely compensating for something, so desperate for attention that he will take negative attention”, as an automotive analyst told the New York Times. Many drivers of various Tesla models rushed to distance themselves from the CEO with bumper stickers that say, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.”
The Cybertruck, meanwhile, “became this totem and symbol of Elon Musk himself”, says Dan Neil, an auto columnist for the Wall Street Journal.

While Cybertrucks took to the streets, Musk was taking a literal chainsaw to the US government as head of the department of government efficiency (Doge), which bore plenty of similarities to the truck, beginning with the empty promises. Musk said Doge could cut $2tn from the federal budget; its website now claims it has cut just $215bn. In the process, hundreds of thousands of workers left the government due to workforce reductions, early retirement and other reasons – before, in a move reminiscent of the Cybertruck’s recalls, many were rehired. And like the Cybertruck, it all came to an embarrassing end: Musk left government under a cloud as he feuded with Donald Trump over spending in his “big, beautiful bill”.

Now, when it comes to the Cybertruck, “you’ve got this expensive luxury product with a very off-putting aesthetic and all this political baggage,” Dyer says (the 2026 model runs from about $72,000 to $102,000). So it’s little surprise that sales have struggled. “It’s following the trajectory of any cult vehicle,” Dyer says. The hardcore fans line up, but once they’ve all got theirs, demand fizzles.

As it reaches the end of its short road, the Cybertruck – outwardly mighty, inwardly fragile, a poorly conceived product of an increasingly oligarchical system – feels alarmingly apt as a symbol of Trump 2.0 Phase I. Ten years from now, spotting an ageing Cybertruck on the street will serve as a reminder of the bad old days.
It will join the ranks of other vehicles symbolic of their eras – for better or for worse.

The Cybertruck is to the 2020s what the Volkswagen Transporter – AKA the VW Bus – is to the 1960s. In many ways, the two are opposites: the VW Bus calls forth images of peace and music, flower decals, and a crowd of well-meaning hippies packed inside. Sixty years after the summer of love, the Cybertruck suggests an isolated middle-aged man hiding from the apocalypse.
The vehicles do have a few things in common, however. One is drugs, but while the VW conjures cannabis, the Cybertruck is more ketamine. The other is a reputation for putting looks over safety.

A few decades later came another icon of its era – in many ways the progenitor to the Cybertruck: the Hummer H2, introduced in the early 2000s. Like the Cybertruck, the Hummer was inconveniently enormous and associated with a certain kind of aggressive masculinity.

And with its military ties and gas-guzzling reputation, it was bound up with imagery of the Iraq war. “It became a lightning rod for pro and con militarism, and so people drove them or bought them as a political statement as much as a style statement,” says Neil.

A similar perception may have plagued the Cybertruck, as Tesla showed off its ability to withstand bullets. “All of that was childish,” Neil says. “It didn’t speak with any seriousness to the mindset of people preparing to put down $80, $90,000.” The Cybertruck “represented a kind of a militarized vision of the future” to an American public tired of war.

As for Tesla’s clientele, “the wager was they were emotionally immature and it looked like a toy-slash-weapon,” Neil adds. Indeed, as the Guardian’s Arwa Mahdawi put it, the Cybertruck “looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old”. In that sense, it might best be compared to another icon of American vehicle design: the Little Tikes Cozy Coupe, the plastic red and yellow car that was for a time the bestselling vehicle in the world.
But perhaps that’s unfair. To Neil, the Cybertruck represents both a “failure of management” and “a phenomenal piece of engineering.
“Its ambition and its vision and its willingness to break the mold of convention – that I think is its legacy,” he says.

Dyer agrees. “I’m glad in a way that it exists because it’s interesting, and I’m in favor of more interesting cars. Period,” he says. In this case, however, that difference “is a towering monument to overconfidence.
“There’s never been anything like it,” Dyer adds, “and I guess there never will be again.”

items.title: Polestar Formula 2030 concept car "screams performance"
paragraphs: Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.

The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the company’s production cars in the coming years.
It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers said “scream performance”.
With signature “Dual Blade” headlights, the front of the car previews the face of the next-generation Polestar 2, a saloon scheduled to launch in 2027.

Meanwhile, the tail of the Formula 2030 mirrors the upcoming Polestar 7 crossover SUV, moving away from the continuous rear lightbar that has become widespread among electric cars in favour of separate “Single Blade” lights.
Unlike Polestar’s most recently released production vehicles, the Polestar 4 and Polestar 5, the Formula 2030 also has a conventional rear windscreen.
“Design should always reflect the values and mission of a brand and that is exactly what we did with Polestar Formula 2030 concept,” said Römers, who joined Polestar from Audi in January 2025.
“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”
At 1.35 metres tall, 4.68 metres long and 2.02 metres wide, the Formula 2030 has a very low roofline but a broad stance.
Its styling was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and substantial 22-inch wheels.
Other sporty design elements include a deep front splitter and a single vertical windscreen wiper.
The Formula 2030 showcases a newly developed paint colour called Nitrogen, with accents of gold dotted throughout the car.
Inside, the design echoes efforts in recent concept cars from other carmakers to emphasise the driving experience.
The cockpit features a curved screen band mounted above the steering wheel, presenting information to the driver.
Another screen is integrated into the centre console, which slopes gently up to the dashboard.

A sliding “drive mode selector” on the centre console would allow the car to alternate between three modes – Performance, Normal and Autonomous – changing the angle of the central screen, seating and steering wheel to allow for a more passive or active driving position.
The Formula 2030 embraces a wider trend in car design back towards incorporating physical buttons, rather than only touchscreens.

Also occupying the central console is an interface of eight large mechanical controls. These can be configured to the user’s preferences, with choices between different types of buttons and switches capable of being programmed for specific functions.

In a modest nod to sustainability, the seat backs are made from a bio-based composite combining European flax and bio-based polypropylene, while the insides of the doors are made from a single material in order to be recyclable.
Headquartered in Gothenburg, Polestar has emphasised design and sustainability since it was spun out of Volvo as a premium EV brand in 2017.

Amid heavy financial losses, it has increased its production of SUVs, which tend to be popular with consumers and deliver higher profit margins. SUVs or SUV-adjacent cars now account for three of the five models in its lineup.
SUVs are often associated with a greater environmental impact than other types of cars, but Polestar denies watering down its ambitions on sustainability.
According to its most recent sustainability report, published in April, the company is ahead of schedule on a target to halve greenhouse-gas emissions per vehicle sold between 2020 and 2030.
It is the only car brand that publishes life-cycle carbon assessments for all its models. Assessments for the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 have not yet been calculated.
“Learnings from the cars we have already produced will be channelled into the new cars to bring the CO2e figures in as low as possible,” a spokesperson told Dezeen.
In 2021, Polestar announced a project to produce a “truly climate-neutral car” by 2030. Earlier this year, it pushed this target back to 2035 owing to the “scale and complexity of the challenge”.
Other concept cars recently covered on Dezeen include the flying Tesla Roadster and a Fiat that transforms from an SUV into a pickup truck.

items.title: How do you redesign a cult kids’ product? I asked Yoto’s new designers
paragraphs: I’ve been obsessed with Yoto since 2019, when a friend introduced me to the tactile, lo-fi audio player for kids. My children have used it daily ever since, and it’s one of the most interesting brands out there. It arrived just as parents were looking for an alternative to endless high-stimulation screens, and it has grown from a community-led, Kickstarter-style product with its foibles into a polished, self-assured brand that still listens closely to its community.

So when I heard a new generation was on its way, I asked to speak to the design team behind the biggest shake-up of its physical design yet. It’s a fairly tricky proposition: a product used by children but invested in by parents, with a clear mission and a feature set that’s still evolving. The new players have a mischievous new look, a green dial (big news in the world of Yoto) and a few other added features. Most importantly, the design team and Yoto chose not to lean any harder on the screen’s capabilities. For families trying to rely less on screens, that’s a crucial decision.

Below is my conversation with Jack Godfrey Wood of design studio Heirloom, covering the design mission, how the players were prototyped and tested, and the challenge of designing for a product with such a clear purpose and such a vocal community.

We knew people there. One of our colleagues worked on the original Kickstarter version, the wooden cube with the two blue dials, and two of our team designed the later generations at another company. When we started Heirloom, we took on the current fourth-gen players, so our team has been involved in and out from the beginning. It made sense straight away, because we all had that Fisher-Price cassette deck as kids and this felt like this generation’s version. Once Tom and Ben showed us the community they’d built, I knew it would work.

There were technical aims and design aims. Yoto wanted more storage, more battery and more internal robustness, and they wanted the player to be splashproof. That meant a lot of work on keeping dust and liquid out. Inside, the downloads are faster, there’s more storage and the sound is better, so they’ve fixed the things I wanted fixed as a parent. Our job was to make the players fit better in kids’ hands, travel better, and be easier to hold, carry and drop without anything breaking.
Where did your design decisions come from?

Both the community and our own experience, plus writing some rules. Yoto’s core goal is “kids in control and parents in charge”. We also knew we didn’t want addictive, distracting moments. Both screens have more resolution than before, but we kept everything in pixel world, because to us that’s Yoto. It’s a fun menu, not a distracting screen. We could have added motion, like a character that waves at you if nothing happens for 15 minutes, but we felt the community would say that was wrong.
Does Yoto’s approach feel different to other consumer tech clients?

Yes. Yoto’s goal isn’t to keep eyeballs on the screen. It’s how often the player gets used and whether it adds value to a child’s and a family’s life. It’s a very clear moral code, which makes design decisions easier. A lot of the pixel work we did is artful, precise and beautiful, but we kept it happily lo-fi and didn’t turn it into another Apple product.

Yoto wanted the backup content stored in each player to be available on the player itself. That way, if you can’t find the card, your kids can still listen to what they like, and you don’t have to get your phone out at 9pm when nobody’s going to bed. The hard part was doing that without turning the screen into an iPod or an iPad.

It was our way of giving kids access to what they want without overwhelming them with 200 cards. Daily radio and podcasts have moved onto it, along with 20 favourites. It populates automatically, but parents can set up day and night versions in the app. At night, all 20 can be sleep or relaxation content. In the daytime, you can have Elton John and Harry Potter. It also means your favourites are there wherever you go, which is really good for holidays. We still love cards, though. In all our research, they’re still the main way younger kids want to use it.

For one of the players, up to 10 to 15 concepts across a few different areas. When we gave the more pebbly form to some children, it was obvious how naturally it fitted their hands and how much they wanted to hold on to it, so we presented that one with a strong recommendation. For the other, we looked at five or six directions, but Yoto wanted it to feel like a continuation of the previous products. The concept was quite singular, and we spent a lot of time on the detailing: where the dials sit, how sharp they should be, and so on.
What did you change about the dials and finish?

The dials used to be crisp. We softened them so kids can reach them from different angles, and made them slightly longer for more grip. The smart button isn’t in the middle, which most designers would do. Because it’s a kids’ product, kids can use it from the front as they hold it.
How do you work with such an opinionated community?

Because we’re external to Yoto, they do most of the community work and the feedback is funnelled to us through the Yoto team. We’re forthright about what we think is right within Yoto’s mission, and we don’t try to do everything people ask for. The challenge is that the community is always ageing up, but we also have to look after new families who’ve never used Yoto. A new user shouldn’t have to learn anything, and an existing user shouldn’t be thrown off because every feature suddenly does something else. The community’s feedback is great because it comes from hard-won experience, not assumptions.

By keeping the mischief, fun and wonder, and the underdog spirit, rather than suddenly feeling like a big corporation. My favourite bits are the hidden details. There are little faces between the dials, and the charging cable has four tiny Yoto logos, one of which is winking. No one’s going to talk about it, but one day someone will spot it and get a little flutter of appreciation.

Georgia has worked on Creative Bloq since 2018, and has been the site's Editor since 2023. With a specialism in branding and design, Georgia is also Programme Director of CB's award scheme – the Brand Impact Awards. As well as immersing herself with the industry through attending events like Adobe Max and the D&AD Awards and steering the site's content streams, Georgia has an eye on new commercial opportunities and ensuring they reflect the needs and interests of creatives.

items.title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
paragraphs: Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.

After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.
Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.

Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.

Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.

A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

items.title: National Trust takes back land for nature restoration
paragraphs: Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the owners.

The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge".
There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period.
The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit.

Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge".

Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like."
The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come.
Community drop-in sessions about the vision, external will be held between Saturday 21 November and Friday 27 November.
Feedback will be used to help inform the next stage of planning before proposals are developed during 2027.

items.title: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run
paragraphs: Fast rising pop star Skye Newman began her November five-gig run at Brixton Academy on Thursday - a record for a British female solo artist
The BBC Sound of 2026 winner is set to overtake rapper Little Simz, who headlined three nights at the legendary south London venue in 2021.
It will cap an incredible few years for Brit Award nominee Newman, 23, who performed at Radio 1's Big Weekend in Sunderland, external last month.

Speaking to BBC News's Mark Savage ahead of her record-breaking run, Newman said it had given her "goosebumps and chills". She added: "It's crazy. My jaw drops all the time. I feel honoured to be the first woman, and I don't take it lightly."

Born in south-east London, the "loud, raw and strikingly honest" Newman - according to our music correspondent - exploded onto the scene last year when her debut single, Hairdresser, went straight into the top 20.
The follow-up, Family Matters, reached number five in June. It was the first time a female artist had made the top 20 with their first two singles since Ella Henderson in 2014.
The husky-voiced soul and R&B singer has previously supported Ed Sheeran and Lewis Capaldi on tour, and been called "incredibly talented" and "something else" by Sir Elton John.
Now she stands on the shoulders of pop giants.
Watch: The BBC's Mark Savage sat down with Skye Newman after she won BBC Radio 1's Sound of 2026
Historically, US pop-punk icon Debby Harry and Romy Croft, frontwoman of the band The XX have also enjoyed big Brixton residencies, as well as Phoebe Bridgers, Chappell Roan and Tash Sultana.
But after three more gigs this weekend and one added one next, Newman will newly lead the way for UK female solo stars at one of the country's most prestigious venues.
She also insists on having an all-female band on stage with her.
"Women are the centre of my world," she said. "They're the people that built me. They allowed me space to grow and find myself. So, I definitely had to take that out on stage with me.
"I had to stand by what I stand by. It's quite scary at the minute how much social media is [affecting how women are being treated] so I'm just really big on trying to keep women everywhere."
She continued: "If I can have a woman in place, I will. I'll give a job out. I'll give my helping hand always."

Newman recently paid tribute to another soulful London singer to have graced the same space back in 2007, the late Amy Winehouse, with a rendition of her song Addicted during a special Back to Black anniversary gig for the BBC.
"The thing with Amy's music is it's so incredible that you don't want to touch it," she admitted.

"No-one would ever do it like Amy, and I think it was definitely scary for all of us... that feeling of, you've got to live up to that expectation. You've got to fill her shoes, and they're big shoes to fill.
"But I think we all smashed it, and I think it was honestly the most beautiful, inspirational day I've had in a very long time."

Next month she will head off to Australia with Harry Styles for a series of support slots, which the childhood One Direction fan says is "surreal", and something she agreed to with "no questions asked".
"'Whatever I've got, cancel it'," she joked she had told her team on hearing about the request.
"It felt like a dream because I was the age of One Direction [fans], so that was around when I was a child and obviously I loved them and Harry and Zane were my favourites.
"So then now to go and support Harry Styles is just mental."

items.title: Brand will face 'hell on earth' in Wandsworth prison, says former inmate
paragraphs: Russell Brand has been in HMP Wandsworth for a week
Russell Brand will face "hell on earth" inside HMP Wandsworth, a former inmate at the London prison has said.
Brand, 51, was convicted a week ago of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault and was sentenced on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison.
He is currently being held at the South London jail, which is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons.
Chris Atkins, who served eight months at HMP Wandsworth for tax fraud, described the prison as "hell on earth".

He continued: "The first month is hands-down the worst. The mental shock is absolutely colossal. It was colossal for me and it's going to be 10 times worse for him because of the nature of his offences and the height from which he's fallen.
"He has to come to terms with it and the pure physical shock of suddenly being trapped in a dungeon for weeks on end with nobody to talk to most of the time is ghastly."
A source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing in the prison.
A member of staff at Wandsworth said there was "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival.

"Prisons are boring and Russell Brand being in their space has given them some fun - they've been slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. He is a rapist, so there's also been some anger about what he's done.
"We're very aware of that feeling," they said.
Brand will have had his possessions confiscated when he arrived at HMP Wandsworth
Brand is likely to still be in a cell on his own. It would usually have a bed, a basin and a toilet. He may have a television and kettle depending on where in the prison he is housed.

On arrival, Brand's possessions will have been confiscated. That will include his mobile phone, clothing, and any other valuables. He will have been issued with a grey prison tracksuit - a uniform that has been described by some of those who've been inside as "itchy" and "often the wrong size".

The former media personality and comedian will have been given a night pack. It contains items such as biscuits, teabags, a small bag of cereal, some sugar and a carton of milk. According to the charity, Prison Reform Trust, this is to help inmates until they can buy goods from the prison shop.
Brand, who has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, would be able to register for the weekly Sunday service in the prison chapel, inmates said.
"Many sign up just to get out of their cell," one added. They said Brand could probably get regular time with the prison chaplain, if he wanted.

Inmates receive money through prison work or from their family. But several former prisoners have told the BBC there are a limited number of jobs in places like workshops, laundry rooms and libraries.
They say it is much harder for sex offenders to get work because their conviction means they are more at risk of assault from mixing with other inmates.
Staff at other prisons say Brand's fame and the offences he has been convicted of could make him a target among other inmates.
Sex offenders are often among those most at risk of being attacked. One prison governor said: "When a trial gets plenty of publicity it highlights the crimes the offender has committed.
"This in turn makes him vulnerable to the inmates own 'justice' system of arbitrary beatings and assaults, especially where sex crimes are involved."
The South London jail is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons

The prison paperwork is also said to be a huge challenge for newcomers. Getting permission to make phone calls and filling out visitor requests can take a long time and have to go through the system to be signed off.

Atkins said: "He won't have anyone set up on his visitor account - visitors need a series of checks. Phone numbers need to be approved. These checks are not quick and you need to know how to make these applications.
"There is often nobody there to tell you how this all works so you have to work it out." He said it took five weeks to see his young son.
It's just days since Brand was sentenced to more than a decade in prison.
At this stage nobody knows what the future holds for him. In time he may be transferred to a different jail with a less harsh regime and more modern facilities.
The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.

items.title: ‘Hurry, hurry, get your tickets now!’ The last of the great Australian showmen – photo essay
paragraphs: My uncle Teddy Trevor remembers Casey Nelson, a fellow showman, spruiking his double-jointed horse to sideshow punters in the 1960s. The horse, Nelson warned, was “showing here for the last time”. “Too late, too late will be the cry, when Happy Harry has passed you by,” he called. The act continued for another two decades.
The Casey Nelson tent show, featuring Happy Harry the double-jointed horse, circa the late 1940s

I’ve been hearing stories like this my whole life. Ted laughs at Casey’s line as he pours another cup of tea and passes the biscuits at the kitchen table of the family home in Brisbane. At 91, after a lifetime in Australia’s travelling shows, he has no desire to quit the showgrounds yet. While their mid-century heyday may have passed, these grounds are still the lifeblood of his friendships and family.

Ted feels blessed, he says, to belong to two great show families: the Trevors, circus people on his father’s side, and the Fosters, sideshow people on his mother’s. Born on the showgrounds in 1935, he comes from more than eight generations of show folk.
Ted in his kitchen with his cockatiel, Sweetie Pie

Ted’s grandmother Cora Trevor performed an iron-jaw act, hanging upside-down and spinning grown men by her teeth, including her 14-stone (88kg) acrobat father. My great-grandmother Alice Foster, known as LuLu, arrived in Australia in 1913. She was a widow with six sons and a daughter. Lulu kept her whole family fed while running a dancing duck as a sideshow act.

Clockwise from top left: Ted Trevor aged five; Cora Trevor Williams, Ted’s grandmother, performing an ‘iron-jaw’ act; Billy and Vera (left), who performed trapeze and iron-jaw acts, and Ted’s grandmother, Cora (right); Ted’s mother, Frances ‘Girly’ Foster, on stilts on Pitt Street, Sydney

Uncle Teddy’s own entry into work coincided with the second world war, which brought the showgrounds to a halt. He started his career selling fabric door to door from my grandmother’s vardo caravan. As a young man in the 1950s, he worked with my uncle Frank Foster, promoting Slim Dusty’s tent show on the sideshow alley. Those days were hectic. “You start at nine in the morning, you don’t finish till after 11 at night, and you do a show every 20 minutes,” Ted tells me.

“The show was a big event for the town,” Ted says – the biggest day of the year for some places. The men wore suits, hats and ties, the women their best dresses. “Now they go in a pair of shorts and thongs,” he says.
‘The reason they call it the old-time showman is because that’s exactly what it was. You had to be a showman to work with whatever you got’

Teddy says the atmosphere of the sideshow was what everyone came to the show for. He can still recite the lines they used to entice the crowds: “The Slim Dusty show is just about to start! Australia’s top country-and-western recording star, the only Australian to top the hit parade in England, our only gold record-holder, is on this next big program. Hurry boys, hurry girls, get your tickets now! The cowboys, the cowgirls, the knife-throwers, the jugglers, you’ll see and meet them all on the inside.”

Uncle Teddy says that between the advent of TV, RSL clubs offering sideshow talent a new touring strategy, and state-based showground permits hindering showpeople from pivoting beyond the scope of their trade (for example, a clown joint can only do clown business), the landscape of the showgrounds drastically changed in the early 1970s.
Frances Foster with Slim Dusty at the Brisbane Exhibition in the early 1960s
Performers could sing half a dozen songs at an RSL, Ted tells me, “for what three or four days and hundreds of songs paid them on a sideshow”.

Participator numbers also declined, while costs climbed, he says. The big rides came in, worth millions. “The showgrounds are saturated with equipment now,” he says. “There’s no more ground available, so there’s no permits for the young showman.”

The cost escalated, too. “They’re charging $12 for a game on the clown joint. It’s all ridiculous,” he says. In Ted’s day, it used to be “only four bob [40 cents] to go and see the show”. Some shows were three shillings, and a shilling for a child. As he puts it: “The money was sort of nothing.”
Ted in his pool room, where all his favourite photographs are on display
In the last couple of years, I had seen Uncle Teddy posting diary-like entries on Facebook, sharing his memories along with photographs It led me to ask him some more questions.

Uncle Teddy often says: “I’m sorry you were born a bit late to see the action.” It’s clear he thinks I’d have loved it. He describes the camaraderie of the sideshow community, with everyone pitching in when they were needed. “Everyone’s got to do their own thing,” he says. “The stars have got to get out in the middle of the night and knock pegs in if a storm’s coming up.”

From left: Shayne Brophy, who was born and bred on the showgrounds, performing a trapeze act. She also did contortions, whip-cracking, wire-walking, and worked in the snake pit; Jan Foster in a knife act in the Foster’s big tent show in the late 1960s. Johnny Foster’s son Pikey was the one throwing the knives, and no one dared to be the target except Jan, his wife. Over many years and thousands of knives thrown, the worst she suffered was one small nick to the ear; Ted’s twin daughters, Sonia and Tracy Trevor, working on their Knock ’Em Can joint in the early 1980s
“I always loved the showgrounds because of the people,” Ted says.
My cousins still travel the showground runs, working joints, food trucks and rides. The skills of a modern showman are totally different from the past.

“Today you buy a $2m ride and you don’t have to be a showman,” he says. “People either like the ride or they don’t. It’s just got to be a spectacular ride, a thrill ride, and they’ll queue up and go on it … it’s a different ballgame.[Showpeople] don’t have to get up and tell a tale. They just say, ‘Next ride, hurry now, get your tickets for the next big ride,’ and that’s it.”

These days, Uncle Teddy visits his friends and family at the Beenleigh or Brisbane shows, and chats on the phone to his friends across Australia. “You get friends in different towns. You meet their kids, and when you get old, you meet their grandchildren, and they all become like family.”

I take my own child to the Royal Easter Show when it’s on in Sydney, and the moment I spot a laughing-clown joint, I half expect to see Uncle Teddy come around the corner, his eyes sparkling, a joke on his lips and coins jingling in his waist pouch. I tell them the stories Ted told me, alive with dancing ducks and my iron-jawed great-grandmother. Their eyes widen the way mine did at Ted’s kitchen table, and the show rolls on to another generation.

items.title: Flood victim, 95, lived in Wetherspoons after her home was destroyed and died before she could return
paragraphs: Jean Powell was temporarily staying in one of Monmouth Wetherspoons' guest rooms while her flat was being refurbished after it was flooded a year ago
ByPeter ShuttleworthReporting fromMonmouth and Lucy VladevBBC Wales
When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home.

Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales last November.
But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded.
"Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that."
The BBC report from November 2025 when Monmouth town centre was hit by severe flooding after Storm Claudia
Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of November 15 last year as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours.

It has been officially described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in Monmouth during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town.

Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her.
"She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms most days.
"The Wetherspoons staff were brilliant with Jean, they'd take her food and really looked after her."
Wyn Smith helped her neighbours to safety when floodwaters swamped their block of flats in Monmouth and now she's awaiting their return as renovations near the end
"We never thought she'd be there that long," said Wyn. "It's nobody's fault, it took a long time to dry her home out. It had to be done properly."
Residents have been with family, some are in rented accommodation, some have been in an Airbnb while another is in a care home.
Their story is typical of many in Monmouth who have been out of their home since Claudia struck - and that trauma and anxiety from the devastation of 12 months ago is never far from the surface.
"Some had been through the war and they said it upset them more than that. It was just awful," said Wyn.
This was how ground floor residents in Jean's Chippenham Court retirement complex found their flats after Storm Claudia
"But unfortunately it could happen again. There's that fear. If they see water coming, it'll freak them out. They need to feel at home and not worry about the weather."
The Met Office estimates that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events.

Wales' environmental body has warned long-range forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual this winter with Natural Resources Wales (NRW) saying people should prepare for "the unthinkable".
Monmouth's main shopping street was submerged after the nearby River Monnow burst its banks as it reached record levels during Storm Claudia

Apart from three nights at the local Premier Inn over Christmas when Wetherspoons was shut - where Jean had sandwiches from the nearby petrol station for Christmas dinner because she wanted to "remain independent" - she stayed above the pub in the town's main square for almost 10 months.
"As time went on, living in one room was awful for her," recalled Wyn, 70.
"When Jean got ill, it wasn't a place for her to live. Her health deteriorated and she didn't come back home, which is sad."
Jean's death will be acutely felt when the first displaced residents return to the Chippenham Court retirement complex she called home following its £1m refurbishment in the next few weeks.
Emily Frost recalls how she had to wake her two boys in the middle of the night and evacuate their family home before it was flooded during Storm Claudia last year

One in seven properties in Wales are at risk of flooding, including the Frost household on the other side of Monmouth where Emily says she and her young family will never recover from being evacuated on a lifeboat last year.
The mum-of-two breaks down as she recalls being woken by the coastguard telling her she's got five minutes to evacuate her family as the floodwaters surge towards her end-of-terrace cottage.
"Opening the door, I completely freaked out to the lifeguard," Emily told the BBC.

"They were waist deep in water and said our house was at risk. I just needed to get our boys, who were then aged three and five, and they'd be back with a raft. We didn't have time to think about it."
What was supposed to be a night of celebration for her and husband Jake's 10th wedding anniversary, turned into a nightmare.
This was what Emily Frost saw of her house on the left of this picture as she looked back while their family were evacuated on a life raft during Monmouth's flooding in November 2025
Emily and Jake didn't take their boys when they returned home the following day where more than a foot of water had penetrated their home.
"There was sludge and mud everywhere," she recalled.
"We didn't bring the boys home for a good while because we didn't want them seeing everything that they'd treasured had been destroyed.
"It was the toll it would take on them that worried us the most."
The Frosts lived in rental accommodation nearby for six months as they ripped out the downstairs of their home and started again.
Emily and Jake, who had also been flooded in 2020, have seen their boys "playing floods" so know their children have been "trying to process" their ordeal.
This was Emily Frost's kitchen the day after her family home was flooded for the second time in five years
"They couldn't really understand why we weren't able to go home or have their things" said Emily.

"Because it's the time of year, even now when it rains they'll ask "are we staying home, is it okay? Luckily they're resilient as kids, but you still worry. People don't recover, it's something you'll just live with."

Environmental bodies estimate about 275,000 properties in Wales are at risk of flooding with another 400,000 in Scotland, while in England about 6.3 million properties - around 11.3m people - live in flood risk areas.

An official report said the River Monnow swelled to more than six-and-a-half metres after significant rainfall locally and upstream over the Black Mountains during a week where more than half-a-dozen Met Office rain warnings were issued.
Jennifer and Alan Morgan's 18th Century cottage near the banks of the Monnow had two more doors to hang after a five-year renovation when Claudia struck and they had to start it all again.
Alan and Jennifer Morgan said they spent their life savings renovating the house Alan grew up in and has been in his family for three generations so "it means a lot to us"
"I've not slept well for a year as it's been an absolutely living nightmare," said Jennifer, 70.
"The flooding was awful and the renovation has been so stressful, it's had a huge impact on us. We're not anywhere near to going back home, we probably won't be in until next summer.
"People might think because some of the shops and businesses are open that Monmouth is back to as it was before, but that's not the case - and we're proof."
The River Monnow burst its banks and the official report into the flood said floodwater reached depths 1.5m high, almost 2.5m in some extreme cases

The official Section 19 report, external into the flooding said flood warnings - where action is required as properties are in danger of flooding - were issued for all of Monmouth hours before the floods hit.
Wales' highest state of flood alert - the "risk to life and significant disruption" severe flood warning - was issued by NRW for the northern part of Monmouth on the Friday evening.

The severe flood warning for the rest of Monmouth was issued at 03:31 on the Saturday morning - but that was more than two hours after its flood defences were breached and after shops and homes had been flooded.

Emily had signed up to NRW's free flood alert service, external but went to bed because at midnight the rain had stopped and there was no water visible - half an hour before her young family were evacuated.

Prince William was in the Monmouth area last month visiting communities affected by the 2025 flooding caused by extreme weather conditions and met with Natural Resources Wales, the Welsh Government and Monmouthshire County Council
"When it stopped raining everyone probably thought 'oh well this has passed and we don't need to worry'," she said.
"Then the deluge of water just appeared from nowhere. It just shows how quickly it can change."
The official report recommended a review of the timing of severe flood warnings throughout the Monnow catchment "to ensure adequate advance notice is provided for people to respond effectively."
It also called for a review on the "uptake and understanding" of the flood warning service for those who live and work near the River Monnow.
NRW has said it reviews their "response, recovery and flood warning thresholds" after every serious incident to "identify lessons".
Of the one in seven properties in Wales classed as being at risk of flooding, NRW said less than a third of those eligible to receive flood warnings to their phone or email were currently signed up.
This is how the River Monnow usually looks at Monmouth but it swelled to 18-times its normal depth in November 2025 after torrential downpours during Storm Claudia

NRW argues Wales' geography makes it particularly vulnerable - with a vast coastline and "fast-responding" rivers which can fill at speed as rain runs off steep terrain in places like the south Wales valleys.
The official report also recommended a review into whether Monmouth town centre defences are fit for purpose.
"We're looking at our flood modelling and if there's anything else that can be done," said Sara Pearson of NRW.
"We're seeing flooding that we've never experienced before and with climate change that's set to increase. We can't prevent flooding, but we can help minimise the impact."
The Welsh Government has said it is spending almost £1.4m in flood risk management in Monmouthshire, including £700,000 of NRW funding for works at nearby Skenfrith.
"We have made £85m available this year to Natural Resources Wales and local authorities for flood and coastal erosion schemes across Wales," the government said in a statement.
NRW have said they've done work to clear rivers while the local council insist they've got more workers out clearing ditches, gullies and drains.
Storm Claudia devastated the residents of Monmouth in November 2025 when the historic market town was hit by the worst floods in living memory
"We know how serious this is and how worrying it is for people," said Catrin Maby of Monmouthshire council.

"If it was only down to drain clearance we wouldn't need to worry. We need to look at the engineered defences again, we need to look at how we manage the land, we need to allocate sufficient resources into drainage and clearing those drains."

Insurance companies in the UK paid out £565 million to help homeowners recover from storms and floods in 2025 - and Emily's home is one of them with flood defence measures in place like flood gates and flood doors after advice from Flood Mary, external.
"I feel safer," added Emily. "I'll still be very apprehensive when you get the flood alert, it's whether you're gonna go back to that time or not.
"But you don't feel safe, which you should do in your own house."

items.title: How many sewage spills have happened in your part of Scotland?
paragraphs: It is difficult to assess how the numbers compare to the previous year's figures, when 24,000 spills were recorded because of lower coverage.

The sites are all licensed to release untreated or partially-treated waste but just under 12% of overflows are legally required to report their data to the regulator, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).
Sepa said it has a "risk-based approach" which prioritises areas for monitoring based on population and environmental need.
However, none of the new monitors were required to be reported to Sepa.
Scottish Water figures, external show that Glasgow's River Clyde was one of the most impacted waterways in Scotland last year, receiving almost 6,150 spills - or the equivalent of 17 a day.
When adding in the Clyde Estuary, Firth of Clyde and other unnamed tributaries that run into the Clyde's waterways, this almost doubles to nearly 14,200, or 39 a day.
The Clyde Estuary also recorded the longest duration of spills - more than 25,000 hours - followed by the River Clyde with more than 15,000 hours.
Barcloy Mill Burn in Dumfries and Galloway, which is one of the newly-monitored sites, received the most spills last year, with a total of almost 3,500.
The data suggests that 225 sites recorded no spills and 525 recorded fewer than 10. There may also be errors which suggest a monitor is active when it is not.

items.title: Ukraine looks to international partners to cover growing financing needs
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.

More than 40 leaders of European countries gathered in Ireland for a summit Thursday, with discussions centering around European security and the need to support Ukraine amid increased attacks by Russia on its infrastructure and businesses.

Funding for Ukraine was a top issue in Europe in the run up to the two-day European Pollical Community and the informal European Council summit. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged the European Union to find the money to meet request from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine for an additional $77 billion for the next year.

In his letter to European Council President António Costa, earlier this week, Merz called the new aid an "essential prerequisite" for approving the next EU budget. The content of the letter was first reported by the Financial Times.

The leaders of Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria have already voiced their opposition to linking approval of the EU’s budget to any new funding for Ukraine, which may delay the approval of the money.

Following the meeting with Zelenskyy on Thursday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen assured the Ukrainian leader of the EU's support, covering immediate survival this winter and funds needed through 2027. She announced the European Council will review the Commission's proposal for Ukraine's financing needs by the end of the month.

To alleviate immediate financial pressure, Ukraine hopes to obtain $1.67 billion in fresh funding from the International Monetary Fund by the end of the year. IMF's Director of the Communications Department, Julie Kozack told reporters on October 29 that the money will be released once the IMF completes assessment of its program in Ukraine. The IMF has started the review of the program for Ukraine on Monday.

The U.S., as the most powerful member of the IMF, supports the current Fund's program for Ukraine, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced earlier this year (in April) when met he with Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko.

"Secretary Bessent underscored President Trump’s efforts for a lasting peace for Ukraine, and highlighted the United States’ support for Ukraine’s new IMF program and for the progress that Ukraine has made on its reforms," a Treasury Department statement said.
An analyst told VOA staying on track with the IMF program is an important anchor for Ukraine to secure support from other international partners.

“There are other partners who support us much more,” Yuliya Markuts, head of the Center for Public Finance and Governance at the Kyiv School of Economics, said. “But the IMF is an anchor that demonstrates to our partners that Ukraine is indeed a country they can work with, they can trust and treat as a reliable partner. Therefore, Ukraine is very much dependent on having an IMF program.”

Over the past several months, Ukraine's parliament has approved several laws envisaged by the program. Markuts says she is “cautiously optimistic” that Ukraine will obtain the favorable review from the IMF.
If Ukraine does not get the fresh funding, the situation could be dire, said Markuts, as Ukraine has virtually no room to cut spending.

“This is actually a very difficult situation. Because shelling is taking place constantly. There are ongoing problems with critical infrastructure, particularly energy infrastructure,” Markuts said. “We have to provide the people living in this country with heating, water, electricity, and so on.”
Markuts stated that Ukraine's current investment is geared towards endurance and providing basic services to its people through the war.
