Timothy Ash, chief strategist of BlueBay Asset Management, believes that the IMF supports maintaining the program.

“But the IMF operates in a certain way - the program has to be sustainable," he told VOA. He highlighted that this would require financing assurances from Ukraine’s allies “that those gaps will be met."
Ash says he is confident that Ukraine will be able to secure funding from European partners, despite the opposition from some EU members.

“The big economies in Europe totally get it. Europe has figured out that Ukraine is central to its security in its long-term defense," he said. "Europe needs time to build autonomous defense capability, and the longer Ukraine survives in this war, the longer Europe has to build that autonomous defense capability. So, Europe has an interest now in helping Ukraine defend itself and Europe,” he adds.

items.title: US-based Russian activist sentenced to 6 years in absentia for "military fakes"
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

A court in Ulan-Ude, Russia, has sentenced U.S.-based activist and researcher Maria Vyushkova in absentia to six years in prison on a charge of allegedly “spreading knowingly false information” about the Russian armed forces.
"The kind of persecution in absentia and then attempts to put pressure on relatives who remained in Russia" are now becoming more widespread, Vyushkova VOA's Russian service.

The case stemmed from her research on the killings of hundreds of civilians in Bucha, Ukraine, in March of 2022. Russia has consistently denied any involvement in the killings and has called the evidence staged.
Some media accounts at the time singled out Buryat soldiers in the Russian army as being responsible. Buryats are an Indigenous people who live mainly in southern Siberia near the Mongolian border.

Vyushkova, herself a Buryat, argued that Russian paratroopers from Pskov were in Bucha at the time of the killings. The court said it found her statements were motivated by political hatred, according to the independent outlet Glasnaya.

Vyushkova, a citizen of the Russian Federation and the United States, is one of the co-founders of the Free Buryatia Foundation, which has been recognized in Russia as an "undesirable", "terrorist" and "extremist" organization.
In April 2026, the Russian authorities put Vyushkova on the register of foreign agents, and in July, the Ministry of Internal Affairs put her on the wanted list.
Vyushkova, who lives in the United States and has not traveled to Russia for many years, says she is surprised by the attention of the Russian authorities to her activities.

She says she believes that "this is part of a large, coordinated campaign against activists from regional ethnic groups, because this case was opened against me in the summer of 2026 for an interview that I gave in the summer of 2023."
Vyushkova says she plans to completely ignore the sentencing. "I do not recognize any right of the Russian authorities to put me on trial, to accuse me of something and to judge me," she told VOA.

items.title: Explainer: From undercover employment to corporate data breaches: the "Combating Foreign Threats to Main Street Act"
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

A bipartisan bill that could help U.S. small businesses recognize threats from foreign adversaries, including the risk posed by North Korean workers posing as job candidates, was debated and passed in the House of Representatives on Wednesday. It now moves on to the Senate.

The core provision requires the Small Business Administration to develop and distribute educational materials so that businesses can recognize the risks identified by the U.S. government and learn how to respond.

Its official title is the “Combating Foreign Threats to Main Street Act of 2026." It requires the Small Business Administration to guide businesses on how to identify, prevent, and respond to threats. The bill requires the SBA to develop materials in collaboration with relevant agencies and distribute them through regional offices and existing support programs. The SBA would be expected to use its existing budget to produce new materials.

Rep. Roger Williams, a Republican from Texas’s 25th Congressional District and chairman of the House Small Business Committee, is leading the effort. Williams has specifically identified China, Russia and North Korea as foreign threats the legislation seeks to address. Explaining the need for the bill, he said that “while many small businesses are exposed to foreign threats, they lack the resources and expertise to respond.”
Rep. Derek Tran, a Democrat representing California’s 45th Congressional District, is also involved in the effort. He serves on the House Small Business and Armed Services committees.
Why Is This Important for Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises?
“Even small companies have technology and information that needs to be protected”, according to the proposed bill.

For example, even a small software company may have programs it developed in-house. “If a manufacturer’s blueprints or customer and business partner information are leaked, it could harm the business”.
Chairman Williams’ office explained that “many small businesses lack the resources or expertise to identify and respond to increasingly sophisticated threats”.
The bill goes beyond simply alerting businesses to risk; it also provides guidance on prevention methods and where to seek assistance.
It includes guidelines to ensure that while risks are assessed when conducting business or receiving investments overseas, legitimate commercial activities are not unnecessarily restricted.

The bill relies on the Commerce Department’s definition of “foreign adversary,” which includes North Korea. While it does not specifically address North Korea’s use of covert IT workers in U.S. companies, its coverage of cyber intrusions and its catch-all provision for emerging threats could allow the SBA to include such schemes.
During hiring: North Korean IT workers misrepresent their identities and actual work locations to secure remote work positions.
Once hired: They gain access to the company’s computer networks and the data necessary to perform their duties.
If that access is abused: It can lead to the theft of corporate information or extortion.

Last January, the FBI warned of a case in which North Korean IT personnel stole sensitive corporate data and program source code from a company and, after being discovered, used this as leverage to demand money.
In July of the same year, the FBI stated that companies that outsource IT work to third-party vendors may face additional vulnerabilities because they cannot directly manage the hiring process.
This alert is directed at U.S. companies in general. It does not mean that all affected companies are small and medium-sized enterprises.
What kind of assistance will companies receive?
The bill requires the SBA to guide companies on how to protect intellectual property, trade secrets, sensitive corporate information, and supply chains.
The proposed bill covers not only cybersecurity but also the import of goods produced through forced labor, counterfeit goods and illicit trade, and predatory investment practices.
The bill now moves to the Senate. There is currently no Senate version of the bill, and this session of Congress ends in early January.
- September 10: The bill was introduced by Rep. Roger Williams (R-Texas), with Rep. Derek Tran (D-Calif.) as the Democratic co-sponsor.
- September 16: The House Small Business Committee voted 22–0 to recommend the bill to the full House.
- October 9: The committee’s official report was submitted.
- November 11: Passed by a voice vote. The Senate must approve it with the same wording, and the President must sign it.

items.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
paragraphs: Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.
It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.

Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious.

Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one.

The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it.

First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration, will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job.

Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed.

Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors.

Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive.

Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns as US lawmakers push tougher chip export controls
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday following controversy surrounding an extramarital affair and concerns about potential national security risks, as members of Congress urge tighter restrictions on exports of advanced SI (commonly referred to as AI) chips.
Nvidia has named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO.

The resignation comes amid growing concerns about possible national security risks linked to Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former executive at Singapore-based technology company Megaspeed. U.S. intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang of gathering information for Beijing.
The developments have intensified scrutiny of Nvidia's business ties to China and renewed calls in Congress for tighter restrictions on exports of advanced super intelligence chips.
U.S. lawmakers from both parties are pushing to include new restrictions in the annual National Defense Authorization Act, or NDAA, which Congress hopes to pass before the end of the year.
The House Select Committee on China, led by Republican Representative John Moolenaar, called for stronger export controls following Huang’s resignation.

“Jensen Huang’s firing from the company he founded is an unfortunate end that could have been avoided,” Moolenaar said in a statement, “Nvidia must now change its corporate practices and appoint leadership that makes national security its top priority. In Congress we must act quickly to pass bipartisan export control legislation in the year-end national defense bill.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, told Politico that he supports adding stronger chip export restrictions to the NDAA.
Democrats have also urged Congress to act.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Monday that he would work to ensure chip export restrictions remain in the final version of the NDAA.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer has also urged lawmakers to pass legislation limiting China's access to advanced U.S. technology, warning that Congress must act before it is too late.

Congress is considering several legislative proposals designed to strengthen U.S. oversight of semiconductor exports and prevent sensitive technology from reaching countries considered national security threats.

The AI Overwatch Act, introduced by Republican Representative Brian Mast, would restrict exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China and other countries considered national security concerns.

The Chip Security Act, introduced by Republican Representative Bill Huizenga, would require advanced AI chips to have location-verification technology and require companies to report suspicious transfers of sensitive technology.

The Remote Access Security Act, introduced by Republican Representative Mike Lawler, would expand U.S. export controls to cover remote access to certain technologies when it poses a serious national security threat.

The Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, or MATCH Act, would tighten restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment and improve coordination with U.S. allies.

The Senate version of the 2027 NDAA already includes provisions from several of these bills. The House and Senate must agree on identical versions before the legislation can go to the president for signature.
The current Congress ends January 3, 2027. If lawmakers fail to pass the legislation before then, they will have to restart the process in the new Congress.

items.title: Participating in art and culture has measurable benefits on our wellbeing | Letter
paragraphs: Reading Emma Brockes’ response to a recent Art Fund study, I felt the significance of the research may have been lost in its packaging (Art is good for your health? Allow me a quick eyeroll, 5 November).

The language of “prescribing” art has its roots in social prescribing. I understand why this might make people uncomfortable, particularly if it suggests that culture is being instrumentalised rather than enjoyed for its own sake.

Yet these findings matter for two reasons. First, they provide evidence for what many of us know intuitively: that participating in and experiencing art and culture are not only enriching, but also have measurable benefits for our health and wellbeing.

Second, with budgets for culture under pressure, this evidence strengthens our case for public investment. Surely that’s another argument for keeping our national museums free and ensuring everyone can access their wellbeing benefits.

Rather than viewing this study cynically, we should recognise the opportunities it presents. As Daisy Fancourt, who is quoted in Brockes’ article, explores in her excellent and insightful book Art Cure, the evidence extends far beyond visiting galleries and museums.

In the London borough of Ealing, we’re piloting a free creative health programme bringing residents and council staff together through activities ranging from clay workshops to Islamic geometric drawing. Almost all participants have reported improved wellbeing following these sessions. But beyond the evaluation, conversations have shown me how even an hour spent being creative can positively change the course of someone’s day, while regular participation can have a lasting impact on their lives.

Art shouldn’t have to justify its existence through its health benefits. But understanding those benefits strengthens the case for everyone to experience, participate in and benefit from art and culture.

And if the thought of visiting a museum makes Brockes’ eyes roll, I’d happily invite her to one of our workshops. She might leave having learned a new skill, but I suspect she’d take away rather more than that. William Rees Culture officer, Ealing council

items.title: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?
paragraphs: Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world?

Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run.
This has made the chipmaker arguably the most important player in AI and, at times, the most valuable company in the world. Huang’s departure sent shares in Nvidia plunging 13% in early trading.

Nvidia is not the only company that designs these chips. Most leading tech companies, including Microsoft, Meta and Google, are trying to make their own lines of AI chips. Some of these, such as Google’s tensor processing units, appear to be at least as good as Nvidia’s, and even better for certain purposes.
What makes Nvidia irreplaceable – and far more integral to the AI economy – is its web of relationships, most of these led by Huang himself.

One aspect of this is Nvidia’s complex web of ties with the companies actually building AI infrastructure, a mess of circular finance that implicates US tech giants and many of the world’s governments.

In recent years, Huang has been the kingmaker when it comes to AI. In 2025, he met numerous world leaders – including Mohammed bin Salman, Keir Starmer and Emmanuel Macron – persuading them of the urgency of developing “sovereign AI” with his product. His presence served as a guarantee of those nations’ AI plans. These meetings were followed by deals in which Nvidia announced it had arrangements to supply those governments with precious, hard-to-get chips.

None of these agreements were particularly transparent. While Nvidia appears to have promised 260,000 advanced chips to South Korea, for example, it was never immediately apparent when those chips would be delivered, who would pay for them, and on what terms.

Meanwhile, Nvidia financed a web of companies called “neoclouds” to buy its chips and put them in datacentres, there to be rented to the world’s biggest AI companies. These neoclouds have done wonders for Nvidia, propping up demand and keeping the risk associated with building datacentres and finding customers for them off its balance sheets.

Neoclouds are not the only thing financed by Nvidia. It has become known as the “central bank of AI” because it is enmeshed in almost every layer of the AI economy. Nvidia has invested in a spate of AI startups that could become future customers. It has offered massive sums of cash to companies such as OpenAI, to be used to buy its chips. This investment runs to hundreds of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s money, circling again and again through a limited set of accounts.

Then there is Nvidia’s relationship with a Taiwanese company called TSMC, or the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. TSMC makes the world’s AI chips, churning them out across several fabrication plants on the north-west of the island.

As far as geopolitics goes, TSMC is arguably more important than Nvidia or any other chip designer. Other companies can design AI chips, but TSMC manufactures the overwhelming majority of them and has no real competitor. This is because manufacturing AI chips is one of the most expensive and challenging industrial processes to date.

Each chip is etched with nanometre lines by lasers working in the extreme ultraviolet spectrum, which cost billions of dollars and two decades of research to develop. While TSMC has refined its process to make these chips for more than two decades, it still has only a 60% yield rate for its most advanced chips, which means that 40% of them have defects. It’s a staggeringly high rate for one of the world’s most expensive technologies.

Nvidia has worked closely with TSMC to help it develop its processes and products. Lore has it that Huang wrote the chief executive of TSMC a letter introducing himself in 1997. These are high-trust relationships built over decades.

Will it all be the same without Huang? This is almost impossible to answer because Nvidia’s relationships are so opaque. Investigators following the supply chain of its chips run up against secretive corporate contracts and tangled export records. There is known to be a years-long queue of customers waiting to obtain its chips, but questions regarding who is in that queue, in what order, and how many chips have been shipped remain open.

This murkiness was brought into sharp focus by Megaspeed, a small Singaporean company that was getting access to lots of GPUs, even as other companies struggled. One of Megaspeed’s executives, Alice Huang, was later revealed to be having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive, and to be an alleged Chinese spy. This relationship appears to have allowed Megaspeed to secure roughly $7.5bn (£5.67bn) worth of Nvidia chips, which were allegedly smuggled into China.

Was Huang and his glad-handing a source of this opacity? Perhaps a new chief executive could bring some transparency and predictability to the business, at least in terms of chips contracts and supply chains.

But what else could be laid bare if the “central bank of AI” became more transparent, or came under external scrutiny? Many questions surround its contracts and relationships; lots of elaborate debt structures and handshake agreements may yet be uncovered.

Huang dazzled the world in his leather jacket; he convinced heads of government that his technology held the keys to transformation and to power. When the patina wears off, will this still seem the case?

items.title: Fuel shortages in Iraqi Kurdistan spark dispute over separate queues for women
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

Fuel shortages in Iraq's Kurdistan Region have sparked a dispute over how subsidized gasoline is distributed, with women drivers in Halabja complaining of discrimination after authorities introduced restrictions on their access to filling stations.
Long queues have become a common sight outside government-run fuel stations across the region since U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began in late February, disrupting fuel imports.
Despite being OPEC's second-largest oil producer, Iraq relies heavily on imported petroleum products because domestic refineries cannot produce enough gasoline to meet demand.
In Halabja, in Northeast Iraq near the Iranian border, motorists spend hours waiting for fuel, while others queue overnight to secure gasoline at government-subsidized prices.

According to the most recent information from August, a liter of gasoline costs 750 Iraqi dinars at government stations, compared with around 1,150 dinars at privately operated stations, a price gap that has encouraged drivers to endure lengthy waits.
To ease the burden on women, who generally face greater social constraints on waiting overnight, Halabja's fuel committee initially introduced separate queues for male and female drivers.

But the arrangement prompted complaints from some men, who argued that women were receiving preferential treatment. Some also accused female drivers of bringing their husbands' vehicles to obtain cheaper fuel.

Authorities subsequently changed the system, allowing one female driver to enter a station after every 10 male drivers. Women are also required to present driving licenses; a requirement not imposed on men.
The changes have angered women who say they face longer waits, additional scrutiny and harassment from male motorists.
"Many men go through, eight or 10 of them, before one woman is allowed in," said Kurda Jamal, a local driver.

"They then ask women for their driving licenses and accuse them of driving cars belonging to their husbands," she said, adding that such accusations were embarrassing and made the experience increasingly difficult.
Another female driver, Kizhan Osman, called for equal treatment.

"If a man gets gasoline, the next person should be a woman," she said. "It should not be 10 men followed by one woman. We want this discrimination to end at all fuel stations in Kurdistan Region, particularly in Halabja."
Male drivers have also expressed frustration, saying the shortages have disrupted their work and daily lives.
Aram Abdullah, a local motorist, said teachers, government employees and other workers were losing valuable time waiting for fuel.
"You might spend half your day just getting a few liters of gasoline," he said. "What time is left for the rest of your life?"
Residents also complained that the allocation of just one gasoline tanker a day to Halabja was insufficient to meet demand.
Halabja district administrator Simko Salar attributed the congestion to reduced fuel allocations and defended the revised distribution system as fair.

"Equality does not mean allowing one woman and then one man through," Salar said, arguing that the much shorter queues for women under the previous arrangement meant men could wait seven hours while women received fuel in half an hour.
"Both are human beings," he said, adding that authorities respected women and would investigate their complaints.
For many motorists, however, the financial incentive remains difficult to ignore.

The lower price of subsidized gasoline has prompted some residents to begin queuing a day before deliveries arrive, spending the night outside filling stations in hopes of securing fuel the following morning.

items.title: UN representative urges Taliban to end child recruitment and recognize 18 as age of adulthood
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

The United Nations has urged the Taliban to align their definition of a child with the Convention on the Rights of the Child, amid growing concerns over the recruitment and use of children by the group in Afghanistan.

The U.N. Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflict, Vanessa Frazier, told VOA that the age of adulthood must be set at 18, warning that physical signs of puberty cannot replace the internationally recognized legal definition of a child.
The Taliban leader issued a decree banning the recruitment of children “who do not show physical signs of puberty” into their ranks.
Frazier, however, said that the main problem is how these directives define a child.

“The problem that we have is that the distinguishing element that is used in the edicts of the Taliban is signs of puberty, and not the age of 18, which comes out of the Convention on the Rights of the Child,” said Frazier.
The U.N. special representative called on the Taliban to align their definition of a child with the Convention on the Rights of the Child to which Afghanistan is a party.
A new U.N. report released in September said that the task force verified the recruitment of 557 boys, some as young as 12 years old, by the Taliban from 2023 to 2025.

The U.S. State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, released in October, said that there was a pattern of recruiting and using children both in combat and support roles, as well as a pattern of sexual slavery through bacha bazi, a practice in which men exploit boys for social and sexual entertainment.

The report accused the Taliban of not taking measures to prevent the recruitment and use of children for combat and support roles, and that the Taliban did not make efforts to protect the victims of bacha bazi.

However, the report acknowledged that the Taliban established a commission to identify and demobilize children among its forces and that an international organization was able to secure the release of 58 children from their ranks.
Frazier said poverty and economic hardship could also leave Afghan children vulnerable to recruitment.
“Families struggling to feed their children may see joining an armed force as a source of food, security and income,” she told VOA.
Frazier said that boys are reportedly used in a range of roles, including cooking, carrying weapons, fighting and serving as border guards.
She also said that the militarization of schools and ideological indoctrination of children under the Taliban is concerning.
"And so, when they are recruited, there's already been some indoctrination that has happened in madrasas,” Frazier added.

The Annual Report of the U.N. Secretary-General on Children and Armed Conflict for 2025 reported 1,070 verified grave violations against children, including recruiting and using 204 boys by the Taliban in combat, 62 in support roles and 142 verified.
The U.N. also reported the killing of 100 and maiming of 290 children, including the killing of 103 children in the air strikes by Pakistani forces.
The report called on the Taliban to “immediately take all actions to better protect and uphold the rights of children and ensure accountability.”

items.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
paragraphs: The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.
Associated Press contributed to this report

items.title: Schools, libraries and parents face 'difficult decision' over David Walliams books
paragraphs: Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Mr Di'Iasio urged the government to give schools national guidance, so they are "not leaving this open to one or two head teachers making one decision and others making a different one".
Darren Morgan, head of Kings Road Primary School in Manchester, told the programme that he has taken the decision to remove Walliams' publications.
The stories have been useful to promote reading, but "when there are these allegations it's really difficult to keep these books on the shelves", he said.
Steve Chalke, head of Oasis Academies, which runs more than 50 schools, said it was impossible to stop children seeing the current stories about Walliams.
"So when a child wanders into a school and into the library and sees his name or perhaps sees his photograph on a book, it can be very traumatising for some children," he said.

Author Chloe Combi, who has written about "how it feels to be young in modern Britain" and Generation Z, said banning Walliams' books is not appropriate, and could mean that important conversations about him "get swept under the carpet".
"I think by talking about it and what has happened - and the responsibility of parents to have that conversation with their kids - that actually makes more sense," she told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"I'm totally sympathetic with schools for withdrawing him and bookshops withdrawing him as an individual decision. But the point is, none of that is going to erase what's happened."
The Department for Education has been asked for comment.
Retailers including Waterstones, TG Jones, and The Works, say they will no longer sell Walliams' books, and his publisher HarperCollins cut ties with him in September.
Public libraries have also faced calls to remove his books.
Librarians' body CILIP said it "recognises that dealing with challenges made to books or other resources can be an extremely complex and stressful situation for library staff".
Decisions about stocking books are made by local councils.
Among them, Kent County Council said it had no plans to remove Walliams' titles from its libraries.
"The starting point is that books should be available to readers unless their content is unlawful," a spokesperson said.

"Decisions about library stock are not made through blanket bans on individual authors. Collections are regularly reviewed and refreshed to reflect factors such as reader demand, condition and relevance of stock."

A Telford and Wrekin council spokesperson added that after the "recent media coverage and allegations published in the press" they had taken the decision to "remove all Walliams' books and audio books from their library catalogues".
Surrey County Council said that demand for Walliams' books had "fallen significantly in recent years", but his titles are "not illegal" and "remain available for readers to borrow".
Camden Council in north London said it was putting Walliams' books in storage.
A spokesperson told the Camden New Journal: "We are committed to making Camden a safer place for women and girls, to challenging harmful attitudes, and promoting healthy relationships.
"Following these allegations, we believe the most appropriate action is to remove these books from display."

On Tuesday, ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including some who accused him of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.
In a letter to journalists published by the paper, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

items.title: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'
paragraphs: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone".
Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.
But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.

In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.
Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.
He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office.
Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.
As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri.
Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates."
As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.
This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year.

The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.
Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words.

"The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said.
On tackling the causes of climate change, Burnham said his government remained committed to meeting the country's target of net zero by 2050 whilst also getting bills down.
He said key to this was cutting our "dependence on fossil fuels" and increasing electrification - the amount of our energy needs met from renewable electricity.
The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.
Turkey, the co-hosts of COP31, wants a key outcomes of this year's summit to be a commitment by countries to meet 35% of their energy supply from electricity by 2035. Currently, it is around a fifth.
But Burnham has been accused of having double standards.
"The Prime Minister simply cannot call for clean power across the world while saying yes to more fossil fuels in the UK," said Beth John, climate adviser at Oxfam.
Last month, the government approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on the grounds that it provided energy security.
And in the budget last month Chancellor John Healey announced a funding cut to the Warm Homes Plan, which provides grants and loans to support the installation of heat pumps.
Whilst this week there has been media speculation that the government is considering watering down electric car sales targets, although the government insists no decision has been made.
Successfully switching petrol and diesel cars to EVs and moving from gas boilers to electric-powered heat pumps are key ways to achieve the 35% electrification target, external.
Although there was no royal presence this year, King Charles III sent a message ahead of Burnham's speech.

"As the world gathers for Cop31, I can only hope that this same spirit of partnership and common purpose can help inspire the collective action that our planet – and future generations – so urgently need.
"Our children and grandchildren will not judge us by the promises we made, but by what we chose to do."
Burnham was the only G7 leader to speak at this year's conference in a sign of faltering support for the COP process - something he acknowledged in his speech.

In an almost word for word copy of Sir Keir Starmer's address last year he said: "The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate has gone, and the reality is now the world will reach 1.5 degrees."
Other leaders expected to speak on Thursday include many island states like Tonga, Tuvalu and the Solomon Islands.

For these nations, the impact of climate change is already at their front door. With most of their land just metres above sea level, rising water levels have caused many to abandon their homes in recent years.
Last year, Australia - the co-host of the COP31 summit - opened up the world's first climate visa for Tuvalu citizens wanting to evacuate.
The first intake was massively oversubscribed, with more than a third of the population entering the ballot.

As glaciers continue to melt and oceans expand, average sea levels are expected to keep climbing and potentially accelerate. The World Meteorological Organisation said on the opening day of this conference the global mean sea level was at its highest level since records began.

items.title: ‘You can almost smell the sweat’: striptease artists and steel pans light up this week’s free art shows
paragraphs: A vast red concrete wall splits Maxwell Alexandre’s work in two. It’s the wall of the Flamengo sport club in the painter’s native Rio de Janeiro, a towering crimson monolith of division, literally separating us and them, rich and poor, black and white.

Alexandre joined the upmarket club in the early 2020s. He’d walked past its red walls countless times as a kid – the club is on the edge of the favela he’s from, the biggest in Brazil. What he found inside was serenity, sunbathing, prosperity, and whiteness. He’d spent his early career painting the black figures of his favela, but now he was surrounded by pasty bodies with rippling pink skin.

With success in his career, he’d bought access to this new world, and knew he couldn’t paint the same black figures he’d made his name with. So this is the result, dozens of paintings of lush tropical trees and white bodies in repose, lounging, chatting, playing by the pool within the confines of that red well, all part of his new approach to what he calls “white figuration”.

The red walls dominate the works in the first space as a figure stands on a diving board and palm fronds wave in the distance. The second room is covered floor to ceiling in paintings on brown paper of the club’s members, some shown next to figures from art history. Boys stand in the sun, men splash in the water, girls talk and women sunbathe. It’s idyllic, hazy, almost nostalgic painting.

But it’s full of emotional complexity. The work is a rejection of the expectations placed on black artists to make black work, to churn out paintings of black figures to sell to white audiences and collectors. It’s Alexandre refusing to play the game. But there’s also an introspective exploration of what happens when your life changes, when you stop being young and poor and desperate and become something different. This doesn’t feel like Alexandre mocking white flabby bodies, it feels like him trying to make sense of a divided city, an art history that doesn’t represent him, and a world that expects you to be something you no longer are. It all looks like heaven, but even heaven is a complicated place.
Carlos/Ishikawa, London, until 28 November

The exhaustion in Susan Meiselas’s photos is so palpable it’s almost draining. She spent three years in the mid-70s following a group of striptease performers as they toured the endless American sprawl, slowly gaining their trust, capturing them at their most intimate, unguarded and knackered.

She photographs them from backstage. Night after night the women dance seductively for wide-eyed, drooling, dumbstruck men – you see them gawping from between the dancers’ legs, anonymous pervs desperate for an eyeful.
And then the dancers crash from the effort of it all. They smoke distractedly, lounge on sofas or crumple into bed. This is the end result of physical labour: total collapse, utter exhaustion.
In lots of the photos dancers peek through the curtain back on to the stage, waiting their turn, watching things turn ugly for the poor performer on stage.

The more posed images don’t give the viewer much, but when Meiselas captures the dancers unaware, lost in the moment, they’re pretty special. These are stories of exploitation and entertainment, work and exhaustion, leaving behind nothing but physical, emotional depletion.
Huxley Parlour Photographs, London, until 21 November

Hyun-Sook Song says so much with so little. With just a handful of brushstrokes, the Hamburg-based Korean painter opens up a whole world: written into every mark are her memories of life in deeply rural, mid-century South Korea, her shock at the monstrous urbanity of modern Germany, her desperate need to find sanctuary in painting.

The minimalism of the whole thing is made obvious by the titles. The works are called things like 11 Brushstrokes or 6 Brushstrokes over 1 Brushstroke because that’s all they are, but they’re more complex than that implies.

She lays each canvas flat first, and paints every mark in a long, sweeping, full-body motion, physically trying to communicate her ideas into the work. The paintings are all on dark green or black backgrounds, each swooping brushstroke creating a gossamer white veil across the darkness. Cutting across almost all of them is a brown line, a stick that seems to almost lift the impossibly thin curtains. The white marks reference the raw silks collected in her youth, the brown marks nod to boundary posts that delineated her childhood landscapes. There are all these ideas of separation and division, of veils being lifted, of quiet and peace. They’re almost unbearably fragile paintings, but all the more beautiful and meditative for it.
Sprüth Magers, London, until 23 January 2027

Way before London’s Carnaby Street was one the capital’s main tourist taps, it was a proper cultural hub, a place for fashion and music to flourish. And No 50 Carnaby Street was home to six different music venues between the 1930s and 80s which helped totally change the cultural landscape of the country. Whether it was the Sunset Club in the 50s or Columbo’s in the 70s, this address is where activism met music, where jazz gave way to steel bands and sound systems, where black met white.

This tiny show in Sadie Coles’ downstairs project space by Studio/Chapple gallery celebrates 50 Carnaby Street just around the corner from the original address. The walls are painted deep brown, handmade speakers by Maya Ramnarine play out the sounds of old jazz and ska records, paintings show dancers moving in tightly crowded spaces, performers playing to packed rooms. I don’t love all the works here, but the idea is good, and the two paintings by Georgia Semple and Amida Deen are great. Semple’s is a dark, atmospheric vision of the Russ Henderson Steel Band, Britain’s first steel pan ensemble, playing to a crowd of joyful figures slowly swaying to the music. Deen’s work travels to the 1970s, with people pressing themselves together in a room of fiery red and heat-soaked orange as dub pours out of the speakers.
The show is a tiny love letter to music history, clubbing and dancing. You can almost smell the sweat.

items.title: How much art does your council own and is it locked away or on display?
paragraphs: Councils across England own hundreds of thousands artworks, but what are they doing with it all?
Fewer than one in 20 artworks owned by English councils are on public display, the BBC has found.
More than 500,000 pieces of art are held in the collections of 225 councils, but the vast majority is being kept in storage.
Local authorities remain "the biggest single constituent of public funding for arts and culture", according to the chief executive of the charity Art UK.
Yet many face a strain on storage space and resources, with a real-term fall in spending for museums leading to challenges in displaying council-owned art.
Council art collections include works by notable artists like Tracey Emin, David Hockney, LS Lowry and Antony Gormley.
Some of those collections include tens of thousands of pieces, with the largest collection of 125,000 works belonging to Waltham Forest Council.
Only a fraction of councils were able to provide the value of the collection but even individual collections had insurance values worth millions of pounds.
As of April, just 26,856 of more than half a million works were being displayed by the 225 councils who shared data with the BBC. But what options do these local authorities have?
Only one responding authority with more than 100 pieces of art - Rugby Council in Warwickshire - had them all on display.
All of its 257 artworks were exhibited together for the first time in April.
Sally Godden, manager of Rugby Art Gallery and Museum, said art had the power to connect communities.
"If things have been squirrelled away, then it's not going to do that," she said.
"It's not just a picture on the wall. It's how it connects to somebody and makes people think."
Sally Godden said the museum team aimed to ensure the council collection instilled "pride in the people of Rugby"

Godden said: "We can have the best collection in the world, but if they're not accessed, if they're not seen, if they're not enjoyed, if they don't make people think, then what's the point of them? They are so much more than an asset.

"We are very lucky to have such a great collection and continue to collect as well. By continuing to do that, we're growing stories, we're growing the diversity of the town, we're growing the views of people."
The council has backed a funding bid for the redevelopment of Rugby Art Gallery and a museum which would include a permanent space to display the council-owned collection.
Many of the council art collections are still growing and only 10 councils actively disposed of any of the art they own during the past six financial years.
Derbyshire sold 356 artworks in 2021-22, while North Lincolnshire sold 22 at auction in 2023-24.
The other eight councils said the items moved out of their collections had been donated, transferred to other museums, or disposed of.
For Derbyshire, the sale came as part of the closure of its Schools Library Service which had loaned art to schools.
When the service was closed after 72 years, the council did not have the space or staff to keep the collection.
Rugby, which is among the councils adding to their collections, recently acquired a painting selected by students and pupils living in the town
Kent did not respond to the question, but previously confirmed to the BBC it had sold 418 artworks in the 12 months to April.
At the time, councillor Paul Webb said: "The reason for selling is a practical one, with the closure of the basement store where the art works are kept.
"I am sure the works have brought a lot of joy over the years to many people, and will now continue to do so."
The council also recently sold a sculpture back to Gormley, the artist who created the Angel of the North.

The chief executive of Art UK, Andew Elis, said that if all councils were to sell off art, our lives would be stripped of "these extraordinary artworks that should be there to enrich and engage us and brighten up our lives".
Art UK has spent years photographing public art collections to create a digital record of more than one million artworks, external.
Ellis said it was "really important" to give communities access to publicly owned art.
"We own in the UK arguably the greatest public collection of art in the world," he said. "Art changes lives, it enriches lives, it enriches our sense of place.
"The beauty of bringing all this together on one platform is that you make this art available for everyone, everywhere, all the time.
"From our point of view, this is not just about getting the art up online, this is about telling the stories behind the art and giving people agency over it."
He added councils should make more use of the shared resource, especially with increased strain on finances.
Councillor Mick Barton, who chairs the Local Government Association's culture committee, said communities should be able to enjoy local art and historic exhibits.
But he said councils continued to face significant financial pressures which were leaving them with less money to provide "discretionary services, such as museums".
Once adjusted for inflation, the net spend on museums across English councils has fallen by a fifth between 2017-18 and 2025-26.
Keeping the collections in storage does not always mean there is no access to the work.
Three of the responding authorities that owned more than 100 artworks said none were on display.
One of them, Rochdale Council in Greater Manchester, is not currently displaying any of its 1,701 artworks due to the regeneration of its Touchstones museum.
Its temporary closure saw the entire collection moved into the council's stores, which had to be reorganised to accommodate the works.
Senior curator Sarah Hodgkinson said they had been "taking a bit more risk than we have in the past" by bringing items from the collections directly to the public.
That has seen a "lively" programme, including taking pieces to schools, picnics in the park or events.
It has also let them catch up on the "behind-the-scenes" tasks of looking after a collection, like the storage and preservation.
Mark Doyle said it was "fair to say that when we reopen, there will be more of the collections on display at any one time than there ever has been"
Hodgkinson said: "We've taken loads of collections out into the community as part of our collections on tour programme.
"We've been working on repacking all of our sculpture collection, making sure our documentation is being worked on."
Mark Doyle is director of arts, heritage and wellness at Your Trust, which delivers culture and leisure service on behalf of Rochdale Council.
"A lot of people don't understand what's involved in looking after a collection and making sure that it's there for future generations to be able to access and see," he said.
Doyle said they often came across the "misconception" that the museum should have all of the items on display at the same time.

"Obviously that's not possible," he said. "But also there's other stuff that people don't understand about not having things on display for too long because it begins to deteriorate or they begin to be affected by the environment."
Additional reporting by Lauren Woodhead and Jonathan Fagg.

items.title: Significant drop in levels of toxic 'forever' chemicals in England's rivers
paragraphs: Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA).

The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment.
One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue.
Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated.

PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties.
They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally.

The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer., external
As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020.
The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last ten years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively.
Levels in fresh-water fish have fallen 49%.
"It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University.
There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used.

The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one.

The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment.

The regulator is now regularly testing for 60 other PFAS to build a picture of contamination across the country, and earlier this month the government announced it would begin monitoring levels in people's bodies.

The EA report acknowledged that while concentration levels have fallen, because the chemicals take so long to break down, the overall amount still in the environment is likely to have remained unchanged - they have simply been diluted and been washed into the sea.
"There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused," said Megson.
One of the few ways to permanently destroy PFAS is by high-temperature incineration - there are just two such suitable sites in the country currently.

items.title: Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
paragraphs: Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.

The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.

Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.

The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.

“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.

The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.

“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.

Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.

During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.

“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.

It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.

Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.

Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.

The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.

Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.

“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

items.title: 'Summer was a wake-up call, winter could be dire' warning over food supplies
paragraphs: Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.
It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.
Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust, external, which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.
Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture, external, only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture, external.
Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.

"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires, and overheating," said Fisher.

Food security has become a hot topic, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.
Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".
He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.
"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber attacks.
"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."

Dibben said she believed people in the UK thought it would be able to "avoid many of the real challenges of climate breakdown" and "just be able to grow grapes and peaches" but the reality is very different.
"We're going to have to really think a lot harder about how we're producing food, even in this country," she said.
This includes looking at which vegetables work best in hotter climates.
Dibben described the past summer as the hardest she had experienced in five years of growing.
"The hours I was keeping were just insane," she said.
"I was getting out to the field at 05:00, and then working until it got just too hot to be outside, which was like 11:00 some days, maybe even earlier."
She said working in polytunnels was impossible by 09:00 due to the heat.
When it became too hot to work, she had to go indoors and "just survive until it was cool enough to go back outside at probably 17:00".
She then worked until midnight to try and get everything watered.
Dibben said she did not usually have to worry too much about not having enough water, but this year was completely different.
"Even the things that you felt like you were giving as much water as you could were still not growing as much as they should be," she added.
"We've not had the water bill yet for this summer, but I dread to think.
"We've just not had the crops to make it worth it."
She does not believe it will necessarily be as bad every year, but Dibben accepts there will be more hot summers and unpredictable weather such as flooding.
Dibben thinks there will always be a need for bigger scale farms producing wheat, barley, beef or sheep.
"But I think if there was a farm like ours every 10 miles throughout Wales, that would be a pretty great future in my eyes," she added.
The Welsh government said "significant progress" had been made on its plans to create a national food strategy to "target a more resilient, integrated and sustainable food system".
"There will also be a focus on how to grow more fruit and vegetables in Wales, and we have already begun mapping the current position of the sector with key stakeholders," said a spokesperson.

The UK government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: "We recognise the hurdles that our vital fruit and vegetable growers face, which is why we are slashing planning red tape and investing £200m to help farmers trial crop boosting technology.
"The prime minister has made clear that food security is national security, and we're working across the farming sector to make supply chains more resilient."

items.title: Elliptic analytics say North Korea launders stolen Binance funds via homemade meme coins
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

North Korea is laundering cryptocurrency stolen from Binance through homemade meme coins, according to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, describing it as a scheme designed to resemble ordinary trading and delay investigators.
The FBI on October 31 attributed the theft of than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from Binance to North Korea.
North Korea Pyongyang has denied being involved but the FBI says it has identified this specific “North Korean malicious” cyber activity as "TraderTraitor."
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
In its November 9 analysis, Elliptic said those laundering the funds created at least six meme coins on the NEAR blockchain between November 5 and November 7.
About 117,000 NEAR — worth approximately $430,000 at the time of the analysis — passed through them.
Meme coins are tokens inspired by internet jokes, animals, or celebrities, with prices driven by online attention and speculation.
Elliptic assessed that these tokens have no apparent practical purpose other than to move funds within the laundering network.

Elliptic says the launderers created exchange pools holding their tokens and NEAR wallets that contain stolen NEAR, while other wallets in the network sold the same tokens into those pools and collected NEAR.

This replaced direct transfers between wallets with purchases and sales, potentially making recipients look like investors earning legitimate trading profits. Elliptic said network wallets conducted all sales of the six tokens. They were traded intensively soon after creation, with no trading since November 8. Each cost about $90 to create.

All transactions remain publicly recorded on the blockchain, enabling investigators to trace them. But additional steps take time to unravel, helping launderers move funds before the associated wallets are identified, and transactions can be blocked, Elliptic said.
The Binance theft occurred October 29 across 11 blockchains. Elliptic estimates losses at $6.43 billion, which is the largest cryptocurrency theft ever, according to the FBI.
Elliptic’s November 9 update put conversions into bitcoin at approximately $225 million, with $2.85 billion frozen or seized and roughly $3 billion remaining in theft-linked addresses.

items.title: Moolenaar urges next Congress to continue bipartisan China committee amid questions over its future
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on China, in a statement released November 9, urged the next Congress to renew the panel’s mandate, saying it should continue its bipartisan work on China policy when lawmakers return early next year.

Moolenaar said the select committee had brought Republicans and Democrats together over nearly four years to address what he described as serious threats posed by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to American interests and values.

"For nearly four years the Select Committee has brought together Republicans and Democrats to address the grave threats the Chinese Communist Party poses to U.S. interests and values," Moolenaar said. "We have worked hand-in-hand with other committees and administrations of both parties to secure vital policy changes that strengthen our nation and protect the American people."

The Michigan Republican said the committee had exposed the CCP's exploitation of the U.S. economy, American workers, and innovators. He also highlighted its bipartisan efforts to secure critical supply chains, deny Beijing access to resources and technologies needed to advance what he called its dangerous ambitions, and advocate for people fighting for freedom and dignity.

Moolenaar warned that the challenges facing the United States were becoming increasingly urgent, particularly as technological competition in artificial intelligence intensifies and China's coercive actions against U.S. allies and partners continue to escalate.
“The coming two years will be a critical period—and an opportunity to meet the moment through the Select Committee’s bipartisan mandate and work."
History of the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

The Select Committee on China was established in January 2023, during the 118th Congress, after Republicans gained a majority in the House of Representatives in the 2022 midterm elections.The committee was created under House Resolution 11, introduced by then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-California). The resolution passed the House on January 10, 2023, by an overwhelming bipartisan vote of 365 to 65, with 146 Democrats joining all but absent Republican members in supporting its creation.

Its creation reflected growing bipartisan concern in Washington over China's expanding economic, technological, military, and geopolitical influence, as well as the implications of the Chinese Communist Party's policies for U.S. national security and economic competitiveness.

Unlike a traditional standing committee, the Select Committee on China was established as a temporary investigative and policy-focused panel. Its mandate was to build bipartisan consensus on the challenges posed by the CCP and develop policy recommendations to counter these threats.
The 120th Congress is scheduled to convene on January 3, 2027, when newly elected lawmakers will be sworn into office.

items.title: Russian prosecutors seek 15-year prison sentence for lawyer Maria Bontsler in treason case
paragraphs: Editor's note: This story was adapted from the original VOA Russian article.
Russian Prosecutors have asked a court to sentence Kaliningrad lawyer Maria Bontsler to 15 years in prison on charges of high treason.
Bontsler is known for representing defendants in politically sensitive cases. She was detained in late May 2025 and has remained in pre-trial detention ever since.

Slovo Zashchite, translated in English as "A Word to the Defense," first reported the news, citing attorney Ilya Sidorov, who visited Bontsler in pretrial detention. Sidorov was on Bontsler's defense team until July 2026, when he was removed from the case.
Bontsler could deliver her final statement in court Wednesday before the verdict is handed down.
She was initially accused of confidential cooperation with a foreign state. Investigators say Bontsler passed information about Russian security officers to Ukraine’s SBU security service.
Authorities later reclassified the case as high treason, a charge that carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years under Russian law.
She is currently being held in a detention center in Kaliningrad, and according to Bontsler's lawyer, her health has deteriorated in prison due to complications related to diabetes and hypertension.
Valeria Vetoshkina, a lawyer with the independent human rights group OVD-Info, told VOA that Bontsler's physical condition remains a major concern.

"Unfortunately, she is not feeling well. Everyone knows that Russian detention facilities and prisons are extremely difficult places. People are often treated poorly, and adequate medical care is frequently unavailable."
Human rights advocates have repeatedly expressed concern about Bontsler's health and the conditions of her detention as she awaits the outcome of her trial.

"If a person has chronic illnesses, they can worsen significantly in custody, and that is what happened in her case," Vetoshkina said. "She lost consciousness at one point and was not provided with proper medical assistance."
Vetoshkina also said she "would not be surprised if the sentence is close to what prosecutors are seeking."
Treason cases can carry a life sentence. But Russian law prohibits life imprisonment for women, so according to Vetoshkina, "the maximum punishment is 20 years."
The human rights lawyer also highlighted an unusually harsh approach by local security services.

"It appears that the local Federal Security Service (FSB) has taken a particular interest in this case. We see an extraordinary level of severity and a very negative attitude toward her," she said. "Given everything that has happened, I would not be surprised if the final sentence is close to the term being requested by prosecutors."
Vetoshkina also pointed out that Bontsler had frequently defended people prosecuted in cases initiated by the local FSB.

items.title: A warrior poet shares her views on the Russia-Ukraine war
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.
The war in Ukraine has been going on for well over four years, with U.S., Ukrainian, and Russian negotiators meeting this week to find a way to end the conflict.
There are currently more than two million Ukrainian veterans of the war, and the number continues to grow.
Yaryna Chornohuz knows the reality of what they are experiencing. She is a Ukrainian poet, UAV operator, and sergeant in Ukrainian Marine Corps.
VOA spoke to her during her current tour of the United States, where she is talking about the war and reading some of her poetry, much of it written about the struggles of Ukraine's military.

Chornohuz says Ukrainian soldiers are “tired and exhausted, especially those of us constantly on the front lines without any rotation." She and her husband served seven and nine years in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, respectively.
“Yet, at the same time, we all know that we have fought for and earned the right to have a voice," she says. "We live, after all, in freedom - even on the front line, even in a war of attrition.”
She also makes the case for a postwar Ukraine being led by veterans.
"They are the ones capable of building the nation-unburdened by the legacy of corruption or a focus on personal gain and instead driven by a commitment to the common good," Chornohuz tells VOA.

The poet also spoke about the current debate over female conscription. She says it's not currently being considered but, "in a war of this scale, regardless of whether or not there is a formal mobilization of women, it is essential to prepare everyone so that, if necessary, they can become soldiers."

She tells VOA she likes to joke that "if you gathered all of us - all 75,000 women serving in the Armed Forces of Ukraine - we could defend an entire small European nation. The audience at that event joked back that they would love to have an army of women like that to defend their own country."
